Uniform Title: *Mantrakaumudī* Author: Devanātha Thakkura Description: The *Mantrakaumudī* is by Devanātha Thakkura, who was born circa 1490.

He lived and worked in Mithilā. He is the author of numerous works on various subjects, not only Tantra. He composed the *Mantrakaumudī* at the age of seventy-five in 1564. This work mentions ninety-nine treatises on Tantra and deals with their various aspects.
Through the general acceptance of this work on the practice of mantra, Thakkura established a new school of Tantra in Mithilā that is free from vāmācāra practices.

He who possesses the flavor of the stream of honey-dew shimmering within the lotus of his own philosophical tenets—
Victorious is the lion of sound reasoning, who acts as a bee to the honey of the minds of the spiritually immature. || 5 ||

Victorious on earth is Devanātha, the son of Govindapañcama, renowned throughout the world for his great devotion, who has mastered the essence of all philosophical systems, and who is a lion of courage in traversing the forest of logic. || 7 ||
Tell me, what difference is there between the bliss that flows naturally from the speech of the learned master Vāgdevanātha— whether one follows the right path or a wrong one—
and the bliss found upon tasting the soft, tender lower lip of a deer-eyed woman, whether on a bed or in a forest? (8)
He who knows meditation, the yantra for worship, the various stages of worship, the seat of the deity, and the specific details of ritual placement and so forth— he alone knows the Kaumudī.
Even that which is established has been abandoned by me if it contradicts the tradition; conversely, even a novel construction is being stated if it conforms to the tradition. (1)
Furthermore, there is no validity whatsoever for a scripture that is inconsistent with reality, as evidenced by the Bhaṭṭavārtika, which establishes the lack of authority of the Pañcarātra. (2)

Because even by means of Vedāntic statements, one ascertains their lack of authority therein; nor can that which contradicts the Veda serve to communicate a lack of authority [regarding other matters]. (3)

This [restriction] should be stated as applying only to the *Pañcarātras*, for if it were restricted further, there would be a loss of authority; moreover, the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭas*) is not observed here to serve as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Since its arising occurs according to the analogy of a continuous stream of water from a ewe's udder, why is its lack of attention-worthiness being investigated? (5)
It is said: In this way, there would be a lack of authority for memory, the Vedas, and so forth; for, in some cases, they would be devoid of corroboration due to the absence of a restrictive factor.

The conduct of the learned, being devoid of any [scriptural] basis, is exactly the same as that which arises from a defect in the seed; moreover, it has been established by you yourself through your own words. (7)
Its authority is thus stated in the *Vārāha-pañcalakṣaṇa*: "In the absence of Vedic mantras, the ritual procedure proclaimed in the Pañcarātra [is to be followed]. (8)
It shall not even reach the path of the ears of women and Śūdras;
the Pañcarātra is prescribed only for the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
It shall not even reach the range of the ears of Śūdras and others;
this was stated in the Brahma Purāṇa as well, in the account of Pauruṣottama.

Having worshipped Madhusūdana according to the ritual procedure of the Pañcarātra, [one realizes that] those [doctrines] which have the statements of the Vedānta as their object are therefore in contradiction with the Veda. (11)
(4) There may be other scriptures; however, this specific injunction [of ours] is now being defined here: the Vāmas, the Pāśupata practitioners, and likewise the Pāñcarātrikas. (12)
In that Kali age, there will be Brahmins devoted to the Kṣatriyas, as well as [adherents of] Vāma,
Pāśupata, Soma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Cauryava.
This which has been spoken is improper, and likewise it is outside the Veda; even that which is thus stated in the Purāṇas is intended solely for the purpose of censure. (14)
For this very reason, the Pāśupata and other such systems were not mentioned in the Purāṇas; rather, the Pañcarātras and Saptarātras were indeed proclaimed by me.
The sages have categorized these separately in the world according to the number twenty-five; the *Hayaśīrṣatantra* is the primary tantra, which deludes the three worlds. (16)
The Bhairava, Pauṣkara, Prāhlāda, Gārgya, Gautama, Nāradīya, Māṇḍavya, Śāṇḍilya, and likewise the Raiṇuka Tantras. || 17 ||
The *Tantra* spoken by Satya, the *Śaunaka*, the *Vāsiṣṭha* which is an ocean of knowledge, the *Svāyambhuva*, the *Kāpila*, the *Tārkṣya*, and that which has Nārāyaṇa as its essence. || 18 ||
The Ātreya, the one called Nārasiṃha, the one called Ānanda, as well as the Āruṇa, the Baudhāyana, and the Aṣṭārṇa—thus has its detailed exposition been stated. (19)
First, I shall describe the method for the inquiry into a mantra; a wise person should receive from a true guru a mantra that has already been proven effective. (1)

Likewise, wealth and other matters favorable to the lunar mansion and the zodiacal sign [should be determined] by means of the numerical letters arising from the *kaṭapayādi* system, up to the end of the *piṇḍa*.

One should know that *ṅi* is again empty when it occurs with a pure vowel; [the syllable] *prāpa* generally becomes *paṭu* due to elision (*lobha*), and *rudraḥ* here becomes *ruruḥ* through the addition of the suffix *kara*.
Generally, the multitudes of wicked people are divided among the various classes; then, the letters in their respective order, having departed from the vowels, enter into Revatī. (4)
The practitioner should calculate in sequence from the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) of his own birth sign: Birth, Prosperity, Misfortune, Welfare, Enemy, Benefactor, and Death. (5)

One's friend, one's supreme friend, and again and again one's births and so forth—surely, is there not the purification of the zodiac sign and lunar mansion based on the first letter of one's name? (6)
How could it not be so? It is said:
"By means of which the zodiac sign and lunar mansion of birth are grasped; of these two, these [two] are primary. (The reading enclosed in brackets is missing from manuscript *k*; it is corrected.)

Likewise, it is stated in the science of astrology (Jyotiḥśāstra): "Nine stars from one's own birth star... [In all the Jyotiḥśāstras, something was said by the author of the Dīpikā: "In the various names of the birth stars, when the qualities are combined for the Manu..."]

Nor is this [term] even one that possesses various constellations and zodiacal signs; for if that were the case, the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) applied to the birth-place would be rendered rootless. || 9 ||

This figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is well-established and is necessarily required here; moreover, this sentence will not serve the purpose of investigating both [the literal and the figurative meanings]. || 10 ||
Nevertheless, the examination of one's birth star is indeed required; if you also agree with this, how could this [name] be accepted? (11)
In reality, this word (*padam*) would be connected independently;
therefore, it is understood that there is no dependence here even upon [the categories] such as *siddha*. || 12 ||

"For this very reason, the Tantrikas maintain that there is no need for purification through ritual success (*siddhi*) and so forth here. Having thus composed his mind, let the one possessed of reasoning investigate. 13.

For one whose birth asterism (janmabha) is manifest, [the calculation] should be made from that birth asterism; for one whose birth asterism is lost, one should infer it from the name asterism (nāmarkṣa).
Calamity, a killer, and an enemy are to be avoided by the wise;
however, otherwise has it been declared by the practitioners of mantras who are knowers of the Veda. (15)
The eighth and ninth notes are auspicious when situated in the Vedas (fourth) and the couple (second); those others are not auspicious—this should be known by those skilled in mantra.

The letters *bāṇa* (ba), *gaura* (ga), *khura* (kha), and *śoṇa* (śa) shine beautifully when arranged in groups; these letters are joined in sequence, while the letters beginning with *śa* are situated in the *kanyā* (virgin) group. || 17 ||
Some here have stated otherwise: "The letter *kṣa*, having reached the subsequent position, together with the four letters beginning with *ya*, resides in Pisces. (18)
The zodiacal signs (rāśis) should be abandoned— namely those corresponding to eight, four, and twelve days—
for the tantric practitioner who thus recites the text at the beginning of the autumn season and other such times.
I shall also describe that which investigates the principles of the zodiacal signs: the ascendant, wealth, siblings, kinsmen, children, enemies, and wife. (20)
Death, dharma, karma, and the future—these are the twelve zodiac signs (*rāśi*).
Let him recite this reading here, which is not in contradiction with the previous recitation.

This is the sequence in the Bhairava Tantra; one should contemplate it in this very way: in the Moon, in Fire, likewise in Rudra, in the Planet, in the Eye, in the Pair, and in the Sun. (26)
In the directions, in the sixth and eighth lunar digits, in the Śrutisoma [eleventh], in the Bhautika [fifth],

The wise man should write the letters contained in the script within the squares numbered according to the modifications; by this sequence, he shall then know the "Siddha" and other [categories].
Having divided [the grid] into four by fours starting from the square containing the first letter of one's own name,
the wise practitioner should count up to the square containing the fourth letter of the mantra.

In the sequence of *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari*, one should circumambulate clockwise. That which is already accomplished (*siddha*) is perfected in time; however, that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is perfected through recitation and fire-offerings.
Even by merely seizing [the enemy], one who is well-perfected cuts through the roots of his foes; in that case as well, the practitioner of mantra should calculate according to the grid of names.
They declare the results of these [mantras] according to the distinctions of *siddha-siddha* and so forth: a *siddha-siddha* [yields fruit] as stated, while a *siddha-sādhya* yields double that. (32)

A *siddha* becomes *susiddha* by half the recitation; a *siddha-ari* destroys one's kinsmen (or relatives). A *sādhya* becomes *siddha* through double the recitation, while a *sādhya-sādhya* is fruitless.

The *sādhya* and *susiddha* [mantras] are [attained] from three times [the recitation]; however, the *sādhya-ari* (enemy of the sādhya) kills one's kinsmen. The *susiddha-siddha* [is attained] by half the recitation, and that *sādhya* [is attained] by a recitation three times [that amount].
When [the planet] is well-established (susiddha) through its acquisition, it is remembered as the destroyer of the enemy's caste; when established by the enemy (arisiddha), it kills the son;

when to be accomplished by the enemy (arisādhya), it kills the daughter; when well-established by the enemy (arisusiddha), it kills the wife; and when the enemy itself is destroyed, it destroys the enemy.

The purification of the stars is for the Vaiṣṇavas, the purification of the square (koṣṭha) is for Śiva, and the purification of the zodiac signs (rāśi) is for the Traipuras; so the Vārāhī Tantra has declared. (36)

Having ascertained [the presence of] wealth and so forth, as well as the attainment of supernatural powers (siddhi) and the like, the wise should proceed; for otherwise, there would be fruitlessness. || 1 ||
One should draw five excellent lines extending from south to north;
likewise, one should fashion solar lines extending from east to west.
The wise man should write two vowels each in five cells, and likewise others;
having written one [consonant] each in six [cells], he should then [place] the letters from *ka* to *ha*.

One should cause the intellect to write down each [number] one by one within eleven groups of three, using the sequence of ten directions, earth, mountains, Vedas, elephants, ṛṣis, oceans, six, and three. (4)
One should multiply the letters of the practitioner, distinguished as vowels and consonants,
by four, fifteen, twelve, seven, and five.

Then, one should place the numerical values of the syllables of the name, starting from the first and ending with the last, in order within the nine squares [formed by] the Vedas (4), fires (3), weapons (5), lord of serpents (1), and the Manus (14).
Just as one might destroy the fifth [term] by means of the qualities of the [first] five, so too,
in brief, do those multipliers of the qualities terminate.

In the syllables of the practitioner, there are the forms of the ruru deer, fish, man, and garden; within the letters of the mantra, there are those very [elements]: mountains, earth, sun, and rivers.
Having understood the debt of both from the names, letters, and the like— such as *ga*, *ja*, *bha*, *kta*, and so forth— the wise mathematician should know the remainder to be the greater [debt].
One should take a share from both [the debtor and the creditor] according to their respective wealth; he in whom a greater abundance is observed is proclaimed as the debtor (adhamarṇa). || 10 ||
One should indeed employ those mantras by which [the object] is held;
in their absence, one should never [use] a wealthy creditor who possesses equal wealth. (11)
Alternatively, one may perform the clearing of debts in another manner: taking the first letter of one's own name, and then those that follow it.
All [the syllables] from the beginning of the mantra up to its final letter should be counted;
they are to be multiplied by seven and then divided by three.
Whatever number remains is declared to be the debt; taking the first letter of the mantra, those others which follow it [are counted]. 14.
The letters beginning with one's own name and ending with the final letter should be counted by the wise;
that resulting number should then be multiplied by three. (15)
That which is to be subtracted by seven is called the remainder of that wealth;
now the method for examining the *kulākula* is being described. (16)
Air, fire, earth, water, and space are the fifty letters in sequence;
there are five short vowels and five long vowels, ending with the bindu, which arise from the junctions.
The consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṣa*, *kṣa*, *la*, *sa*, and *ha* are proclaimed in groups of five.
The first syllable of the practitioner [is the seed], as is the syllable of the mantra itself. (18)
If one should know that [the deity] belongs to a single element and its entire family—whether it be earthly, watery, friendly, fiery, or even airy—[then one should proceed accordingly]. (19)
The air element is considered the enemy of the earth, water, and syllables; likewise, the fire element is the enemy of water, and the ether element is the enemy of fire.
Furthermore, for all of these, however, there is no awakening that is not based on the sky; a wise man should not effect a union of things that are mutually contradictory. (21)
Hasta, Svātī, Śravaṇa, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Puṣya, Anurādhā, Aśvinī, Revatī, and Punarvasu—these, the reciters say, are the asterisms belonging to the gods. (22)
The three stars beginning with Pūrva and Uttara, as well as Ārdrā, Bharaṇī, and Rohiṇī—these constellations are declared by the learned to be the group called "Martya. (23)
In the Citrāśleṣa [group], Mūla, Maghā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Jyeṣṭhā are likewise included;
Varuṇa, Kṛttikā, Indra, and Agni are declared to be the Rakṣogaṇa. (24)
The highest affection exists between two gods; that between a god and a human is middling; and it is said that there is great enmity between gods (and humans) and demons.
Thus the awakened one should apply the mantra to himself according to the ritual procedure;
for from the various distinctions of the letters of the Mātṛkā, all mantras were born. (26)
The classes of mantras are twofold, distinguished by the division into *mantra* and *vidyā*:
*mantras* are considered to be those of male deities, while *vidyās* are considered to be those of female deities. (27)
Mantras are considered to be of three kinds, consisting of female, male, and neuter natures: those ending in *svāhā* are of female form, and those ending in *namaḥ* are neuter. (28)

Those mantras which end with *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* are proclaimed to be masculine; these three types of mantras are recommended for the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*), pacification (*śānti*), and malevolent magic (*abhicārika*).

The times for the awakening from sleep and so forth of the mantras are now declared. It should be understood that the mantras are of the nature of Agni and Soma, corresponding respectively to the cruel and the gentle. (30)

For the two types of ritual action, the mantras are said to consist mostly of fire (ra), stars (u), the end of the sky (ha), and space (kṣa); those of the Fire-god (Āgneya) are predominantly composed of these, while those of the Moon-god (Saumya) consist mostly of the syllables of nectar (the vowels).
When the vital breath moves in the southern channel, the fires belonging to Agni awaken; and when the breath is situated in the other part, those belonging to Soma attain awakening.
When the vital breath has entered both channels, they all attain awakening; once awakened, they always bestow their fruit upon the practitioners of mantra.

Having encapsulated the letters from *la* onwards, together with the *bindu*, by means of the mantra, one should then recite those same letters along with the *visarga*, followed by the letter *kṣa* alone. (34)
Having thus recited and instructed [the disciple], one who is awakened bestows all accomplishments;
this applies to the mantras of Nṛsiṃha, Arka, and Varāha, as well as the Prāsāda and the Praṇava.

One should not examine the success (siddha) and other qualities of a mantra whose syllables are combined, nor of one obtained in a dream, nor of one given by a woman, nor likewise of a garland-mantra (mālāmantra). (36)
In all Vedic [mantras], one should not purify the *siddha* and other [categories]. This applies to the *siddha*, the *kūṭa*, the three seeds, the power (*śakti*), and the single-syllable mantra. (37)
Some maintain that even for a favored mantra, these [practitioners] have no requirement for ritual purification;
furthermore, mantras consisting of more than twenty syllables are declared to be *mālāmantras*. (38)
Mantras consisting of more than ten syllables, those below that known as *bījas*, and *sapiṇḍākṣara* mantras such as the Śrī Cintāmaṇi and others [are likewise included]. (39)
In childhood, the Mālā-mantras and other mantras bestow success;
in youth, the five-syllabled mantra and others do so; and in old age, other [mantras] always grant success.
Now, in accordance with all the tantras, I shall state the auspicious months, lunar days, asterisms, times, and so forth, for the reception of mantras.
Commencing the recitation of mantras in the month of Caitra yields the fruit of all suffering;
in Vaiśākha there is the gain of jewels [or, according to variant *k*: destruction]; and in Jyeṣṭha, death is certain.
In Āṣāḍha there will be the acquisition of kinsmen; in Śrāvaṇa, the arising of auspiciousness;
in Bhādrapada, the destruction of offspring; and in Āśvina, happiness in every respect. (3)
In Kārttika there shall be an increase in knowledge; in Mārgaśīrṣa, the dawning of auspiciousness; in Pauṣa, there may be a loss of knowledge; and in Māgha, an increase in intelligence.

In the month of Phālguna, there shall be complete success; one should cause the commencement of the mantra practice. The second lunar day of the bright fortnight is considered to bring about the increase of sons.
The third is considered to yield middling results; the fourth is held to cause loss; the fifth is declared to grant success;
and the sixth is censured in all respects.
On the seventh there shall be the gain of wealth; on the eighth, the destruction of one's elders; the ninth is the loss of inheritance; and the tenth portends happiness.
On the eleventh day there will be the gain of strength and a bull; on the twelfth day there will be prosperity through cattle;
on the thirteenth day there will be the dawning of auspiciousness.

On the fourteenth day there is the loss of disciples; on the full moon day, the loss of intellect; on the new moon day, the loss of strength; and on the first day of the lunar fortnight, the destruction of wisdom.
"Especially the tenth and seventh days of the bright fortnight are [auspicious], while the sixth day is always to be censured; thus it is stated in another Śaiva Āgama. (10)

In the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), neither inauspicious nor auspicious results are seen; however, in the bright fortnight (śukla), there is the attainment of one's desires, the acquisition of jewels, and the arising of good fortune.
One should cause the commencement of the mantra practice during either the bright or the dark fortnight;
this is taught for the sake of all desired aims in the *Śrīmantradarpaṇa*. (12)
Excepting Mars and Saturn, all weekdays are considered auspicious; likewise, the asterisms Citrā, Mṛgaśiras, Rohiṇī, and the Sun (Sunday).
The last three [signs] are considered friendly; among these, the taking up of mantras is held to be auspicious and constantly bestowing happiness, starting from Virgo and ending with Pisces. (14)
Some describe it differently; that too is examined here: one who possesses the color of a horse, enjoys happiness, and relies upon wealth. (15)
Under Bharaṇī, death occurs quickly, there is loss of wealth, and the destruction of progeny;
under Kṛttikā, one will always be constantly distressed by disease and grief. (16)
Under Rohiṇī, one becomes like the lord of Rohiṇī herself, a temple of fortune; under Mṛgaśīrṣa, there shall be gain favored by the king and accompanied by kinsmen.
Under Ārdrā, there will be oppression by the king and the loss of wealth arises; under Punarvasu, there is an increase in progeny and constant stability in the commencement of undertakings. (18)
In Puṣya, the Flower-armed One (Kāma) is pleased, and he who enjoys happiness is dear to his beloved;
likewise, in Aśleṣā, the minister goes to destruction constantly.
Under Maghā, one becomes highly fortunate, always possessed of wealth, and happy;
under the three Purvas as well, one reaches the further shore of the three complete Vedas.
In the latter triad, one is endowed with generosity and the knowledge of the Vedas; there is always prosperity in the hand, as well as the acquisition of learning. (21)

Under Citrā, there is the attainment of auspicious knowledge; one becomes beloved by the world and successful. Under Svātī, one falls under the power of death, and likewise, there shall be a loss of strength.
Under Viśākhā, one constantly meets with ruin, slaughter, and imprisonment;
but when the moon has entered Anurādhā, one becomes auspicious, dear, and radiant as the sun.
In Jyeṣṭhā, there will be the loss of the eldest [son] as well as the loss of wealth; in Mūla, one becomes highly intelligent, wise, and possesses many descendants.
Under Śravaṇā, one is always distressed and likewise suffers the loss of wealth;
under Dhaniṣṭhā, however, one is wealthy, a delighter of young women, and accomplished.
In Śatabhiṣaj, one possesses the wealth of truth and is endowed with riches and grain; and in Revatī, one is long-lived and finds refuge in wealth and grain. (26)
In this world, a person certainly becomes truthful through the commencement of mantra practice; the commencement of mantra practice under the asterisms of Ārdrā and Kṛttikā is highly praised. (27)
If the commencement of the mantra-ritual for the Lord or for Agni occurs in due order during Aries, one becomes afflicted by grief;
in Taurus, one is beset by disease. (28)
One born in Gemini lagna will be miserable; likewise in Cancer. In Leo, he will be an enemy to the assembly of poets; in Virgo, he shall partake of the fruits [of his actions]. (29)
In Libra one is an enjoyer of happiness; in Scorpio one meets with destruction; in Sagittarius one is wealthy; in Capricorn one is prosperous; and in Aquarius one is destitute. (30)
One who is devoted to the six duties, wealthy, and always eloquent in Pisces— when one is fully endowed with these qualities, one should have the initiation performed on that day.
One should employ a Vaiṣṇava mantra for a Vaiṣṇava, a Śaiva for a Śaiva, and a Śākta for a Śākta;
however, one should not apply them perversely even toward a Great Guru who is omniscient.
In accordance with the tradition, I shall describe the initiation consisting of the Kalās, even more concisely than before,
for the benefit of practitioners of mantra.
Since, without this [wisdom], the fruit of all mantras cannot be obtained—[for it is so called] because it contemplates all beings and protects them from the ocean of saṃsāra. (34)

For one who possesses the nature of mantra is engaged in the activity of both reflecting and protecting; having directly realized the chosen deity according to the path of mantra, [one proceeds]. (35)
The guru should awaken the disciple; therefore, that is called *dīkṣā*, because it bestows divine knowledge and effects the destruction of sins. (36)
Therefore, it is proclaimed as *dīkṣā* by the teachers who are experts in the Tantras; for it bestows the entire essence of knowledge and destroys the cage of sins. (37)
Therefore, that is called initiation (dīkṣā), which is auspicious and cuts through sin;
it applies to the three castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas regarding their own duties, Vedic study, and so forth. (38)
Just as there is no entitlement here for one who has not undergone the initiation ceremony (upanayana), so too there is none for those who have not been initiated into the use of mantras,
yantras, worship, and the like.
Since there is no entitlement [to practice] from such [sources], one should make oneself consecrated by the mantra.
A mantra heard by chance, or through deception, or by force—[is ineffective]. (40)
Even that which has been examined by the teacher and prescribed according to the verses is fruitless; therefore, initiation is indispensable, and its procedure is now being declared. (41)
On the previous day, both the teacher and the disciple should observe eating only once; then, on the following day, the most excellent teacher, having performed his daily rites, [should proceed].
One should worship the deity of the mantra to be given with devotion through ritual services; then, having taken up a conch shell and washed it with water consecrated by the syllable *phaṭ*.
There, being well-restrained and knowing the ritual procedure, one should write the seed-syllable of Hṛllekhā with the *hṛdaya* mantra;
one should offer water and the eightfold perfumes with the root mantra and the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, coraka, saffron, gorocana, jaṭāmāṃsī, and kapi—these are known as the eight fragrances of Śakti. (45)
Sandalwood, agallochum, hrībera, kuṣṭha, saffron, sea-foam, jaṭāmāṃsī, and murā—these are considered the eight fragrances for Viṣṇu. (46)
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, tamāla, water, saffron, kuśīta, and combined with kuṣṭha— this is considered the eightfold fragrance (gandhāṣṭaka) dedicated to Śiva.
There,
the digits (kalās) of the Moon, which are produced from the sixteen vowels and begin with Amṛtā, should be invoked and established according to the prescribed sequence.
Then, having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the installation of the breaths (asus). Likewise, there are twelve kalās of the Sun and ten of Fire.
The twelve solar [kalās] beginning with Kābhā and ending with Ṣāntā are proclaimed; those ten fiery kalās beginning with Yā are likewise celebrated. || 50 ||
They say that the worship of these [goddesses] should be performed all at once according to their sequence; however, when worshipping them individually, one should follow the order of their names.
One should employ the letters together with their bindus as seed-syllables; indeed, in the ritual worship, they should arise simultaneously from the vowels. || 52 ||

Having uttered "Amṛtā and the others," one should say the word "sixteen. Then, with these words and all the [other] items of worship, one should worship the digits of the moon (candrakalā) in due order.

p. 16) Having thus addressed [the deity] according to the rule even in the subsequent stages, one should perform the worship. This very same procedure is considered applicable for the installation of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) and other such rites. || 54 ||
Then, having invoked the ten digits (kalās) born from the syllable *tva*, the wise one should mutter the mantra *haṃsaḥ*, perform worship, and establish the vital breaths (*asūn*).
Thus, O wise one, the ten external kalās are produced from the syllable *ukāra*; having recited this mantra, Viṣṇu should be worshipped and the vital breaths (*asūn*) should be established.
Then, having invoked the ten digits (kalās) produced from the syllable *ma*, the wise one should recite the mantra of Tryambaka, perform worship, and establish the vital breaths (asus).
Then, having invoked the five [elements], the *kalā* arising from the *bindu*,
and reciting the mantra "Tatsavitur," one should worship and establish the vital breaths (*asūn*).
Then, having invoked the sixteen digits (kalās) born from the Sound (nāda), and having worshipped while reciting the mantra "Viṣṇur yonim," one should establish the vital breaths (asūs).
The Kalās beginning with the letter *ka* and ending with *binduja* are said to be proclaimed in sequence; those born of *nāda* should be known in order as being preceded by the sixteen vowels.
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, Dhṛti, Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, and Aṅgadā. (61)
Pūrṇā, Pūrṇāmṛtā, and Kāmadāyinī are proclaimed, respectively,
as the sixteen digits of the moon (indukalā) situated in the solar orb (bhānumaṇḍala) in due order.
Tāpinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Ruci, Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā. || 63 ||

These twelve digits (kalās) have been declared; furthermore, the ten digits of Fire are Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Rukmā, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī, Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, Havyavāhā, and Kavyavāhā. These belong to the Tāra.
From the five divisions, there are fifty digits (kalās) residing in the phonemes.
Creation, prosperity, memory, intelligence, splendor, fortune, fortitude, stability,
persistence, and accomplishment— these are declared to be the ten forms of the Kalās in their respective order.
Jarā, Pālinī, Śānti, Aiśvarī, Ratikāmikā, Varadā, Hlādinī, and Prīti—these, born from the syllable "Oṃ," arise in sequence as Dīrghā. (67)
Tīkṣṇā, Raudrī, Bhayā, Nidrā, Tandrā, Kṣutkrodhinī, Kriyā, Utkārī, and Mṛtyu—these are the kalās consisting of the letter *ma*, in their respective order. (68)
The five born of the *bindu* are declared to be yellow, white, reddish, black, and infinite (*anantā*), situated in their own respective groups; and the *kalās* born of the *nāda* follow in sequence.
Withdrawal is its foundation; knowledge follows immediately as peace. It is Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, Mocikā, and the Supreme (Parā).
The subtle, the very subtle, the immortal, the nectar of knowledge, and the nourisher—these are considered the pervasive powers of the vowels, which are of the nature of space and infinite. (71)
Immediately after the placement (nyāsa) and other rites of the digits (kalā) of the moon, the sun, and so forth, one should likewise recite the Tryambaka mantra,
the Gāyatrī, and the Jātavedas mantra.
"Having placed [the mantras] and worshipped them according to the rules, one should establish their vital breaths (asūn)"—
thus some say here as well, out of a stubborn adherence born from ignorance regarding the oral instruction.
First, one should extract the Śakti conjoined with the noose and goad; [then] the letters beginning with *ya* and ending with *sa*, with their heads adorned by the bindu. (74)
At the end of that, the wise one should extract [the syllable] joined with Vyoma (Ha), Sadya (Sa), and Indu (I);
then [he should utter] Haṃsa and Parātman; then he should speak the word *amuṣya*.
One should say "the vital breaths" (prāṇāḥ), and after that, "here the vital breaths"; then one should say "the life-soul (jīva) of so-and-so is stationed here," and utter the word "of so-and-so."
May all his senses— speech, mind, sight,
hearing, and smell— along with his vital breaths, come here and dwell happily for a long time.
Let the wife of Agni (Svāhā) remain as before;

then, having applied the word "prati" followed by the name of the person [to be affected], and likewise the noose (pāśa) and other [knots] (granthi), one should extract the life-mantra (prāṇamantra). || 78 ||
In place of the word "amuṣya," one should utter the name of the person for whom the rite is intended; having performed the touching, one should recite it three times or recite it only once.
The procedure for the re-establishment [of the deity] has been declared according to all tantras; or else, the practitioner of mantra should re-establish the vital breaths with this mantra.

Having extracted the [vowel] *a* from that [word], one should then utter "prāṇā iha" (the vital breaths are here); likewise, one should say "jīva iha sthitaḥ" (the living soul is situated here). || 81 ||

p. 18) "In the same way, [the mantra] 'all the sense organs'—likewise speech and mind as well; from that, let the vital breaths come here, svāhā"—thus is the mantra declared, ending with svāhā. || 82 ||

The name of the person for whom the rite is performed (*sādhya*) and so forth are the same; everything else is as previously stated. Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are declared to be the sages (*ṛṣi*), and the meter (*chandas*) has been described. The deity (*devatā*) is Consciousness (*caitanya-rūpa*) whose nature is Power (*śakti*), consisting of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The heart is uttered with the guttural class [of consonants] preceded by the vowels beginning with *viyat* (the letter *i*). || 84 ||
One should worship the head with the letters beginning with *śa* and the sense organs (*dhīndriyas*) beginning with the letter *i*;
likewise, one should worship the tuft of hair with the letters beginning with *ta* and the organs of action (*karmendriyas*). One should worship the body-armor with the letters beginning with *ta*.
The eye is said to be formed by the letters beginning with *pa* (the labials) joined with those beginning with *va* (the semivowels);
the weapon (*astra*) of this [deity] is proclaimed to be formed by the letters beginning with *ya* (the palatals) joined with those beginning with *b* (the gutturals). (86)
The limb-mantras (aṅgamantras) of the same class are declared to be self-sustained;
the Praṇava is the seed (bīja), and the wife of Agni is said by the sages to be the power (śakti). || 87 ||
Seated upon a red lotus in a boat upon a sea of blood, she holds in her hands a noose, a goad, a bow made of sugarcane,
an arrow, a trident, and a skull-cup.
The wise man should worship the red, three-eyed Goddess, the destroyer of wretchedness and suffering,
after first reciting the root mantra in reverse order.
Having duly invoked the splendor of the root mantra from one's own heart into the conch,
one should worship it with excellent offerings.
In the case of the ritual installation of the water-pot (kalaśa), one should worship the Sarvatobhadra mandala and duly place rice grains and other offerings therein.

One should worship, beginning with the Ādhāra-śakti and ending with the Pīṭha-mantra; [one should place] a pitcher made of gold or other materials, its interior washed with the water of the Astra-mantra.

The mantra-practitioner [should prepare] an auspicious vessel with nine gems within, encircled by triple-stranded threads, worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and provided with dūrvā grass and unbroken rice grains.
Uttering the syllable *oṃ*, one should place [the vessel] there and then fill it with a decoction of milky trees or with that derived from the bark of the *palāśa* tree.
With pure water from a sacred ford or with cow's milk, the Guru, having recited the *vilomamātṛkā* (the mother-letters in reverse order) as well as the root mantra, [should perform the rite]. (95)
Then, having consecrated the conch according to the prescribed rite, one should pour its water into the pitcher,
cover it with mango leaves and the like, and place upon it a fruit and unbroken rice grains (akṣata).
Having placed a wine-cup made of the fruit of the celestial tree (kalpavṛkṣa) in his mouth, the Guru should then wrap it with a pair of stainless linen cloths.

There, at the mouth of the pitcher (kumbhavaktra), one should worship one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) according to the rules with the sixteen offerings beginning with the seat; this specific distinction has been declared. || 98 ||
Pearl, ruby, lapis lazuli, agate, diamond, coral, ruby, emerald,
and sapphire constitute the nine precious gems.
Gold, a diamond, sapphire, ruby, and pearl—
these five jewels, or alternatively, one should place them into the pitcher.
Then the disciple, having satisfied the guru and the brahmins with meditation, wealth, cattle, clothing, and other such things, should offer his own body to him.
Then, with divine vision, the most excellent Guru should look upon the disciple standing nearby and draw that consciousness into his own heart.
Then, having placed [the hand] up to the knees for *nivṛtti* and up to the navel for *pratiṣṭhā*, one should place *vidyā* as far as the neck.
Having assigned Śānti from the throat up to the forehead,
and Śāntyatītā from there up to the head, one should awaken [the deities] by means of the reverse order.
The Guru should then project that consciousness residing within himself into the disciple; having placed dūrvā grass and unbroken rice grains upon the head of that disciple, he should do so. (105)
Reciting the *mātṛkā* of the root mantra mentally in reverse order, the most excellent teacher, being satisfied, should consecrate his beloved disciple. (106)
Then the disciple, having risen and put on his two garments, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana),
should grasp the feet of the teacher with his hands placed apart.
With his body adorned, he should stand to the right of the Guru;
thereafter, he should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and the ritual placement of the kalās upon the disciple.

Then, one should perform the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) and the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa) with devotion; one should contemplate the deity within oneself as having been transferred into the disciple.

Then, first of all, the Guru should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. Having placed a *jāla* (water-offering vessel) in the hand of the disciple, he says: "O [Name], this is the mantra of both of us. (110)
The disciple should likewise say, "May it be so," and then,
perceiving the oneness of the deity, the guru, and the mantra, he should prostrate like a staff.
The disciple should bow to the Guru and worship him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, [saying]: "O Goddess, abode of compassion, refuge of all prosperity! (112)
O Mother, who are a refuge and full of affection, show mercy toward this child, O Sovereign of the Gods, for he is bound by the fetters beginning with the *āṇava*.
O Goddess, whose essence is compassion, show mercy to this wretched man; may he be fully nourished by auspicious fortunes both in this world and the next. 114.
With palms joined in reverence, one should pray: "O Noble One, remain forever firm here. Then, [one should recite] the mantra, together with its seer (ṛṣi) and other components, into the right ear.
The teacher should say this, and then the disciple should give the threefold fee (dakṣiṇā) to him; so it has been stated in all the tantras by the practitioners of mantra who know the tantras.
Abandoning stinginess regarding his wealth, the disciple, with a contented mind, should offer either his entire property, half of it, or a tenth part as gold. (117)
For the sake of the successful completion of the mantra-initiation, the wise man should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru— either his entire property,
half of it, or according to his capacity.
"A king should give half his kingdom as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru";
thus says the Śrī Gārgyasaṃhitā in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtitantra. (119)

For both he who has not obtained [the fruit] despite being initiated, and he who has obtained it but failed to give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), have performed their actions in vain; since the fruit arises from the Śrauta rite when it is performed with all its constituent parts (sāṅga). || 120 ||

Then, one should recite the mantra obtained according to one's own capacity a hundred times; having recited it eight times, the wise practitioner of mantra should do so for the sake of attaining the goal of the mantra.
One should offer all items, such as the conch and the garments, to the preceptor; one should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the twice-born and also feed the Brāhmaṇas. || 122 ||
And for three days he should not even abandon the observances such as celibacy; by this procedure, the disciple becomes initiated and his impurities are destroyed.
He obtains enjoyments both in this world and the next; of this there is no doubt.
This is the power of the mantra that has become manifest for the practitioner who has received the mantra. (124)

By reciting it one thousand and eight times, that [obstacle] is removed; the disciple [should likewise perform] the assignment of the seer and other [limbs] of the mantra, as well as the ritual placements and worship. (125)
Terrified by the falling of the *śakti*, one should investigate with great haste; at the time of a solar eclipse, there should be nothing else to seek. (126)
There is nothing whatsoever equal to the time of a solar eclipse; whatever is performed there, all of it yields infinite fruit. (127)
He does not instruct on the purification of the day and so forth during a solar eclipse; for at that time, whatever is desired or received from a guru among men is [efficacious]. (128)
The mantra becomes effective quickly and without effort; therefore, initiation and other rites should be performed right there, provided that the possibility exists. (129)

When performing the initiation into the mantra at a sacred ford (tīrtha), during an eclipse of the sun or moon, or on the specific days of the *āmāvāsya* and *pūrṇimā* festivals, one need not purify the month, the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), and so forth.
In that regard, it is declared to be a solar eclipse and not considered a lunar eclipse; thus, what has been stated by some is held to be without foundation. (131)
This initiation has been described in brief for the delight of the virtuous,
according to the procedure for immediate consecration (sadyodhivāsa) and in accordance with all the traditions of the learned.
[* * * * * * * *] First of all, there is no perception of the mantra; nor does he even give it away, due to the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). 133.
The determination of its being both the seed and the fruit is established through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); for in this way, one may effect the destruction of sin here. (134)
In such cases, the accumulation of karmic results would accrue to the donor alone;
what then would be the fate of one who is devoid of initiation and sacrifice, as stated in the passage beginning "even [one who is] devoid of initiation and sacrifice"? (135)
Moreover, that which has a different locus [from the word] cannot be the cause for its application on account of its complexity;
for if it were so, then even a heavy [property] would function as such. (136)
There is neither the status of an initiated disciple nor even the attainment thereof; for this contradicts such statements as "he performs the initiation" and so forth regarding the disciple. (137)

To this it is replied: "The initiation of the *mantra* and the grasping of the *mantra* according to rule. And the phrase "according to rule" is stated as an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the various procedures (*vidhā*). (138)
This is not merely a qualification; otherwise, there would be a violation of the injunction: "I shall perform the sacrifice with the initiation-rite; in that matter, you be my guru. (139)

For this very reason, it has been stated by the practitioners of mantra in the *Ratnākara* and other works that the general time for initiation is now being declared for the mantras. (Note: The text enclosed in brackets is not present in manuscript *ka*). 140.
Instructed by the Tattvasāgara with the desire for the welfare of practitioners, initiation should be performed whenever there is a wish, in accordance with the command of the Guru. (141)
Neither the lunar day, nor a vow, nor fire-offerings, nor ritual bathing, nor the practice of recitation is the cause for initiation; rather, it is simply the spontaneous meeting with a true Guru.
The wise are not able to perform the initiation in full detail;
therefore, one should proceed according to this concise method.
In the Sarvatobhadra mandala, one should place a new jar filled with water,
honored with perfumes and flowers, and adorned with cloth.

Then, having performed the worship of the deity with all medicinal herbs, five jewels, and five sprouts, one should offer [or, according to another interpretation, recite] one hundred and eight oblations. 145.
The mantra-practitioner, having brought the well-adorned disciple onto the altar, should cause him to sit down,
sprinkling him with the waters from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel as well as the waters from the *śāntikumbha* jar.
One should perform the consecration with [water] empowered one hundred and eight times with the root mantra;
then, while accomplishing the mantra, one should place the hand upon the head. (147)
Saying "Namo'stu," he should offer unbroken grains (akṣata) and then address the mantra to the disciple: "Surā, māṃsī, vacā, kuṣṭha, śaileya, and the two types of rajanī."

Likewise, the *campaka*, *mustā*, and the entire collection of medicinal herbs are prescribed. If someone is unable even for this, they should worship the lotus—meaning the conch shell—along with *akṣata* grains.
Having sprinkled that [water] eight times with the root mantra alone, one should perform the placement (vinyāsa) and recite it into the ear; this is the procedure for the oral instruction (upadeśa).
When the moon or sun is eclipsed, at a sacred ford, or in a pure temple of Śiva, the mere recitation of the mantra is called "instruction" (upadeśa). || 151 ||
(23) Furthermore, that method of instruction has been declared by the wise even regarding a mirror.
Having taken water from a conch shell together with flowers, *kuśa* grass, and sandalwood, (152)
Having sprinkled a devoted, intelligent, and peaceful person, one should cause [the mantra] to be given; at the conclusion of the worship, O Śrī Gārgya, the Saṃhitā speaks this mantra to him. (153)

Having performed his daily rites, the best of gurus, as a practitioner of mantra, should recite the mantra— along with its seer (ṛṣi) and other components— three times into the right ear of the disciple.
Then, having abandoned stinginess regarding wealth, the disciple should rise and give the teacher a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); he should prostrate before the guru like a staff. || 155 ||
One should offer one’s body, wealth, and life to the guru; from that time forward, with undivided mind, one should do what is pleasing to the guru. (156)
One should renounce food, clothing, and other gifts to the Brahmins according to one's capacity;
one should observe the rules such as celibacy (brahmacarya) and others, just as in the rite of initiation (dīkṣā). || 157 ||
If one should, out of negligence, receive or recite the mantra of an enemy, he should recite the mantra one thousand times over a *droṇa* measure of cow’s milk.
Having drunk milk or likewise water, one should then cast it away; by this very procedure, one is quickly liberated from the enemy mantra.
Having written the enemy mantra on a banyan leaf, one should cast it into a stream;
thus one becomes liberated from the mantra—so says the tradition of the learned.
Now, for the benefit of the world and for those of limited intellect, I shall today briefly state the characteristics of the teacher and the disciple. (1)
One who acts according to his own will, who is not vain, whose intellect is pure, and from whom desire has departed—
such a person is called a "guide" (deśika) in every land, regardless of place or time.
Foremost among the hosts, omniscient, and with his physical form utterly stilled;
even by inflicting suffering upon himself, he was solely intent on the happiness of others. (3)
Like a mirror for all branches of knowledge, he did not corrupt their vision; he was a devotee of the deity, tranquil, and free from desire even for sense objects. (4)
That best of Brahmins was a knower of the self, a proponent of Brahman, and skilled in the meaning of the Vedic branches; he was capable both of uplifting and of destroying.
He is a knower of the Tantras, one who does not pierce the vital points of mantras, and a possessor of secrets;
he is intent on the victory of the six limbs, powerful, and possessed of an expansive mind.
Pure, with pure limbs, his actions unblemished and his mind undaunted,
he was ever devoted to the worship of the two enemies of the cities and the demons.
One whose undertaking is endowed with the [proper] group [of attendants], who is profound and free from hypocrisy,
who has achieved success through the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa), whose mantra is perfected, and who knows the ritual applications (prayoga).
A householder who is ascetic and truthful is called a guru;
those born in Madhyadeśa, Kurukṣetra, Lāṭa, and Aṅkola [are eligible]. || 9 ||
Those established at Antarvedi, the Āvantyas, the most excellent Gurus, the Gauḍas, the Sāndhodbhavas, the Sauras, the Māgadhas, and likewise the Keralas; || 10 ||
The Kośalas, the Daśārṇas, the Guravas, the Saptamadhyamas, those born on the banks of the Kārṇāṭa, Narmadā, Rāṣṭra, and Kaccha,
as well as the Kaliṅgas, Kadambas, and Kāmbojas— these are likewise considered inferior. [The followers of] Āstika...
Devoted to the guru and desirous of knowledge, together with faith. || 12 ||
Having developed detachment from women and other objects due to the suffering arising from desire, anger, and the like,
he long practiced their service with his body and his wealth.
Adorned by even a single speck of dust arising from his lotus feet, one who has not yet attained the bath [of initiation] generally attains what is intended by the mind of the Elder (Vyāsa). 14.
A disciple, being himself diligent in mind, should constantly devote himself to service with body, speech, and mind for a period of three, two, or one year. (15)
Having observed him to be such a person—one who always speaks truthfully, pure of both mother and father, intelligent, and free from greed—[he appointed him]. (16)
One who follows the practice of non-stealing, is endowed with faith, exerts proper effort, is stainless, free from falsehood, and possesses a mind that does not covet another's property. || 17 ||
Constantly observing the vow of celibacy, devoted to the service of the guru, having mastered the Vedas, self-controlled, free from mental anguish, and devoid of physical disease. || 18 ||
With limbs ever perfectly tranquil, always remaining in the presence of the Guru, devoted to the welfare of others, and refraining from censuring others; (19)
He regarded the wife of his guru as his own mother and her sons as his brothers;
he was free from the affliction of forgetfulness, endowed with a smile, and devoid of pride.
A teacher should accept a disciple only after examining him in this manner; a teacher should never accept a disciple who is not of such a kind.
If one accepts [the gift], that fault will likely touch even the preceptor, just as the fault of subjects falls upon the king, or as the fault committed by a wife falls upon the husband. || 22 ||
Likewise, there is no doubt that the fault committed by the disciple falls upon the guru, whether he favors the disciple out of affection or out of greed by initiating him without the proper rite.
If a curse from a deity should fall upon that guru together with his disciples, or upon the enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu), upon Mahādeva, or upon one's mother, father, or king; || 24 ||
Devotion to the lotus feet of one's own guru should always be maintained; whatever is commanded by the guru, whether it be desirable or undesirable, however great it may be, [must be accepted]. (25)
One should always be devoted to the guru with supreme haste, through devotion that is perfect and sincere, by means of action, mind, and speech. (26)

For the sake of accomplishing his own purpose, the disciple should worship [the mantra] without artifice; for that which causes distress to the world and that which cuts into the vital points [of others must be avoided]. (27)
One should never utter speech that causes agitation to those who are settled, nor even that which is delightful, excessively intense, or desired by the mind. (28)
One who is devoted to the teacher and properly honors the teacher should never assume an appearance that is loathsome to the world. (29)
That disciple, having accomplished his purpose, indeed rejoices both in this world and in the next.

Now I shall describe the supreme mandala for the purpose of worship at the beginning of initiation and other rites: it is a square divided into four compartments, with four lines drawn to the corners. (1)
At regular intervals, the mantra-practitioner should cast [lines] such that there may be fish-patterns; two lines each should extend from east to west and two from south to north.
One should drop four equal threads across these fish-marks. || 3 ||
As before, one should drop the thread into the corner squares; then, upon the fish-figures produced therefrom, one should apply four threads.
Then, there should be fish in the compartments; therein the practitioner of mantra should drop the lines, extending up to two hundred and fifty-six squares.
Then, by that very same procedure, he should drop the threads there; in the center, with thirty-six squares, he should draw a lotus possessing all its characteristics.
One should draw the pedestal (pīṭha) with one row [of squares], the pathway (vīthikā) with a pair of rows,
and the doors, ornaments, and secondary ornaments with the remaining two rows.
Then, following the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, the mantra-practitioner, being wise, should draw a lotus after setting aside one-twelfth part of the lotus-field.
In the middle of that, one should divide it with three circles in equal proportions: the first shall be the place for the pericarp (karṇikā), and the second for the filaments (kesara).

There, the third [measurement] is the tip of the petal at the shoulder of the pearl [ornament]; this is the measurement of the space between the outer and inner circles according to the rule, O wise one. (10)
Having placed small moon-disks all around the tips of the filaments and having drawn lines situated at the joints,
one should drop the threads there.
The wise practitioner should draw a circle with the same measurement as that of the tips of the petals; within that space, on both sides of the central line, he should proceed.
One should draw the tips of the petals all around with the outer hand; at the bases of the petals, one should fashion the filaments in pairs. (13)
This common lotus design has been proclaimed by those who know the tantras; one should sweep out three squares for the purpose of the quarters in the corners of the pedestal.
With the remaining squares, the learned one should fashion the limbs of the pedestal; he should then sweep the squares situated along the pathways, ensuring there is no confusion in the rows.
Then, one should construct doors in the directions starting from two or four squares;
likewise, the *śobhās* on both sides of the doors should consist of three and one square respectively.
The secondary ornaments (upaśobhās) should be formed with one square each, followed by three squares;
the four corners should be formed with the remaining six squares.
One should color that captivating maṇḍala with five colors: yellow should be made from turmeric powder, and white from rice flour. (18)
The five colors are said to be: red from safflower powder, black from burnt rice husks, and dark (śyāma) from the leaves of the bilva tree and others. (19)
The auspicious boundary lines, one finger in height and width, should be white;
the pericarp is yellow in color, and the filaments are reddish.
The practitioner of mantra should color the petals with white pigment and their joints with black; alternatively, the pericarp may be yellow.
The filaments should be yellowish-red, and the petals should also be reddish;
the joints should be black in color, or alternatively, yellow or black.
One should color the interiors of the pedestals; the feet should have a reddish glow, and its limbs, as well as those in the four walkways, should be white.
One should draw wish-fulfilling creepers endowed with leaves, flowers, and fruits,
variegated with various colors and enchanting to the sight of all.
The doors are white in color, the ornaments (śobhā) are said to be red,
the secondary ornaments (upaśobhā) are yellow in color, and the corners are black.
One should draw three lines on the outside, white, red, and black in sequence; this is considered the universal *sarvatobhadra* mandala.
Having divided the square ground into twelve parts from the cardinal directions, the wise one should drop threads there; thus, one hundred squares are seen. (27)
One should fashion the pedestal (pīṭha) with forty-four squares, followed by thirty-six lotuses; there is no pathway (vīthikā) here in this row.
Just as the secondary ornament (upaśobhā) was previously seen at the door-ornament (dvāraśobhā),
the knower of mantras should form the corners with the remaining six squares.

One should perform the remainder as previously described; thus is the mandala considered. For the worship of the deity at the beginning of initiation and other rites, the Sarvatobhadra mandala is proclaimed according to all tantras as bestowing all prosperity. (30)
Having thus obtained a favorable mantra from the guru, one who is well-restrained should perform the preliminary rites;
this is declared with its authoritative measure.

But the initiated one [should perform this] in a pure place during the rising of Jupiter and Venus at an auspicious moment, when the ascendant is in a state of growth (upacaya) and is free from the aspect of malefic planets. || 32 ||

Then, during a meritorious month and on an auspicious day free from the *riktā* dates and other such inauspicious times, and joined with favorable planets and so forth, one should perform the *puraścaraṇa*.

Recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), libation (tarpaṇa), ritual sprinkling (mārjana), and feeding the twice-born (dvijabhojana)— thus indeed is the five-limbed preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) declared.

By some of the best of mantra-practitioners, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consisting of five limbs has been declared as performing worship here at all three times of the day after offering [the materials] in the place of purification.
O ascetic, whatever one desires, one shall obtain it even by mere thought—be it unattainable even for the gods or located in another continent. (36)
Having performed the five-limbed worship, one shall obtain whatever is desired;
the wise person who performs this five-limbed *puraścaraṇa* [shall achieve the same]. (37)
He indeed triumphs in the world through knowledge, sovereignty, sons, and other blessings, provided he possesses a mantra obtained from a guru with a deeply serene inner self. (38)
This five-limbed worship is prescribed as preliminary to the attainment of perfection; he who performs the *puraścaraṇa* excels among all. (39)
Through knowledge, sons, grandsons, and the abundance of wealth, grain, and so forth— there is no dharma equal to this,
nor is there any austerity equal to this.
By this [statement], nothing whatsoever is ever established regarding the desired object. (41)
Now, what indeed is their preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa)? It is said that it consists of the fivefold performance beginning with recitation (japa);
however, this is not tenable.

Since each of these individually would be over-extensive as a definition, if it is claimed that their combination constitutes such a definition, then the combination does not exceed the sum of its parts. (43)

The claim that "the five, beginning with *japa*, joined together are likewise [the *tathatās*]" is also refuted by this. If it is argued that they are called the "five *tathatās*" because they are performed without interruption, [that too is incorrect].

"Do not say so, for that would contradict the state of having five members (*pañcāṅgatā*)... [and] because the status of being a member is established [only when combined]. If it is argued that each [member] individually would be a member when combined, we say no, because of the aforementioned fault. (45)

Or what would be the recourse in such cases as "it should consist of only two members," and so forth? Furthermore, does this term "five-membered" (pañcāṅgatā) have the meaning of "having five parts" (pañcāvayavatva)? (46)

Even this [objection] is not convincing by virtue of the procedure of the six-limbed sacrifice (*ṣaḍaṅgayāga*); because it results in the fallacy of a definition that lacks a basis, the example is simply not applicable. (47)

Because sacrifice is a particular form of desire, it is called its "worship. Just as recitation and the rest have five constituent parts, so too do recitation and the others. Sacrifice, which is of the nature of desire, is called "volition" (saṃkalpa) and "vow" (vrata). (48)
The statement that [the rite] would consist of two limbs and so forth is inconsistent, because in that case, five-limbedness is established by resorting to a secondary alternative (anukalpa).
Because the ritual procedure is one, there is a scriptural teaching that all [subsidiary rites] possess the status of being limbs;
thus, the statement beginning with "if any limb should be omitted" and so forth is also consistent with this.
The Agastya-saṃhitā itself declares with its own voice: "The worship of the five limbs performed with devotion is called *puraścaraṇa*. (51)
That by which a mantra is accomplished—either independently or in dependence on the internal perfection of the mantra—and which is approved by all authorities, is considered *puraścaraṇa*. (52)
"Without which a mantra would not be accomplished even in hundreds of years"—this very point is established in various tantras as well. (53)
In this context, "siddhi" is proclaimed as the state of mantras being fit for application; or, as those learned in logic know, it is a specific desired result. (54)
Devotion to the Guru is proclaimed as the foremost benefit for the worlds. At dawn, one should [meditate on] the Guru, who has three eyes and two arms, upon a white lotus on the head. (1)

One should meditate upon Him as peaceful, endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, preceded by His name: "Obeisance be to You, the Guru, who possesses the very form of the chosen deity. (2)
The nectar of whose speech destroys the poison known as saṃsāra—he is the Guru; the Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, and the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara.
The Guru alone is the Supreme Brahman; therefore, one should worship him first. For one whose Guru is well-pleased, there is no lack of accomplishment; otherwise, it is not so.
For one whose devotion toward the mantra, the deity, and the guru— these three— is unwavering and never interrupted, spiritual accomplishment is not far off.
As is Śiva, so is Vidyā; as is Vidyā, so is the Guru. When the Reality is revealed by the Guru, one becomes identical with it at that very moment.
When Śiva is angry, the Guru is the protector; when the Guru is angry, there is no one at all. Whether ignorant or learned, the Guru alone is always the refuge.
For the wise person who possesses supreme devotion for the Divine, and for the Guru as for the Divine, these truths that have been declared indeed shine forth clearly. (8)
But that lowest of men who, having served his teacher, acts contrary to him out of delusion, shall be cooked in hell for ten million eons.
Just as copper becomes gold through contact with an alchemical elixir, so too does a disciple become identical with Śiva through the mere presence of the Guru. 10.
One should never step over the teacher’s bed, seat, vehicle, sandals, garments, stool, bathing water, or even his shadow.
In the presence of the Guru, one should avoid separate worship and the doctrine of non-duality (*advaita*).
One should renounce before the Guru such things as initiation, exposition, and authority. (12)
And at the end of their bodies, those most sinful and lowest of men who show contempt for their guru are reborn among the animals after passing through the hells.
When will the liberation from the sufferings of hell come about for those disciples who have constantly served their gurus yet have shown them contempt? (14)

Those who, having fallen from the abundance of prosperity consisting of sons, friends, wives, and so forth, and being afflicted by misfortune, out of delusion revile their teacher and speak harshly to him; || 15 ||

Those fools who are hostile toward their guru and are constant evildoers will indeed become pigs for even hundreds of births; there is no doubt that this shall last as long as their merit and their demerit endure. (16)
Devotion should always be cultivated toward the mantra, the deity, and likewise toward the guru who bestows the mantra; for that is the primary means of accomplishment. (17)
Instruction in the mantra at a sacred ford, faith in the practice of recitation, and the conviction that it will bear fruit— this is the characteristic of one who has attained perfection.

One should perform the *puraskriyā* (preliminary rite) for the sake of attaining the fruits mentioned in the Tantras; without this, a mantra will not succeed even in hundreds of years. When this has been performed, the practitioner obtains his desired fruit—what need is there for fire-offerings (*homas*)?
What is the use of mutterings of prayers, and what is the use of the elaborate ritual placement of mantras?
For if there were no preliminary service (puraskriyā) for secret mantras,
the preliminary service of a mantra is indeed said to be its first seed.
Just as a living being devoid of vigor is incapable of performing any action, so too is a mantra declared to be ineffective when it lacks the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa). || 4 ||
Now, in order to perform the preliminary honors (puraskriyā), the fixed locations are stated: a sacred field, the bank of a river, a cave, or a mountain peak. (5)
Sacred sites, the confluence of rivers, purifying forests, secluded gardens,
the foot of a bilva tree, and the slope of a mountain.
A grove of Tulasī, a cow-pen, a temple of Śiva devoid of bulls,
the roots of an Aśvattha or Āmalakī tree, a cow-shed, and the midst of water— [these are auspicious places].
A temple of the deities, the shore of the ocean, one's own home, the presence of teachers, and likewise a place of one-pointed concentration of the mind. || 8 ||
And likewise, the realm of the hungry ghosts and so forth, as shown in their respective Kalpas—
one should perform the recitation while taking refuge in any one of these places.
Listen to the seats which have been described by the sages: a seat of *kuśa* grass brings prosperity, while a woolen blanket (*kāmbala*) grants liberation from suffering. (1)
A deer-skin seat brings about knowledge; one made of reeds increases prosperity; a cloth seat removes disease; and a tiger-skin seat bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
In the rite of sorcery (abhicāra), it is black; in rites such as subjugation (vaśya), it is red; for pacification (śāntika), it is said to be white; and for all rites, it is multicolored.
For the rite of immobilization, an elephant hide should be used; likewise, for killing, a buffalo hide; for expulsion, a goat's hide; and for the rite of subjugation, a sword-sheath (or tiger) skin.
For inciting enmity, a seat of jackal-skin is prescribed; for rites of pacification, it should be a cow-hide. Poverty results from a bamboo seat, and misfortune from a wooden seat.
On the bare ground there arises suffering; on a stone seat, the occurrence of disease;
on a grass mat, the loss of reputation; and on a leaf mat, the delusion of the mind.
In the case of burnt bricks, however, this [mantra] should be used for the general recitation;
this has been stated in the Siddha-Śaiva Āgamas and other scriptures regarding the meanings of the Āgamas.
A person of fortune should avoid a seat made of bamboo, stone, earth, wood, grass, or leaves,
as it bestows the suffering of poverty and physical ailments.
One should prepare a soft seat made of black antelope skin, tiger skin, silk, cane, cloth, or woolen blanket.
No one who has not received initiation should enter while holding a black antelope skin;
however, an ascetic, a forest-dweller, a student, and a graduate may enter.
It should be richly provided with kusha grass, deerskin, and cloth, raised four finger-breadths high, and one or two cubits square on all sides. || 11 ||
p. 35) Thus, free from affliction, one should enter there by means of the sequence beginning with the *svastika* posture.
O best of beings, I shall now describe the postures, beginning with the *svastika*. 12.
The fourfold [mudrās] known as Svastika, Padmaka, Vīra, and Vajra are recommended for recitation;
among these, the first is further praised when used for worship.
Now I shall describe the characteristics of these [mudrās], beginning with Svasti, in their proper order:
having placed both soles of the feet correctly between the knees and the thighs. (14)
Sitting with the body straight is declared to be the *svastika* posture; the wise man places his right foot upon his left thigh. (15)
Then, the knower of the ritual procedure, having crossed over by placing the left foot upon the right thigh,
should hold [the posture] with both hands and place the chin upon the heart.

The wise man should gaze at the tip of his nose; this is considered the lotus posture (padmāsana). This lotus posture is thus described by the learned for the beginning of recitation (japa) and other such practices.
Having observed the passage beginning with "having joined the palms in reverence," one should place the right foot upon the left thigh and likewise the left foot upon the other. (18)

Having performed only this much, one should carry out the recitation of mantras, fire offerings, and so forth; it should be understood that by this very statement, [the goal] will be accomplished. (19)
For in the Nāradīya [Purāṇa], the sage spoke thus regarding the mind of Nārāyaṇa: "From both thighs and from the soles of both feet... (20)

Having placed [the foot] upon [the thigh], one should sit; that is the seat called Padmāsana. Likewise, placing one foot upon one thigh and the other foot similarly upon the other thigh is declared to be Vīrāsana. (21)
Having placed the left ankle above the penis, and likewise having placed the other ankle upon that,
the vajrāsana is thus described.
Now I shall describe the mudrās, which should be displayed with great care;
by performing them, the deities of the mantras rejoice. (1)
Various seals are manifested here and there; [the Lord] fashioned the flute, the lotus, the garland, and the mace, known as the *bilva*, in sequence.
The Knowledge Seal (jñānamudrā) belongs to the Blessed Lord Rāma; the bow with arrow, the Śrīvatsa mark, the Kaustubha gem, the axe, the Gāruḍī, and the supreme Mohanī [are his emblems]. || 3 ||
Nārasiṃhī, Vārāhī, Hayagrīvī, and his beloved Kāmamudrā—these are proclaimed as the [consorts] of this Viṣṇu. || 4 ||

The linga, the yoni, the trident, the eye, the boon-granting gesture, the fear-dispelling gesture, the deer, the khaṭvāṅga, the skull, the hand-drum (ḍamaru), and the auspicious mudrā—these are the [emblems]. || 5 ||
For Sūrya, there is only one [hand], called Padma; for Danta and Vighna, they hold a noose and a goad respectively;
and for Gaṇeśvara, they hold a battle-axe, a sweetmeat ball, and a citron.

In their worship, the mudrās are: the noose, the goad, the boon-granting gesture, the gesture of fearlessness, the sword, the spear, the bow, the two arrows, the shield, the mace, and the one belonging to Durgā; these are the mudrās of Lakṣmī.
A lute, a book, and a rosary are for the worship of Vāgvādinī;
the mudrā called Saptajihvā is to be known for the worship of Agni.
In the worship of Tripurā, ten mudrās are proclaimed:
the first is the Saṃkṣobha-mudrā, and the second is considered to be the Karṣiṇī.
The third is to be known as Drāviṇī, considered to carry the three sections; likewise Unmādinī, Yoni, and the supreme Āveśakarī.
The Mahāṅkuśā, the Khecarī, and the Bījamudrā follow in sequence;
the Kumbhamudrā is for consecration, and the one called Prārthanā is for making requests.
(37) Those called Vāsudeva are declared by the experts in Tantra to be meditations known as Kālakarṇī, Kumbha, Nāda, Bindu, and Vismaya. (12)
The Karakacchapikā mudrā becomes the supreme Tattvamudrā; whichever mudrā is appropriate for a particular occasion, one should employ that one there. || 13 ||
And their defining characteristics are now stated according to the order of their enumeration. (14)
One should lift the left big toe and join it with the right big toe,
pressing its tip with the collection of fingers of the right hand.

One should press [the heart] with the fingers of the left hand while remaining composed; reciting the mantra, one should establish [it] in the heart—this is known as the practice called *bilva* for subduing Māra.
The wheel mudrā (cakramudrā) should be described for the rite of offering the oblation: having grasped the left thumb with the fist of the right hand. (17)
Then, having made a fist with the palm facing upward, one should extend the thumb;
likewise, the fingers of the left hand should be joined together and well-extended.
This mudrā, resembling a conch shell, has the left thumb joined with the right thumb;
the left little finger is then attached to the [left] lip. (19)
The little finger is joined with the right thumb and extended;
the index, middle, and ring fingers are slightly contracted and moved. || 20 ||
This shall be the Veṇu-mudrā, well-guarded and beloved of Hari; as for that which is called the Padma-mudrā, it shall be described again immediately hereafter.
With both hands joined like a garland, one should touch from the throat down to the feet using the index finger and the thumb; this is the Vanamālikā mudrā.

Having placed the two hands facing each other with the fingers interlaced, and then having the two middle fingers joined and extended outward— this is declared to be the *gadā-mudrā* (mace-gesture) of Viṣṇu, which increases his satisfaction.
With the index finger and thumb joined, one should place them at the front of the heart; this is the Jñānamudrā, and it should be described as a bow with an arrow.
One should join the middle and ring fingers of the two hands so that they touch each other, and fix them with the thumbs resting at the base of the little fingers.
One should form the two index fingers [in this manner]; this mudrā is named Śrīvatsa.
The little finger of the right hand is touched by and joined to the ring finger. (26)
Having bound the little finger with the other [hand],
one should likewise bind the left ring finger at the base of the right thumb with the right index finger.
Furthermore, having joined the thumb and middle finger together, the other four fingers should also be straight and their tips touching; this is the mudrā known as Kaustubha.
Having turned the two hands away from each other and interlaced the little fingers, the two index fingers are joined together,
and likewise the two thumbs are joined.
One should move the two middle and ring fingers like two wings; this is the Garuḍa-mudrā, which brings satisfaction to Viṣṇu. || 30 ||
Placing the thumbs at the crown of the head with both hands in fists, that mudrā becomes the Mohinī;
having placed the hands between the knees, the chin and lips are drawn together. || 31 ||
One should open the mouth wide and flick the tongue; this is the Nārasiṃhī mudrā, which increases his delight.
Placing the left hand above the right with the palm facing upward, the wise one should bend it downward;
this is declared to be the mudrā known as Vārāhī.
On the palm of the left hand, one should press down those fingers of the right hand with their tips facing downward; then, having raised the middle finger among them, one should bend it.
The mudrā called Hayagrīva imitates the form of that deity; it is formed by joining the two hands together with the fingers extended. (35)
With the two index fingers on the backs of the middle fingers and the two thumbs resting upon the middle fingers—
this is declared to be the Kāma-mudrā, which brings delight to all the gods.
Now, the characteristics of those dear to Mahādeva are described: one should raise the right thumb and encircle it with the left thumb.
Having bound that firmly with the fingers of his hands,
the skilled practitioner should bind the left fingers with the fingers of the right hand.
This is declared to be the Liṅgamudrā, which brings about the presence of Śiva; it is formed by joining the two little fingers together and crossing the two index fingers over the ring fingers.
With the ring fingers joined upwards and the middle fingers long and positioned below, one should place the tips of both thumbs [upon them]; this is declared to be the *yoni-mudrā*.
Having bound the little finger with the thumb and joined the three remaining fingers, one should extend them as a rosary; this is the mudrā for the granting of boons and fearlessness.
The five fingers of the right hand should be joined and raised upwards;
the left hand should be placed upon the left side of the body like a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) and bowl.
Then one should raise [the hands] as if to lift up; this becomes the Kāpālikī mudrā. Having formed a loose fist with the middle fingers slightly raised, [this is the mudrā]. (43)
Raising the right hand upward and moving it to the region of the ear—this is the ḍamaruka mudrā;
the mṛga mudrā is used in the fire-sacrifices (juhoti).
Having brought the two hands together facing each other,
with the fingers slightly bent and the thumbs joined at the palms, this is the Padma mudrā of Vivasvat.
Now, the characteristics of the mudrās of Gaṇeśa are being described: with the middle finger pointing upward and palm facing up, the fingers straight and the fist closed. (46)
The tooth-seal (dantamudrā) has been described by those proficient in all the scriptures:
