it is a fist from which the thumb emerges at the junction of the index and middle fingers.
The middle finger is turned downward and elongated; this is the mudrā of Vighna.
The index finger rests upon the left fist, and the index finger rests upon the right fist. 48.
Having joined the tips of the two thumbs, one should insert the tips of the two index fingers [into them];
this is the mudrā called Pāśa, as proclaimed by the learned. (49)
The mudrā called Aṅkuśā should be described for the consecration of the conch;
having joined the palms of both hands together obliquely, one should extend the fingers.
One should form [the hands] joined and then extended; this is the mudrā known as *parśu*.
As for the *laḍḍuka* and *bījapūra*, they have been omitted because they are well known.
Now the characteristics of the Śākteyī mudrās are being described;
the noose (pāśa) and the goad (aṅkuśa) have already been explained according to the rule.
The right hand placed below and extended forms the *vara-mudrā*;
the left hand raised and extended forms the *abhaya-mudrā*. || 53 ||

Having bound the little finger and the ring finger with their respective thumbs on the right side, while the remaining fingers are extended and pressed together, this is the sword mudrā (khaḍgamudrikā). (54)
One should join the tip of the middle finger of the left hand with the tip of the index finger; one should press the ring finger and the little finger with the left thumb. (55)
One should display it on the left shoulder; this is declared to be the bow-mudrā (dhanurmudrā).
The arrow-mudrā (bāṇamudrikā) consists of the index finger extended from the right fist.
Likewise, having turned the left hand sideways, one should extend it;
one should make the fingers contracted—this is declared to be the *carmamudrā*.
Having formed fists with both hands, placing the right over the left, one should perform the *mauśalī* [mudrā] at the head; when thus performed, it becomes the *daurgī*.
Having likewise formed the wheel mudrā and extended the two middle fingers, one should bring the two little fingers together and place the two thumbs at their tips. (59)
This supreme Lakṣmī-mudrā shall bring about all prosperity.
Having positioned the hands as if playing the lute (vīṇā), one should move them over the head;
this is declared to be the Vīṇā-mudrā, which brings delight to Sarasvatī.
With the tips of the right thumb and forefinger joined together, the other fingers extended, held close and turned upward— this is called the *vyākhyāna-mudrā*.
One should form the left fist facing oneself; this is the book mudrā.
Having placed both hands with fingers extended at the wrists, [one forms the following]. (62)
Joining the little fingers and thumbs together, one should extend [the remaining fingers] inward;
this is the mudrā called Saptajihvā, which is dear to Vaiśvānara.
We shall now briefly describe the mudrās of Tripurā: having placed the two middle fingers together, the two little fingers are covered by the thumbs. (64)
One should form the two index fingers like staffs, with the ring fingers placed upon the middle fingers; this is the first mudrā, which causes universal agitation. (65)
O Supreme Goddess, with the middle and index fingers, while the little and ring fingers are joined together in the form of a hook, they are placed in the center.
This is the Ākarṣiṇī mudrā, which effects the attraction of all things. O Supreme Goddess, when the two middle fingers of the first mudrā become straight, it is considered the Sarvavidrāviṇī. (67)
Having turned the two hands over, one should make the two thumbs touch and be level; having placed the two index fingers inside the ring fingers, they should be curved in shape. (68)
O Maheśvarī, one should employ the little finger in its own place; this is declared to be the "Three-Parted" (trikhaṇḍā) mudrā for the rite of summoning Tripurā.
Having placed both hands face-to-face, with the two ring fingers positioned between the middle fingers, the two index fingers should be straightened outside of them. (70)
Then, with the two thumbs shaped like staffs and positioned in the middle of the middle fingers—
this is declared to be the Unmādinī mudrā, which causes all women to become moist with passion.
Having made the two middle fingers curved and positioned above the index fingers, likewise place the ring fingers and the little fingers in the middle [of the palms].
Joining all [the fingers] together in one place and pressing them with the thumbs—this shall be the Yoni-mudrā, which brings satisfaction to Tripurā. || 73 ||

Having formed the hands in the shape of a casket, with the two index fingers curved like hooks, one should turn them back by the hand itself, while the two middle fingers are positioned below them. (74)
O Goddess, in that same sequence, having joined all the fingers starting from the little finger and the ring finger, they should be made firm at the tips of the thumbs. (75)
O Supreme Goddess, this mudrā is considered to cause all types of possession. For the Unmādinī [mudrā], one places the two ring fingers below in the shape of a goad.
One should also apply the two index fingers in that same sequence; this is the Great Hook (Mahāṅkuśā) mudrā, which accomplishes all desires and goals.
O Maheśānī, having placed the left arm on the right side and the right arm on the left side, one should rotate the two hands.
O Goddess, having joined the little fingers and the ring fingers according to that sequence, both middle fingers are likewise pressed down from above by the two index fingers. (79)
O Maheśānī, one should also make the two thumbs straight; this is that mudrā known by the name Khecarī, the most excellent of all. (80)
O Beloved, having turned the two hands over so that they are clearly in the shape of a half-moon, one should then simultaneously join the pair of index fingers with the pair of thumbs. (81)
One should place the two middle fingers pressed down below by the little fingers; likewise, the two ring fingers should be joined at the very bottom in a curved position.
This seed-mudrā is considered to bestow all accomplishments without delay;
it is formed by placing the two thumbs of both hands against each other.
One should form a fist with space between the fingers; that is the *kumbha-mudrā*.
With both hands facing each other, the fingers extended and joined together, one should place them at one's own heart; this is the *prārthana-mudrā* [formed] with the *añjali*.
And that [mudrā] called Vāsudeva is the meditation mudrā (dhyānamudrā). || 85 ||
Having raised the two thumbs while the two fists are joined together, one should turn those very same [thumbs] toward oneself for the protection of children's ears.
With the thumbs raised in both fists, one should place them at the tips of the index fingers;
this is proclaimed as the Kunta mudrā, which provides protection from all [dangers]. (87)
The right fist with the thumb raised is the Nāda-mudrā;
by joining the index finger and thumb together at the front is the Bindu-mudrā.
The right fist tightly closed with the index finger placed upon the ring finger is the mudrā known as Vismaya; it causes the manifestation of wonder.
The two hands, joined face-to-face and then placed obliquely with palms raised, should have the thumbs pressed together at the heart; this is the *kacchapikā* [mudrā]. (90)
If the thumb and ring finger are joined on the left hand in the leftward sequence,
this is declared to be the Tattvamudrā, which destroys great sins.
Listen now to what must be done and what must not be done by the one who performs the recitation:
while accomplishing the mantra, he should worship the deity at the three junctions of the day.
One should not recite the mantra alone at two sessions or even one session; rather, the Goddess should be brought into the mind, and the ritual action should be firmly established in the heart.

One should perform drinking and other acts of eating with food and water consecrated by the recitation of the Tattva-mantra; staying constantly in a single village, one should go and pay homage to one's own guru.

One should always perform prostrations in other directions and the salutation of deities; one should regularly perform both obligatory and occasional rites, and maintain association with the virtuous.
The skillful practitioner should bathe with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), or with pure water alone, or with clarified butter, curd, milk,
or sesame paste.

Likewise, in the ritual procedure for *puraścaraṇa*, one should perform bathing for the sake of purification; if capable, one should bathe at the three periods of the day (*triṣavaṇa*), and if incapable, twice or even once.
There is no fruit for one who does not bathe, nor for one who does not satiate the ancestors; the same applies to other rites performed for specific desires and to the company of the virtuous.

One should completely avoid speaking with women, Śūdras, outcasts, those who have fallen from their caste, atheists, or those who have consumed the remnants of food; one should also avoid speaking untruths and crooked speech.

One should not speak even the truth during the recitation of mantras, fire oblations, worship, and so forth; for if the practitioner speaks the truth at that time, his practice will be rendered futile.
Everything performed otherwise becomes entirely fruitless; therefore, one should always be free from desire for women and such through speech, mind, and action. (10)
One should renounce the sight of oil-massages, dancing, singing, and the like; one should also avoid the application of perfumes and the wearing of flowers. (11)
One should avoid sexual intercourse, as well as talk about it, social gatherings concerning it, remembering it, praising it, playing at it, looking at it, and speaking in secret about it. (12)
Intention, deliberation, action, and the completion of the act—thus has sexual intercourse been declared to be eightfold by those who know the Tantras. (13)
A wise man should not take anything from anyone, nor should he be frivolous; at that time, he should certainly not touch women or Śūdras who have not bathed. 14.
One who performs the *puraścaraṇa* rite with a seed-mantra should avoid bathing in hot water, eating food that has not been offered [to the deity], and should not commit injury to living beings. 15.
And one should duly perform the service of cows and other such duties as prescribed in the Kalpa.
Then, out of a desire for the welfare of practitioners, I shall describe what is edible and what is inedible at that time, according to various tantras. (1)
One should eat food fit for sacrifice, milk-rice, vegetables, curd-and-barley gruel, milk, roots, or fruits—whatever is available at that time and place. || 2 ||
Elsewhere as well, the characteristics of edible foods have been declared by the wise:
edible grains, sacrificial oblations, vegetables, milk, roots, and likewise fruits. (3)
The practitioner of the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) should consume either śaktuka or milk alone; likewise, winter rice, white rice steamed with sugar, mung beans, sesame seeds, and barley.
Kalāya, kaṅgu, nīvāra, vāstūka, hilamocikā, ṣaṣṭika, kālaśāka, radish (mūlaka), and kemuka other than that [specific variety]. || 5 ||
Kanda, rock salt, sea salt, curd, clarified butter, milk from which the cream has not been removed, jackfruit, mango, and harītakī; || 6 ||
Long pepper, cumin, orange, and tamarind;
plantain, lavalī, and dhātrī fruits, along with jaggery and sugarcane juice. (7)
Sages partake of sacrificial food (haviṣya) that has not been cooked in oil; among sacrificial foods, barley is considered primary, and rice is traditionally held to follow it.
One should avoid black gram, kodrava, white mustard, chickpeas, wild millet, lentils, wheat, and horse gram— even if all other grains are unavailable.

For those of noble birth, born into a virtuous lineage, who are illustrious, devoted to charity, pure, and possessed of a mind fixed on righteousness, the practice of begging for alms is appropriate. (10)
One should eat from the leaf of Brahmā, but one should avoid the middle leaf;
Dakṣa is on the leaf to the right of Brahmā, Viṣṇu is on the northern leaf, and Maheśvara is on the middle leaf. (1)

When it is possible, fire should not be taken from any source other than a hearth; however, if no such source is available, one may take it from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) even on a day that is not a festival.
In that case, one who is incapable [of fasting] should take food every day;
for if it is taken out of excessive attachment, success will certainly not be achieved.
The practitioner should eat food that is soft, lukewarm, and well-cooked; he should eat in such a way that there is no increase in the [power of the] senses.
Otherwise, from the fault of eating [such food], the loss of accomplishment arises; therefore, practitioners of mantra should always avoid any kind of defiled food whatsoever.
One should eat excellent food with the desire for the perfection of mantras;
for just as a tree grows from water, so do the senses grow from food.
Therefore, with every effort, a man should eat only the food prescribed by the preceptor; he should likewise avoid honey, meat, alkaline substances, salt, and oil.
Food that is steamed, stale, devoid of oil, or defiled by insects; as well as sour gruel, garlic, wood-apple, kalañja, and likewise garlic (repeated for emphasis).
Lentils, kodrava grain, black gram, eggplant, chickpeas and the like, betel-leaf, eating from a bell-metal vessel, and eating during the daytime; || 9 ||
One should avoid these and other such things at the time of recitation; otherwise, the practitioner does not attain success from his food.
The procedure for the rosary (japamālā) is now briefly described, along with its varieties and its fruits, out of a desire for the welfare of practitioners of mantra.
(47) That which is easily accomplished with little effort yet bestows many accomplishments—the very garland of letters—is first proclaimed for those who desire success. (12)
With the letters of the Mātṛkā, together with the Bindu, arranged in both direct and reverse order,
and with the Kṣameruka vowels along with the eight groups of consonants, one fashions a garland of syllables.
When the mantras consisting of individual syllables are recited, they grant swift accomplishment;
this is true even for hostile mantras of men, let alone other mantras. (14)

The letters *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *śa* are declared to be the initial sounds of the classes; regarding the composition of the letters of mantras, one should first utter the initial letter.
Then one should recite the mantra, for it is seen thus elsewhere; by performing the recitation with this [method], its accomplishment is not far off. || 16 ||

In this regard, while performing the counting of recitations (japa) with the fingers, one should count using all the fingers including the thumb; an action performed without the thumb shall be fruitless. || 17 ||
The little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger are considered the fourth;
three fingers should have three joints each, while the middle finger has only one joint.

One should avoid the two joints of the middle finger at the time of recitation; one should know this to be the "Meru," which was itself defiled by Brahmā. Starting from the middle of the ring finger, one proceeds in a clockwise sequence. (19)
One should recite [the mantra] over the ten joints up to the base of the index finger, or alternatively,
over the pair of middle joints of the middle and ring fingers.
Circumambulating Mount Meru, the wise one should count from the base joint of the ring finger up to the base joint of the middle finger.
One should not separate the fingers; one should slightly contract the palm. For if the fingers are separated, the recitation flows away through the gaps. (22)
Whatever is recited upon the tip of a finger, whatever is recited while leaping over Mount Meru, and whatever is recited at the joints of the fingers—all that becomes fruitless. (23)
If one should recite out of negligence, transgressing the rules for counting, the Rākṣasas will certainly seize it;
therefore, the wise person should count with certainty.

One should perform the daily recitation (japa) with the hands, but not the optional (kāmya) recitation, due to a lack of understanding; however, the practitioner should perform both the daily and the optional recitations using rosaries.
Because it is joined with the letters from *a* to *kṣa*, it is celebrated as the "garland of letters" (*akṣamālā*).
One should fashion a rosary for recitation using strings of beads numbering the same as those letters. (26)
Through rudrākṣas, there is the attainment of all desires; through conch shells, for the sake of attaining fame and wealth;
lotus seeds always bestow nourishment and fortune, and bring about the destruction of enemies. (27)
Garlands fashioned from pearls that grant long life to sons, as well as cattle, intellect, and an increase in grain, bestow great good fortune and abundant prosperity. (28)
Just as that [beads made of human bone], a crystal rosary likewise extends the accomplishment of mantra-perception, rites of pacification, rites of prosperity, and liberation. (29)
At the Sārasvata [tirtha], rubies, and likewise at Puṣkala and Dhana, a garland made of gold or silver bestows all desires.

A rosary made of *sārasvata* seeds brings eloquence; one made of sprouts brings subjugation; one made of *adhika-dhana* seeds brings the arrival of great wealth; and one made of materials ranging from *rudrākṣa* to *kuśa* grass destroys sin.
A garland fashioned from all of these would lead men to liberation;
for the purpose of eradication, garlands of horse teeth strung with children's hair are prescribed.
A garland fashioned from the lower tusks of wild asses, strung together with threads of human sinew, is considered a destroyer of enemies. (33)
A rosary for recitation should be made from the lower teeth of a preta;
it should be strung with hair from the body of the person against whom the rite is directed in the act of inciting hatred.

A rosary of *tulasī* is recommended for the worship of Viṣṇu; one made of elephant tusks for Gaṇeśvara; and one of *indrākṣa* seeds or red sandalwood is praised for the recitation of the *Tripurā* mantra. (35)
In the Mantra of Nīlasarasvatī, it should be known that [the rosary] is made of great conch shells;
thus, the counting of finger-joints for recitation is declared to be one.
With *putrañjīva* seeds it is tenfold; with conch shells, a hundredfold; with coral, a thousandfold;
and with pearls and rubies, it is traditionally held to be ten-thousandfold.
That same [arrangement] made with crystal is declared to be a *sphāṭika-lakṣa*; with pearls, it is called a *muktā-lakṣa*.
With gold, it is ten times that, and likewise with all [the aforementioned materials], it is a hundred times that.
With knots of *kuśa* grass and *rudrākṣa* beads, the merit becomes infinitely multiplied;
even with rosaries made of pure lotus seeds, the fruit shall be immeasurable. (39)

The fruit of that [mantra] is also obtained through the *mālā* consisting of the letters of the *mātṛkā*. Alternatively, one may perform it with hundreds [of repetitions] during a recitation common to all. (40)
With fifty-four [beads], there shall be the accomplishment of rites performed for specific desires;
with one hundred and eight beads made into a garland, the accomplishment of all things is said to occur. (41)
One seeking liberation should recite it twenty-five times; one seeking wealth, thirty times;
one seeking nourishment, twenty-seven times; and for malevolent rites, fifteen times.
In the Nāradīya [Purāṇa], however, it is declared that for no one are there fifteen [days];
therefore, between these two positions, there should be a settled option.

And this is the established rule here: that [the mantra] consisting of eight syllables belongs to Anasūya, or it belongs to Puruṣa, or else it is heard to belong to anyone at all; or rather, it should be applied by the practitioners according to their differing opinions.

Now, therefore, I shall describe the stringing of garlands as revealed in the Tantras. At the beginning of the rite, the practitioner himself should string the beads while observing a single meal. (45)
That which is prohibited by the passage beginning with "and [the garland] woven by oneself," is here intended as a flower garland together with sandalwood. (46)

Having performed his daily obligatory rites and being purified, the knower of mantras, having diligently gathered seeds as they are available and according to his desire among those mentioned, [should proceed]. (47)
They should be mutually similar in form, neither too thick nor too thin, free from defects such as insects, and indeed neither worn out nor brand new. (48)
Having washed those senses individually with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), [he should wear] a thread made by a virtuous Brahmin woman, triple-stranded and without knots. (49)

Having tripled that thread, one should wash it again according to the prescribed rule; [it should be] white, red, and likewise black for the rites of subjugation, pacification, and malevolent magic respectively.
The wise one should prepare a thread, or even a silk thread;
he should place fresh shoots of the Aśvattha tree in the form of lotuses.
One should place the thread and the gems into that [liquid] which has been washed with fragrant water;
then, one should [place] the *tāra*, the *śakti*, and the *mātṛkā* upon the threads and the gems.

Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa), one should worship with clarified butter and offer oblations according to one's capacity; if unable to perform the fire-oblation, one should perform a recitation (japa) twice the number of the intended oblations.
(p. 50) Thus some say; regarding this, we shall speak in the context of external worship:
"The wise man, taking each individual jewel, should indeed join it to the thread. (54)
Joining mouth to mouth and tail to tail, it should be made like a cow’s tail or auspiciously shaped like a serpent. (55)
One should place a single eye of the same kind as that [previous one] at the front as Mount Meru; moreover, one should fashion a Brahma-knot within each individual jewel.
Some mantra-experts tie a rosary while reciting the Gāyatrī;
the description of the Gāyatrī mantra occurs during the fashioning of the Brahma-knot.
Their intention here is generally this: how [the mantra] is to be sublated; having thus arranged the rosary, for the sake of its excellence, [one should perform the recitation]. (58)
They should perform the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) as prescribed by the injunctions and taught in their proper sequence;
one should wash [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) using the Sadyojāta mantra and pure water.
One should rub it with sandalwood, agallochum, perfumes, and so forth, using the Vāmadeva mantra; one should fumigate it with the Aghora mantra and satisfy it with the Puruṣa mantra.
One should consecrate each [element] one hundred times with the mantra of Īśa; then, one should consecrate Sumeru with the fifth mantra.

Having thus consecrated the rosary, the wise one should then establish its vital breaths; having prepared the rosary in this manner, the intelligent practitioner should perform recitation with the Mātṛkā mantra.
All mantras were born from the various letters of the Mātṛkā;
therefore, the recitation of all mantras should be performed with this rosary.
Having worshipped the Guru, one should receive it from him for the sake of all prosperity; one who is impure should not touch it, nor should one allow it to fall from the hand.
One should move the rosary resting on the thumb from the tip of the middle finger; it should not be touched by the index finger—this is the sequence of counting that bestows liberation.
The wise man should mutter [the mantra] with the middle fingers during eating, liberation, and drawing;
however, for the highest rite, he should mutter it with the thumb and the ring finger.
Having worshipped this rosary during the time of recitation, one should keep it secret; one should keep one's mantra secret, and one should keep one's guru secret.
One should conceal the rosary and one should conceal one's own seal-ring; the wise man should reveal the Guru, but never reveal the mantra. (68)
One should not show the rosary or the mudrā even to one's guru.
[For otherwise] spirits, rākṣasas, vetālas, siddhas, gandharvas, and cāraṇas [would appear]. (69)
Since they carry [the mantra] away openly, therefore the wise person should recite it in secret;
he should employ a firm thread so that the recitation does not break.
Just as a garland falls from the hand of one who is chanting, so should he act;
if it falls from the hand, there will be an obstacle, and if it is broken, death is certain. (71)
When the thread has worn out, one should string a new thread and recite the mantra one hundred times;
if it falls from the hand through negligence, one should recite it one hundred and eight times.
In the case of contact with that which is forbidden, one should wash [the area] as previously described;
here, the recitation of the Mātṛkā-mantra for a count of one hundred or more is prescribed.

By virtue of the context, because it is this very recitation (*japa*) alone that is taught everywhere, and because it sublates any contrary [view], the author of the *Candrikā* treats it as established. Illustrating this point in his commentaries on the *Candrikā*, he declares:
"Having thus described the rosary (*japamālā*), I shall now state the definition of recitation (*japa*). Recitation.
There may be a repetition of syllables, and that is said to be of three kinds. || 1 ||
It is remembered as being threefold: vocal, whispered, and mental; among these three types of recitation-sacrifices, each subsequent one is superior to the preceding.
When one recites the mantra clearly with syllables possessing distinct sounds and characterized by high, low, and circumflex accents, that is known as vocal recitation (vācika-japa). || 3 ||
One should recite the mantra slowly, moving the lips slightly;
when it is audible to some extent, that is known as the whispered (upāṃśu) recitation. || 4 ||

When one recites a mantra with the mind alone, that is known as mental (mānasa) japa. Loud recitation (uccairjapa) is considered inferior; whispered recitation (upāṃśu) is ten times more effective than the former.
The mental [recitation] is said to yield a thousandfold; they declare these to be its fruits: the verbal for killing, and the whispered for one desiring nourishment.

For one desiring spiritual perfection, mental recitation is declared to be the most excellent; recitation performed at home is said to be equal [to the former], while that performed in a cow-pen is remembered as being ten times more effective.
In a meritorious forest or a grove, it is said to be a thousandfold; on a sacred mountain it is ten thousandfold, and by a river it is declared to be a hundred thousandfold.
They say that ten million (koṭi) is infinite when in the presence of Śiva in his temple; compared to the uncountable, the countable is said to be a thousandfold greater.

Even if performed a thousand times more than the prescribed number, a recitation (japa) made while adorned with the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), having placed the deity within one's heart and having made the heart steady, [is most efficacious].
Having bowed to Śiva and the others, as well as to the Guru, one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind— very slowly, indistinctly, neither too fast nor too slow.
Day after day, one should not perform the recitation with fewer or more [verses] than prescribed;
this is declared to be the rule for uninterrupted practice, and one should not let a single day pass by.
If a day passes [without practice], their attainment of success is obstructed. One should be devoted to celibacy, peaceful, and refrain from censuring others. (13)
Remaining in perfect silence amidst idle talk, eating sacrificial food only once a day, with a mind focused on nothing else,
from the morning until midday.
Free from defects such as anger and with undistracted mind, one should recite the mantra; for recitation is said to be the supreme dharma among all ritual acts. (15)
For through non-violence toward all beings, the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) proceeds; yet one who is angry, deluded, in haste, lying down, or without a seat [is not fit for it]. (16)
Or one whose feet are covered by shoes on a road or a dusty place; or one wearing a turban, or wearing a bodice, or with hair disheveled, or with the neck wrapped [in a cloth]. (17)

One whose hands are not purified, who is impure, or who is prattling, should not recite the mantra; nor should one do so while seated on a vehicle or a bed, or while walking, or while standing up. (18)
A wise person should not recite the mantra with his hands uncovered, nor even if his head is covered, nor with a mind distracted by anxiety. (19)
Neither speaking, nor walking, nor thinking of any other refuge;
with a mind not distracted by yawning, hiccups, or similar disturbances. (20)
One attains the perfection of mantras; therefore, one should be intent upon effort. Being pure, one should arrange for one's own bed upon a couch of darbha grass.
One should wash that garment daily; otherwise, it may bring about obstacles.
One should not wear the garment upside down, inside out, or with its parts reversed.

Due to the occurrence of perversion, there may be a lack of certainty in some cases; therefore, one should avoid such a person with great effort during the performance of the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa).
The practitioner of ritual action should avoid that which causes excessive strain; he should not recite while stretching out his feet or while sitting in the utkaṭāsana posture.
One should not recite the mantra while wearing only a single garment, nor while distracted by many clothes; one should avoid such things and others as well during the time of recitation. (25)

Upon seeing, speaking with, or hearing those who have fallen from their caste or those born of the lowest castes, or upon hearing the sound of passing wind or yawning, one should abandon the recitation of prayers. (26)

Having risen and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with its six ancillaries upon reaching that [place], and then properly recite the remainder; or else, one may simply behold the sun and other such objects.

If the practitioner of mantra, while performing the recitation of mantra, sees something impure, he should perform one breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and then complete the remainder of the recitation; this is stated in the venerable Nāradīya regarding the procedure for the eight-syllabled mantra.

Now, the procedure for the pacification of defects such as "cutting" (chinna) and so forth is stated; likewise, those defects beginning with "cutting," which obstruct spiritual attainment, are described. (1)
Since the defect must first be abandoned, its definition is stated:
that mantra whose beginning, middle, and end contain the seed-syllable of Vāyu (ya) is so described. (2)
Whether conjoined or disjoined, it is again threefold when occupied by its own vowel; furthermore, it is fourfold or fivefold, and thus the mantra is designated as "cut" (chinna). || 3 ||
That mantra which is marked by the pair of seed-syllables of the Earth (la-la) at its beginning, middle, and end is known as "obstructed" (ruddha);
it is devoid of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 4 ||

Alternatively, a mantra that lacks the three principles of Māyā, or one whose seed-syllable (bīja) and Rāva (vowel) are missing, is said to be "devoid of power" (śaktihīna) if it does not possess [the letter] in its middle.
The seed-syllable of desire (KĀM) at the mouth, Māyā (HRĪṂ) at the head, or likewise the goad (AṄKUŚA); this is declared to be the "Parāṅmukha" [mantra], joined with the letter HA as its seed.

If the moon (the letter *i*) does not exist at the beginning, end, or middle, it is traditionally said to be deaf. A mantra that consists of five syllables but is devoid of the letter *ra*, the sun (*r*), and the moon (*i*) [is likewise defective].
One should know that [a mantra] devoid of the *netra* (the eye) bestows suffering, grief, and disease;
likewise, the *haṃsa*, *prāsāda*, and *vāgurī* [mantras] are [ineffective] at the beginning, middle, and end [respectively].

The syllable *ha* accompanied by the *bindu*, the *jīva* (the vowel *i*), and likewise the *vāra* (the consonant *va*) consisting of four *kalās*; followed by *māyā* (*ī*) and the word "I bow" (*namāmi*); that in which there is no [other] syllable is the *kīlita*. || 9 ||
That mantra in which there is one [letter] in the middle and two at the head, but neither the weapon (astra) nor Purandara (Indra), is paralyzed and obstructs the attainment of success.
If fire conjoined with wind is seen seven times at the head of a mantra,
the knower of mantras should consider that mantra to be burnt.
The *astra* [mantra] is seen with two, three, six, or eight syllables; it is called "sloping" (*srasta*) when the *praṇava* (Oṃ) is situated at its beginning. (12)
It is proclaimed as Śiva, or Śakti, or that which is called Bhīta;
there shall be four syllables at the beginning, middle, and end.
One whose mantra is impure should avoid that which possesses the knowledge of mantra; [such a mantra] has either the letter *da* in its middle or the letter *krodha* (*ha*) twice at its head.

The weapon-mantra remains suppressed when it is uttered [without its components]; [the seed-syllables] "bhyaḥ" and "dvayam" are in the heart and the head, while "vaṣaṭ" and "vauṣaṭ" are in the middle.

That mantra which has been thus split must be abandoned by the wise in the pursuit of accomplishments (siddhis). That which consists of three syllables and is devoid of the *haṃsa* is declared to be "deep sleep" (*suṣupta*). || 16 ||
Alternatively, a mantra or a vidyā consisting of seventeen syllables, beginning with five *phaṭ* syllables, is declared to be "Madonmatta" (Intoxicated with Pride). || 17 ||
He whose mantra has that weapon situated in its middle is said to be "fainted" (mūrchita);
he whose mantra is situated in a place of pause (virāma) is called "deprived of potency" (hṛtavīrya). || 18 ||
A mantra that possesses four *asras* at the beginning, the middle, and likewise at the head, and which consists of eighteen syllables, should be known as "deficient. (19)
A mantra of nineteen syllables that is joined with the *tāra* (om), enriched by the seed-syllables of *hṛllekhā* and *aṅkuśa*, is declared to be "asleep. (20)
A mantra of seven syllables is a child; one of eight syllables is a youth; a sixteen-syllable mantra is a young adult;
and a mantra of forty syllables is a mature man.
A mantra of thirty syllables, sixty-four syllables,
one hundred syllables, or even four hundred syllables is designated as "vṛddha" (the aged).
The nine-syllable mantra joined with the *dhruva* is declared to be the *niścitraśas*. At its conclusion is the *hṛdaya*, and the two *śiras* mantras are in the middle.
The *śikhā* and *varma* [mantras] should end with *vauṣaṭ* or *phaṭ*;
or, if they are devoid of the syllables of Śiva and Śakti, that is known as "seedless" (*nirbīja*). || 24 ||
In these instances, if the syllable *phaṭ* is seen six times, that mantra will be devoid of success; such a mantra of ten syllables is considered weak.

p. 57) A *kūṭa* is a single-syllable mantra; it alone is said to be partless (*niraṃśaka*). A two-syllable [mantra] is devoid of power (*śaktihīna*), while a four-syllable one is "squint-eyed" (*kekara*). || 26 ||
A six-syllabled mantra that lacks a seed-syllable (*bīja*) is unbound; a seven-syllabled mantra, or one of twelve and a half syllables, is "smoky" (*dhūmita*) and is therefore censured.

Likewise, there is that which consists of three and a half seeds, that which has twenty-one syllables, that which has twenty syllables, and that which has thirty syllables; this is what is called "embraced" (āliṅgita).
The mantra of thirty-two syllables is proclaimed as the deluding one (mohita);
that which consists of twenty-four letters and that which consists of twenty-seven letters [are also mentioned]. || 29 ||
He who is afflicted by hunger should be known as the twenty-fourth color;
or else, the one consisting of eleven syllables is the twenty-fifth in number. || 30 ||
A mantra of twenty-three syllables is declared to be "proud" (dṛpta);
likewise, those of twenty-six syllables and thirty-six syllables are so described.
That which has twenty-nine syllables, or even lacks a limb [one syllable], is called "deficient in limbs" (aṅgahīna).
That which has twenty-eight syllables, or even thirty-one, [is likewise so designated]. || 32 ||
Being exceedingly enraged, he was addressed and censured in all his activities. [The mantra consists of] thirty syllables, or even thirty-three. (33)
He is declared to be exceedingly cruel and censured in all ritual acts; [this applies] from forty until sixty-three [years of age]. || 34 ||
Mantras of that same number are declared to be named "with shame" (savrīḍa);
those mantras which consist of sixty-five syllables are "tranquil-minded" (śāntamānasa).
Those mantras which consist of from sixty-five syllables up to ninety-nine are declared by the wise to be called "displaced" (sthānabhraṣṭa).
Those mantras that consist of thirteen syllables or fifteen syllables are called "deficient," as are those consisting of one hundred or one hundred and fifty.
Those who are devoid of affection are said to number two hundred and ninety-two, or one less than that, or three hundred. (38)
Starting from four hundred and extending up to one thousand syllables, that which is excessively long should always be avoided by the wise in sacrificial rites.
Mantras exceeding one thousand [syllables] are considered *daṇḍakas* when compressed;
mantras exceeding two thousand [syllables] are considered to be divided into a hundred fragments. (40)

Those mantras should be understood as being in the form of hymns, and they are likewise considered to be so; similarly, the vidyās should be comprehended by practitioners of mantra in all ritual acts. (41)
By means of the Bandha, one should remove the defects of the Yonimudrā, such as its being severed and so forth;
therefore, it is indeed necessary here, as is clearly stated in the Śāradātilaka and other texts.
The person who resorts to a mantra without recognizing these defects will not achieve success even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
One should apply those mantras, which are corrupted by such defects as these, to oneself;
one should purify them by means of the upward-moving breath (ūrdhvapavana) while holding the yonimudrā.
Alternatively, for the sake of purifying defects, one should perform this method: in all [practices] such as mantras, the *hṛllekhā* is the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*). (45)
Alternatively, having inserted the seed-syllable of Śrī, one should recite the mantra for purification;
or else, even a wicked mantra becomes effective when encased by the Tāra (Oṃ).
Now I shall describe the unsurpassed practice of binding the *yonimudrā*; having first conquered one's own enemies, such as desire and the like, one should practice yoga. (47)
They say that desire and anger, greed and delusion, as well as pride and envy—these are the six internal enemies of the self that bestow suffering. (48)
Having conquered these through the eight limbs of yoga, yogins shall attain yoga:
namely, restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), and thereafter—
Withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation, along with meditative absorption—
these they call the eight limbs for the yogi in the practice of yoga.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, straightforwardness, forbearance, fortitude, moderation in diet, and purity—these are the ten restraints (yamas). || 51 ||
Austerity, contentment, faith, charity, worship of the deity, listening to the established doctrines, modesty, intelligence, recitation of mantras, and the observance of vows. (52)
These ten restraints (niyamas) have been proclaimed by those expert in the Yoga scriptures, for the purpose of [controlling] the senses as they roam without restraint among their objects. 53.
The withdrawal from them is prescribed as a forceful extraction [of the breath] at the thumbs, the ankles, the knees, the thighs, the perineum, the genitals, and the navel. (54)
In the regions of the heart, neck, and throat, then in the uvula, in the nose, between the eyebrows, on the forehead,
at the crown of the head, and at the dvādaśānta, according to the prescribed rule.
The retention of the vital breath is called *dhāraṇā*, performed with a concentrated mind abiding within consciousness. (56)
Meditation here is said to be the contemplation of one's chosen deity within oneself, and the constant cultivation of equanimity between the deity, the individual self, and the supreme self. (57)
The sages have declared that samādhi is characterized by eight limbs for one who is moderate in food and recreation, and disciplined in his activities. (58)
For one who has mastered sleep and awakening, yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering; having commenced breath control (prāṇāyāma), his internal channels become purified. (59)
On the seat, the practitioner should place the heel of the right foot; likewise, he should place the left heel upon the anus and the penis. (60)
One who is composed should withdraw the senses from their objects; with body, head, and neck held straight, following the sequence of the crow’s beak.
Having restrained the breath of the world, one should fill the belly; then, with the two thumbs, one should press the ears, and with the two index fingers, the eyes. (62)
Having moderately blocked one's own nostrils with the two middle fingers and the mouth with the remaining fingers, one should restrain one's own mind. (63)
Having stabilized [the breath] at the mūlādhāra, just as a horse repeatedly contracts its anus while abandoning excrement along the path of the rectum; (64)
Then, one should contract this [anus] with the fingers joined at the base; repeatedly, by uttering the syllable *hūṃ*, one should expel the wind from the rectum.
As he practices gradually, Suṣumnā opens its mouth; the vital air enters there, pierces the knot, and [opens] the lotus of the navel. (66)
When it has entered therein, one makes its opening face upwards;
then an internal upward sound arises, which gradually takes on the resonance of thunderclouds, and by that it is awakened.
Then, from the end of the womb where Kuṇḍalinī is deeply asleep, one perceives Smara, who is wandering, radiant like a blooming bandhujīva flower. (68)
Having meditated upon the nature of Śiva, one should contemplate him in the form of a swan;
then the yogi [should contemplate] Kuṇḍalinī, having unified the self with her. (69)
Having fashioned her as endowed with the power of consciousness (citkalā) and accompanied by the Haṃsa, one should lead her upward through the variegated channel to the thousand-petaled lotus.
Having pierced the six wheels and the three signs individually, and having gone there,
one shall attain union with Śiva residing in that pericarp.
From the moon situated in the place called the upper creation of the thousand-spoked [lotus],
she causes a stream of red nectar consisting of mantra to descend.
Having drunk [the nectar], those deities of the six cakras return by that very same path and, being gratified, return to their own abodes. || 73 ||
Thus, repeatedly practicing this coming and going,
the yogi shall remove defects such as those beginning with "cutting" by means of the procedure for the recitation of mantras.
One who practices this yoga with a concentrated mind day after day, having conquered misfortunes, diseases, and the like,
shall live for a long time as one whose nature is that of Smara.
Observing silence and with dark hair, one should accomplish all mantras; within the space between the anus and the penis is the lotus of Brahmā, adorned with petals.
Yogis call this the mūlādhāra, adorned with four bindus resembling gold and ending in the sound 'va'. (77)
At the base of the banner, the station of Śiva known as Svādhiṣṭhāna is joined with the letters beginning with *ba* and ending with *la*, accompanied by bindus, and possessing six petals. (78)
The Maṇipūraka, located at the navel, is endowed with ten petals consisting of ten syllables beginning with 'Ḍa' and accompanied by bindus, which resemble blue collyrium. (79)
In her heart [is the lotus] with the luster of an indragopa insect, twilight clouds, and vermilion;
it is adorned with petals numbering twelve, decorated with the letters beginning with 'ka'.
The wise call this "unstruck" (anāhata) the lotus of the teeth; the lotus known as Viśuddha, however, is located in the throat and is endowed with the luster of bees.
The abode of the Blessed Lady is endowed with sixteen petals and the vowels; it is the lotus of the heart of the Command, shining like the rays of the autumnal moon. (82)
Between the eyebrows is the Dvidala [lotus], adorned with the two final letters of the alphabet and the Moon;
this is declared as the six-chakra system by those proficient in the Yoga scriptures. (83)
Brahmā, Śiva, Gadāpāṇi, Haṃsa, Bhagavatī, and Bindu—these six are proclaimed here as the lords of the wheels (cakreśas) in their respective order. || 84 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—these lords of the wheels (cakreśas) are declared in some places to be, in order, the Bindu. || 85 ||
Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, Kākinī, as well as Śākinī and Hākinī—these are, in order, the deities of the six cakras. (86)
By Svayambhū himself, the Liṅga was established within the interior of the womb;
the two-fold Liṅga is in the heart, and the other is in the intermediate space.
Beneath the creation is a thousand-petaled lotus with red filaments, stainless,
flashing with rays, and possessing three peaks like the moon.
They know that within the space between the guḍa and the dhvaja, there is a liṅga two aṅgulas in height;
it is encircled by a circular form twice its width.
The channels (nāḍīs) that arise therein are proclaimed to be primarily three: the channel Iḍā occupies the left portion of the body, while [Piṅgalā] occupies the right.
Then, Piṅgalā is situated within the body, resting against the spinal column; Suṣumnā reaches the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), and Citrā is the channel between them.
Blazing with five colors, subtle, and joined by the five deities—Brahmā, Janārdana, Rudra, Śiva, and Sādākhya. (92)
The presiding deities of the five elements reside within the channel called Citrā; in the center of the kanda is a triangle, the womb (yoni) of crimson luster.
Like the flash of a lightning bolt from ten million rising suns, the lustre of desire is flickering; therein, its exhaustion should be contemplated as resembling a flash of lightning. (94)
Above, there is a power (śakti) with an exceedingly subtle luster, shaped like the flame of a lamp;
vibrating in the midst of that, it is the very nature of Śiva and Śakti. 95.
Resplendent like ten million suns, the all-pervading one consists of all the gods;
she has the form of a sleeping serpent, her face turning in the whorl of a conch shell. (96)
The auspicious Kuṇḍalinī, encircling the Suṣumnā, is to be meditated upon;
thus is the binding of the Yonimudrā proclaimed. 97.

The ten mantra-purifications are described according to the *Śāradātilaka*: first, birth (*janana*), then life-giving (*jīvana*), followed by striking (*tāḍana*), and likewise awakening (*bodhana*). || 1 ||

Now, consecration (abhiṣeka), purification (vimalīkaraṇa), nourishment (āpyāyana), as well as satiation (tarpaṇa), illumination (dīpana), and concealment (gupti)— these ten are the purificatory rites for mantras.
Having drawn [the diagram] with sandalwood paste and other substances upon a vessel made of gold or similar materials,
the practitioner of mantra should write the letters of the Mātṛkā in their proper order using a golden stylus.
Then, having extracted the syllables [of the mantra], one should write the desired mantra;
having encapsulated it with the remaining letters of the Mātṛkā, one should recite it.

This is declared by those who follow the tradition to be "generation" (janana). Having placed the syllables of the mantra with the *praṇava* (oṃ) interspersed between them, the wise one should perform the recitation (*japa*). || 5 ||
Those proficient in the science of mantras call this "living" (jīvana); having written the syllables of the mantra, one should strike them with sandalwood water.

The practitioner of mantra should strike each [syllable] with the wind-mantra; that is declared to be "striking" (tāḍana). Having written out the letters of the mantra, [one should strike them] with flowers born of the karavīra plant.
One should strike [the mantra] with a number equal to the syllables of that mantra; by that, awakening occurs.
For the sake of purification, one should sprinkle the mantra with leaves of the *aśvattha* tree.
Having intentionally meditated upon the mantra at its root as consisting of the threefold energy, one should then,
through the upward-moving breath and the light arising therefrom, employ the *yonibandha* [mudrā].
The practitioner of mantra should burn away the threefold impurity within the mantra by means of the Vācyajyotis-mantra situated in the heart-lotus;
this indeed is the purification.

The mantra consisting of the syllable *tāram*, followed by *vyoma* (ha), *agnimanu* (ra), *yug* (ya), *dantī* (la), and *jyotiḥ* (sa), is prescribed; with this mantra, one should perform a sprinkling over each syllable using water infused with *kuśa* grass.
This nourishment is considered to be performed according to the rule with that mantra; or, in the Tantra system, the libation is considered to be performed with water and the mantra. (12)
The conjunction of *tāra*, *māyā*, and *ramā* is called the "illumination" (*dīpana*) of the mantra; the "concealment" (*gopana*) of the mantra being recited is its non-disclosure. (13)
Thus, ten consecrations (saṃskāra) of the mantra have been declared, which bestow accomplishment;
by performing these according to the rule, the practitioner of mantra attains the fruit as described. (14)

Now, the procedure for the placement of weapons (astranyāsa) as taught in the Śaiva Āgamas and other sources is described: one should display the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) with the left hand and place the gesture of boon-granting (vara) on the right.
One should properly place a quiver upon the back of the deity, as well as rice, fresh butter, a vessel of curd, and molasses.
One should place the rosary, the deer, and the axe in the right [hands]; and the parrot, the lute, the serpent, the fan, and the water-pot [in the left]. (3)
Likewise, one should place the threatening gesture (tarjanī) on the left and the seat (āsana) on the right; one should apply the Veda, the bird, and the mudrā on the right side.

In the same manner, one should place the conch and the discus; on both [hands] as well, the kusha grass and the lotus. On the two left [hands], one should visualize the noose, the book, and the vessel.
One should offer a skull-cup to the left and a rosary to the right; likewise, one should offer a spear, a fruit, a sword, a trident, and a hand-drum to the right.
One should place a forest garland, a vessel for liquor, a goad, and an arrow;
likewise, a bow and arrow on both [hands], as well as a bracelet, a ring, and a mace.
Having placed the whip on the left, as well as the shield and the chain,
one should likewise offer the vessel of honor (arghapātra) and a handful of flowers to both.
One should give ornaments for both [deities] and a garment described as variegated; or a white one for all the gods, and a yellow one is prescribed for Viṣṇu.

Śaṃ, Gopīśa, Paṃ, Gaṃ, Śa, Pa, Caṃ, Gaṃ, Śa, Go, Pa, Caṃ, Śa, Pa, Caṃ, Gaṃ, Ga, Paṃ, Śaṃ, and Ca; these six, beginning with the conch (śaṅkha), are arranged clockwise. Ke, Ma, Saṃ, Dā, Rā, Mā, Pra, Dyū, Vibhā, Ni, Purva, Dho, Janāḥ, Go, Tri, Śrī, Hṛ.
Nṛsiṃha, Acyuta, Nāga, Peḍhāla, Kṛkara—in this order. || 11 ||
Now, the procedure for recitation as taught in the sequence is undertaken, by which even an unfortunate embodied being may swiftly attain accomplishment. (1)

The omniscient one should perform the formal acquisition of the ground and its measurement for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) of such-and-such a person belonging to such-and-such a lineage. || 2 ||
"May this ground be accepted by her; may my mantra be successful"—thus [he should think], even if the mandala is irregular, extending for a *krośa* or even a *gavyūti*.

In the case of rivers, mountains, trees, and so forth, as well as in measurements down to the tip of a fingernail, there is a standard for the ground upon which the preliminary rites (puraścaryā) are performed;
however, in some instances, no such measurement exists at all.
Regarding this, the author of the *Candrikā* says: "In accordance with various mantras, a site measuring one *krośa* or even two *krośas* [should be chosen] within a village. (5)
For the purpose of moving about during the day and night, one should traverse that much ground, having made each step the measure of a span (vitasti), or perhaps even more.
The mantra-practitioner [should take] stakes produced from milk-trees,
consecrated with weapon-mantras, and having worshipped the Weapon [deity] within them with the fivefold offerings.
One should bury those eight in all directions and extract them from the center; when the field is thus pinned down by the mantra-practitioner, he is not overcome by obstacles.
Then, having duly worshipped Kṣetrapāla along with his own retinue, [one should offer] the milky trees— the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Nyagrodha.

One should offer the bali-oblation to the lords of the directions, and thereafter take recourse to the sacred field (kṣetra). Having taken recourse to the place of recitation, one should contemplate the tortoise-diagram (kūrmacakra).

Having made that [diagram] circular with nine compartments, one should draw it in the shape of a tortoise; likewise, one should write the consonant groups beginning with 'ka' in the northeast and the syllable 'la' in the central compartment.

(67) One should know that the face of the deity resides in whichever square the first letter of the field’s name is situated, following the sequence of the vowels as they occupy the eight directions starting from the east.
The two hands are located on both sides, and the two flanks are in the [adjacent] squares.
Both hands are the two [arms], and what remains is said to be the tail. || 13 ||
Situated in the mouth, one attains success; situated in the hand, one has a short life; situated in the belly, one is indifferent; and situated at the side, one encounters suffering. 14.
The practitioner situated in the tail is afflicted by imprisonment, eradication, and other such calamities;
this is declared to be the Kūrma-cakra, the means for attaining success for practitioners of mantra. || 15 ||
Relying upon its mouth, one should perform recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites, whether in a village or in a forest, or wherever one may look. 16.
One who desires the fulfillment of all wishes should perform the recitation (japa) at the location of the lamp.
He who performs recitation and fire-offerings (homa) without knowing the tortoise-diagram (kūrmacakra) [will find his efforts fruitless]. || 17 ||
For such a person, there is no fruit from recitation; it leads to all manner of misfortune. Having first performed the purification of the body, one should practice eating only once a day.
Then, having bathed in the morning, one should mutter the Gāyatrī mantra for a long time according to one's capacity;
or else, one should perform the gift of gold and other such acts that grant all desires. || 19 ||
First, for the sake of destroying both known and unknown sins, one should then properly satisfy Brahmins with food and clothing. (20)
Afterwards, preceded by his permission. || 21 ||
Even previously, there would have been no contradiction in seeking permission from the guru; in the absence of one's own guru, one should perform it mentally.
Alternatively, one may imagine some person connected with one's guru as being the guru; on that day, one should observe a single meal consisting of sacrificial food (haviṣya).
Then, having risen at dawn during the Brahma-muhūrta,
the wise and illustrious one, having performed his necessary duties, sat down upon an auspicious seat.
In the lotus situated at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), resplendent with a thousand petals, he beholds the venerable Guru,
the Supreme Self, whose hands are graced by the gesture of exposition (vyākhyāmudrā).
One should meditate upon [the deity] who has two eyes, two arms, is joyful, and bestows all accomplishments. Having meditated thus, by means of the stream of nectar flowing from his feet, (26)
The one of steady intellect, having contemplated his own body as washed clean as the deity,
and having meditated upon it within his own heart, should then contemplate his own body [as the deity].
Having bowed to the God, who is pervaded by a mass of that splendor, the wise one should subsequently place the seers and so forth at His command,
while recollecting the meaning of the mantra.
Having gone to the sacred bathing place (tīrtha) by the path arising from his own branch [of the lineage], he should perform his bath;
thereafter, with due care, preceded by the ritual placement (nyāsa) of his own mantra’s ṛṣi and other elements.

Having meditated upon one's chosen deity and invoked the sacred water (tīrtha) with the goad-mudrā (aṅkuśamudrā), one should render that water nectar-like by means of the cow-mudrā (dhenusaṃjñāmudrā).

One should indeed protect that [water] with the arrow [mantra] using the seed-syllable of nectar, *vaṃ*. Having meditated upon the form of the deity within that water, [one should offer it] from what flows from its feet (the *sruva* ladle).

Having immersed himself three times at the sacred ford while reciting the mantra mentally, and having performed the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite, the wise practitioner should then rise, sip water for purification (*ācamana*), put on two garments, and subsequently perform the rituals such as the twilight devotions (*sandhyā*).
Having completed this according to one's own branch [of the Veda], preceded by the nyāsa of the ṛṣis and so forth, one should then mutter the root mantra twenty-eight times.
The officiant should satisfy [the deity] for that long according to the prescribed method; likewise, he should consecrate [the disciple] three times on the head with the jar-mudrā.
One should recite the Gāyatrī of each respective deity ten times; at the end of the word "Kāma," O Goddess Tripurā, one should utter the word "vidmahe."
One should then say "Kāmeśvari," and after that, say "dhīmahi.
Then, having uttered "tanno," one should say "klinne pracodayāt. (36)
This Gāyatrī of Tripurā, which bestows all accomplishments, has been proclaimed;
one should utter the word "trailokyamohanāya" followed by "vidmahe. (37)
"Let us meditate upon Smara; may Viṣṇu then impel that for us. This Gāyatrī of Śrī Hari is said to bestow all desired objects. (38)
"Let us know the son of Daśaratha; let us meditate upon the beloved of Sītā;
may that Rāma inspire us"—having spoken thus at the end, one should say. (39)
This *gāyatrī* of Rāma has been declared, which bestows all accomplishments:
"We know Kāmadeva; we meditate upon him whose arrows are flowers. (40)
Having uttered this, one should thereafter say "Then Anaṅga, may he impel. This Gāyatrī of Kāmadeva is said to bestow all accomplishments.
Let us know that Tatpuruṣa; let us meditate upon Vāmadeva;
may Rudra impel us from that. || 42 ||
The Gāyatrī of Śaṅkara is proclaimed as the bestower of all goals: "We know Sudarśana; we meditate upon Mahājvāla. (43)
Having recited this, the wise one should say: "May that Discus impel us. This Gāyatrī of Sudarśana is said to bestow all prosperity. (44)
"Let us know Caṇḍaghaṇṭa; let us meditate upon Caṇḍeśvara; having spoken thus, one should then recite: 'May Caṇḍa inspire us. (45)
And this Gāyatrī of Caṇḍeśa is considered to bestow all accomplishments: "We know the one with six flames;
we meditate upon the maker of day. (46)
Then the wise one should recite: "Tat naḥ sūryaḥ pracodayāt. This Gāyatrī of Sūrya is declared to be the bestower of all accomplishments. (47)
If the Gāyatrī is not found for a particular mantra in the ritual manual (kalpa), one should construct that Gāyatrī using the name of the deity of that mantra. || 48 ||
The minister recites the Gāyatrī mantra as an illustration here: "Oṃ ghṛṇi sūrya āditya" (eight syllables), and [the name] "Bhānave. (49)
Having offered the *argha* and sipped water consecrated ten times with the root mantra,
one should bow to the lords of the directions and then perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).

One who desires success in this mantra should then perform recitation for this many times; thereafter, the fire-oblation (havana) shall be one-tenth of that, and the libation (tarpaṇa) shall be one-tenth of the oblation.
From that, one-tenth part is for sprinkling (mārjana), and one-tenth part is for feeding the Brahmins;
indeed, I shall thus perform the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) facing the east or the north.
Facing either the east or the north, one should perform [the rite] with kuśa grass, unbroken grains, and water; such is the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) as shown in the scriptures. (53)
(70) But for others, the utterance is considered to be formulated according to what is appropriate.
Some who follow the tradition, however, speak otherwise than this. 54.
Furthermore, the state of being a tenth part applies specifically to their recitation (*japa*), and not even to their presence, which is praised as increasingly superior.
During the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, one should perform the Śrāddha rite day by day;
or for three-quarters of the fortnight, or for one-third, or even for half.
Because such [eating] is not seen among all the learned (śiṣṭa), the feeding of Brāhmaṇas is not prescribed as part of the ritual action. (57)
Because it is an auxiliary to all ritual actions, it is otherwise desired; however, for the recitation of the mantra-deity itself, it is by way of the tenth part. (58)

Reflection should be carried out with ministers, as instructed by the best of counselors; one should also meditate upon the deity of the mantra even for a tenth part of the time spent on the knowledge itself.
The fivefold nature of that very preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is as follows: having gone near the pavilion, one should wash one's feet. (60)
Having sipped water according to the rule, one should perform the general *argha* offering as follows: having purified the vessel with the *astra-mantra* and filled it with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Having invoked the sacred water from the solar orb with the *tīrtha-mantra*, one should cast perfumes and flowers into that water while uttering the syllable *Tāra*.
Having purified this with the Astra-mantra and touched it, one should recite the Mūla-mantra thirty times;
one should then display the Tatva-mudrā, and this shall become the general arghya.
Having sprinkled the door with those waters while reciting the Astra-mantra, one should worship Gaṇeśa and Sarasvatī at the right and left sides of the door respectively.
In the center of the upper archway, one should worship the splendor of the door;
then, on the southern jamb, Vighna, and on the other, Kṣetreśa.
On the two sides of those two [streams] flow the Gaṅgā and Yamunā with waters of flowers; likewise, he [worships] Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, as well as the Śaṅkha and Padma treasures.

One should worship the Weapon-mantra (astra) at each doorway, following this sequence; thereafter, one should worship the presiding deities of those respective doorways belonging to that particular deity.
The gatekeepers of Viṣṇu are known as Ānanda, Sunanda, Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Bala, Prabala, and Bhadra. (68)
Furthermore, Subhadra is proclaimed as one of the Śaiva door-keepers, along with Nandin, Mahākāla, Gaṇeśa, and likewise Vṛṣabha. (89)
Ghiṅgī, Riṭi, as well as Skanda, Umā, and Caṇḍeśvara—these are they;
along with Vakratuṇḍa, Ekadaṃṣṭra, Mahodara, and Gajānana. (70)
Lambodara, Vikaṭa, and another called Vighnarāja—these are the smoke-colored Vighnas; they are known as the Śākteya Mothers.
Furthermore, Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Ananteśvarī, and Cāmuṇḍā as the seventh; || 72 ||
The eighth is Mahālakṣmī; these are declared to be the Mothers of the universe.
Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera are considered the Traipuras.
If there were only one door, then the ritual procedure would be common [to all];
it should be performed once, and one should worship all the gatekeepers right there. (74)
Having thus performed the worship of the door while mentally reciting the root mantra,
one should ward off all obstacles— those of the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms.
"By the command of Śiva, let all indeed go elsewhere from here. Having struck with the heel three times, the wise one contracts his own limbs. (76)
Touching the left branch [of the door], he should enter within with his right foot;
however, this notion that "leftness" is relative to the door is not accepted.
With respect to the person, because there is an absence of sublaters (bādhaka) regarding that [reality],
even this explanation touches upon the portion of skill belonging to the practitioners of mantra (mantriṇaḥ).

It is certainly not appropriate for one who is enveloped by the dense darkness of ignorance; however, in the case of an urgent sacrifice, the wise practitioner should perform it preceded by a strike with the heel, accompanied by white mustard seeds and unbroken rice grains, with the mental intent of the Nārāca weapon. 79.
May those beings depart who are stationed here; may those beings who are creators of obstacles perish by the command of Śiva. 80.
Having thus recited the weapon-mantra at the end, one should scatter [the materials] within the pavilion; then, in the south-western direction, one should worship Vāstveśa and Brāhmaṇa.

One should sprinkle the sacrificial pavilion with the five products of the cow and with water for the guest-offering (*argha*). Now, there may be those present here who are indolent and of limited intellect. (82)

Those men should not perform [the ritual] ending with the worship of the door; having thus performed [the preliminary rites] according to the rule, one should proceed in the place of recitation. Having performed the worship and other such acts that are limbs of the recitation, one should then carry out the recitation itself. (83)
Having adorned the delightful ground and smeared it with cow dung, one should perform the ritual services;
the wise say that these are of three kinds. (84)
A seat, a welcome, the arghya offering, water for the feet, water for sipping, the madhuparka, further sipping water, a bath, garments, and ornaments. (85)
One should employ perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings, as well as prostration, during worship; these are the sixteen services (upacāras). 86.

Then, one should perform the offering of water for honor (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the honey-mixture (madhuparka); furthermore, there is the offering of fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, food (naivedya), and prostration (vandanam). || 87 ||
One should employ the ten services in sequence during worship; from fragrance (gandha) up to the food offering (nivedya), this is the fivefold service (pañcopacārikī) of worship.

The practitioner of mantra, having purified his hands with excellent purifiers (pavitra) and being pure, should place the previously mentioned seat upon the altar after washing his hands and feet. (89)
Having arrived at the site of the altar, one should perform the ritual components of worship according to the rules:
"O you of sharp fangs and massive body, who resemble the fire at the end of an aeon! (90)
"O Bhairava, salutations to you; you should grant me permission. Having thus obtained permission, one should perform the purification of the site. 91.
Having respectfully sprinkled the seat with the fourfold [rites] beginning with inspection,
one should worship [the elements] starting from Ādhāraśakti and ending with the Earth.
There, the knower of mantras [should worship] the deities with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and water; Merupṛṣṭha is the seer (ṛṣi) and Pṛthivī’s Sutala is considered the metre (chanda). 93.
One should remember the deities known as the Tortoise (Kūrma) and those preceded by the sages; the application (viniyoga) of this mantra is proclaimed for the purpose of the seat (āsana). || 94 ||
O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu. Therefore, O auspicious one, support me and purify this seat.
Reciting this mantra, the wise practitioner, with his body held straight, should enter the seat facing either east or north, following the sequence beginning with the *svastika* posture. (96)
A wise person should arrange the proximity of the Guru, Śiva, and the Sun according to their respective magnitudes, as well as that of a burning lamp. || 97 ||
Having placed four full jars in the corners of the seat, beginning with the southeast,
one should worship Gaṇeśa and Sarasvatī within them.
The best of practitioners should also duly worship Durgā and the Lord of the Field; this installation of the water-jars is considered the supreme preliminary rite (puraścaryā). || 99 ||
The practitioner should place the articles of worship on the right side, and on the left, a beautiful jar filled with well-perfumed water. (100)
After washing his hands, he should place the vessel behind him;
he should then set up auspicious lamps, filled with ghee and well-ignited, all around.
One should duly arrange other items such as mirrors and so forth, while standing with palms joined in reverence on the left and right sides. 102.
One should [visualize] the Guru, Gaṇeśāna, and one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) in front; or else, the Guru on the left, Gaṇeśa on the right, and Ambikā in front.
One who knows the ritual procedure should pay homage to Kṣetrapāla in the west; with the mantra of Sudarśana, one should perform protection on all sides.
Oṃ, the thousand-spoked armor-weapon is considered to be the Sudarśana mantra; having perfumed both hands with fragrant flowers, [one should perform the rite]. 105.
The practitioner of mantra should cast a flower to the north with the nārāca-mudrā; having purified it with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra), he should then perform three claps of the hands (tāla).
Having performed the upward progression with that very [mantra], one should then perform the binding of the directions;
[the mantra] which has arisen from the knowledge of light and consists of the nature of truth, knowledge, and bliss. (107)
And immediately thereafter, for his own protection, he should establish a wall of fire all around himself against ghosts, spirits, and demons.

Then the practitioner, for the sake of removing the fire, should scatter water and flowers along with unbroken rice grains (akṣata) consecrated by the fire-seed syllable and the weapon-mantra around [the site]. || 109 ||
(74) One should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*); I shall now describe its procedure: from the feet up to the knees is a square marked with a vajra.
One should contemplate the syllable *laṃ*, joined with *saṃ*, yellow in color, situated on the ground, extending from the knees to the navel, resembling a half-moon and marked with a lotus. (111)
Then one should meditate on water, white in color and joined with its own seed-syllable; from the navel up to the throat, there is a red-colored triangle.
The mandala of fire is marked with a swastika and joined with its own seed-syllable;
the mandala of wind, extending from the throat to the middle of the eyebrows, is black.
One should contemplate a hexagon joined with six dots and the seed-syllable;
it is circular, marked with a banner, extending from the middle of the eyebrows to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). 114.
One should meditate on the auspicious sky as smoke-colored and conjoined with its own seed-syllable;
having meditated thus, one should then cause those elements to dissolve.
Having dissolved the earth into water, that [water] into fire, fire into air,
and air into space, one should likewise dissolve space into primordial nature (prakṛti).
Having dissolved that power of illusion (māyāśakti), which is of the nature of the lower Brahman, into the Supreme Self,
one should remain for some moments in the form of the Supreme Brahman.
One should again generate the pure body of the Supreme Self; that which consists of the Śabdabrahman is Mātṛkā, the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti).
From the Mother of the World, space was born; from space, the wind;
from the wind, fire arose; from fire, water; and from that, the earth. (119)
One should contemplate that one's own body, which consists of light, has likewise arisen from these very elements through the propitiation of the deities.
In that body, one should perceive the Supreme Self— the omniscient, omnipotent,
all-pervading Lord who is the form of all deities and consists of all gods.
It abides within its own body in the form of the self as a seed; this primary contemplation is declared to be the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
That light is full, flawless, unmanifest, and consists of the Praṇava;
it is the source of all mantras and is devoid of the three qualities (guṇas). || 123 ||

Having led [the deity] from the heart-base and the center of the eyebrows to the station of the *dvādaśānta* by means of the best of mantras, one should contemplate the body as being like a pillar. (124)
Then, by means of the wind located at the navel, the practitioner should purify [himself] along with his sins;
then, by means of the fire situated in the heart, he should burn the withered body.
One should contemplate the moon situated on the forehead within the great thousand-petaled lotus— perfectly full, radiant, and consisting of nectar.
Therefore, one should drench the body until it is reduced to ashes by streams flowing from the throat;
likewise, one should drench the body composed of the five elements with [mantras] consisting of the [five] colors.
O Goddess, as before, one should meditate on the mantra-consecrated hearing and consciousness; one should also contemplate the mandalas of the elements within one's own body.
The purification of the elements has been described in this manner, as previously stated in the context of *mohana*; alternatively, the purification of the elements is prescribed by another method.
Born from the bulb of bliss, it has the stalk of knowledge, is most beautiful,
possesses the eight petals of sovereignty, and has supreme detachment as its pericarp.
One should meditate upon one's own heart-lotus, illuminated by the Praṇava;
having placed [the deity] within its pericarp, resembling the flame of a lamp.
The practitioner, joined with yoga, should unite the self with the Supreme Self through the path of the Suṣumṇā, by means of the mantra "So 'ham" according to the prescribed rule.
Space, air, fire, water, earth, and ether, as well as skin, eyes, tongue, nose, mouth, hands, and so forth; 133.
The feet, the anus, and likewise the generative organ; sound and touch as appropriate; form, taste, and smell; and speech, grasping, and movement. (134)
One should contemplate the visarga, bliss, and likewise these others combined, merged there in the state of seed-syllables through their sequential transposition.
One should contemplate the seed-syllable *yaṃ* for the wind in the left nostril—the smoky-colored wind that has become one with the air residing in the *kanda*. (136)
One of steady intellect should visualize the body as withered while situated in the mandala during the stage called pūraka; then, one should exhale through the right [nostril] during kumbhaka.
Then, in the right nostril-passage, one should contemplate the seed-syllable *raṃ* of fire—red in color, with its wind dissolved, and situated within the circle of fire. (138)
Then, having visualized a single body by means of the fire residing in the heart,
the practitioner of mantra should meditate upon that body as being completely filled with fire during both the retention (kumbhaka) and the exhalation (recaka).
The yogi should contemplate it as burnt and exhale it along with the ashes through the left nostril, while keeping his limbs motionless and his senses subdued. (140)
Then, one should contemplate the lunar seed-syllable *ṭhaṃ* in the left nostril—white, situated upon a circle of water, and become one with nectar. (141)
Having taken the seed-syllable for fulfilling what is possible—the moonlight of the forehead—and reciting the nectar-seed syllable, why then would it not be realized? 142.
What is the seed-syllable for that very inhalation (pūraka), and what is its regulator?
And what is the meditation that serves as the regulator here during the recitations of mantras? || 143 ||
Otherwise, how could phonemes (varṇas) and designations (saṃjñās) be subject to recitation? To this it is replied:
because the natural tendency of the *Śāradātilaka* and other treatises [supports this]. (144)
Therefore, for him, meditation alone is considered the recitation of the seed-syllable *svadhā*, setting aside the specific ritual rules as stated in the *Śāradātilaka* and other such texts. (145)
Then, with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, one should flood the entire body; O wise one, why is no such conceptualization not imagined for these two sides? (146)
Wherever an option is proposed, there is no single consistent statement; this is clearly evident in the case of the *dīpikā* and other texts regarding the mixture of phonemes in *kumbhaka*.
One should cause rain from the moon to fall repeatedly as nectar, and one should effect the separation of the bodily humors from the body. 148.

The noble-minded practitioner, having generated the divine [element] and performed the practice up to the crown of the head, should flood it with nectar and exhale through the right nostril (the *dakṣa* wind).
The holding of the nostrils with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb—excluding the index and middle fingers—is to be understood as *prāṇāyāma*. (150)
It is said to consist of three parts: inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka).
The filling of air from the outside into the abdomen is considered inhalation (pūraka). 151.
The retention of breath like a full jar is considered *kumbhaka*; likewise, the expulsion of air from the belly is *recaka*. (152)
Those skilled in yoga declare this prāṇāyāma to be of two kinds: sagarbha (with seed) and vigarbha (without seed); these two are described as follows. || 153 ||
