Those experts in the science of Yoga declare that [practice] joined with recitation, meditation, and so forth is "with seed" (sagarbha), while that which is devoid of them is "without seed" (vigarbha). 154.

The number of recitations for the *sagarbha* [breath control] has been declared in the *Dīpikā* and other works: it is sixteenfold through the recitation in the first [type of] retention (*kumbhaka*), and four times that amount in the subsequent one.
At the conclusion of that *adharma*, however, one should perform the *vigarbha* [mudrā] as directed by the Mother; for as long as it takes in time, one's own hand will reach one's own knee-cap. (156)
That measure is equal to a single breath; one should practice it repeatedly in succession, alternating its sequence. 157.

With that very [nostril] by which one should exhale, one should then fill [the lungs] and retain [the breath]; thereafter, one should exhale through the other [nostril], slowly, in this manner again and again.
Just as a lion, an elephant, or a tiger must be captured very gradually, so too must the moving breath be controlled; otherwise, it destroys the practitioner. 159.

Through the proper practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), there shall be the destruction of all diseases; through improper practice of yoga, however, there arises the emergence of all diseases. || 160 ||
Hiccups, labored breathing, coughing, and pains in the head, ears, and eyes—various diseases such as these arise from the improper performance of breath control (prāṇāyāma). || 161 ||
Therefore, one should practice prāṇāyāma according to the path taught in the scriptures; thereafter, one should lead the dissolved principles back to their respective locations. (162)
By means of the *haṃsa*, one should lead the life-force (*jīva*) of the Supreme Self to its own abode; some here say otherwise, that one should not purify one's own body. (163)
Then [he saw] that evil, resembling a human being, accumulated through beginningless existence, with the murder of a Brahmin as its head and the theft of gold as its two arms. (164)

The drinking of liquor is joined with the heart; violating the Guru’s bed consists of the two hips; association with such persons consists of the pair of feet; and minor sins consist of the limbs and sub-limbs. (165)
One should meditate upon the black [deity] on the right side of the belly as having body hair like minor sins (*upapātaka*), with red beard and eyes, and holding a sword and a shield. (166)

Then, one should indeed purify this [body] by means of the sequence beginning with inhalation (pūraka); this is declared as "purification of the elements" (bhūtaśuddhi) by those expert in the Yoga scriptures. (167)

Alternatively, the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) is prescribed in another manner: [one should place] the individual soul (jīva) through the path of the susumṇā into Sadāśiva, who resides in the lotus.
Having joined [the breath] with the *haṃsa* mantra and reduced the entire body to ashes by means of the seed-syllable of fire (*vahnibīja*), one should mentally disperse those ashes with the wind.
The wise one, withdrawing the entire world by means of the seed-syllable Vāyu (Yam), and flooding it with the syllable Balabhit (Ram),
should contemplate his own self.
The one skilled in yoga should firmly form a net in the shape of a bubble;
then, situated in the middle of that bubble, is a shimmering circle of light.
The wise one should meditate on the egg-born [Brahmā]; the wise one, having contemplated the worlds within that, should then contemplate the beautiful surface of the earth within it. (172)
With a mind fully concentrated, one should contemplate on all sides a grove of *nīpa* trees, adorned with flowers of smiles and intense with a heart-pleasing fragrance. (173)
Within that, the wise man [should construct] a golden pavilion adorned with jewels, possessing the splendor of the solar disc and beautifully decorated with four doors. || 174 ||
It was adorned with four gateways inlaid with jewels,
white as the radiance of the rising moon, and marked by an excellent canopy.
At every door stand Kṣetreśvara and Gaṇeśvara, adorned with garlands and garments, accompanied by their retinues. (176)
One should contemplate the deities stationed as gatekeepers at their respective doors;
thereafter, with an undisturbed mind, one should meditate upon the hosts of celestial women within.

The wise mantra-practitioner should also place those headed by the Gandharvas, who delight in music and song, [therein]; in the center of that, upon a lion-throne, he should place an eight-petaled lotus.
One should meditate on the deity with reddish filaments, resembling the rising sun; having visualized one's chosen deity seated upon her own throne within the pericarp. (179)
One who is proficient in the science of yoga should meditate on the self as being one;
likewise, it should be done in this very same way for whatever form one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) may have. (180)
With a mind disciplined by yoga, the practitioner should contemplate its non-duality; he should then [place] the heart-lotus and the life-force (jīva) in the form of a swan. 181.

One should bring [the soul] from the Supreme Self seated within the lotus of the heart; this is declared as the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) by the best of mantra-experts who know the reality. 182.
Relying on one of these positions, the excellent practitioner, intent on propitiating the deity, should thus purify his body. (183)
This purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) must be performed in every way by the wise at the beginning of worship and other rites;
for without the purification of the elements, the practitioner's acts of recitation, fire-offerings, and worship [are fruitless]. (184)
All [rites] become fruitless, even if performed in every possible manner;
afterwards, one should establish the life-force (jīva) in the body by means of the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā. || 185 ||
Thus, according to the statement in the *Jñānārṇava*, practitioners of mantra (māntrikas) should properly stabilize even their own life-breaths using the prescribed mantra. (186)

Now, moreover, I shall explain the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of the Mātrikā according to the rule; for there is no recitation (japa) or other practice of any mantras without the placement of the letters.

One should know that what has been performed [without this] is fruitless; therefore, one should first place the letters. They say that recitation (japa) without the ritual placement (nyāsa), even if performed by all the gods and asuras, is fruitless.
The Seer is declared to be Brahmā; Gāyatrī is said to be the metre; and Sarasvatī is proclaimed as the deity by the best of teachers. (3)

The six limbs, conjoined with their respective seed-syllables (jāti), should be assigned by the preceptors in due order using the six groups of consonants included within the non-voiced, short, and long vowels.

On the forehead, the face, the circular eyes, the ears, the nostrils, the two teeth, the lips, the upper teeth, the head, the mouth, the joints of the arms and feet, and the tips [of the fingers and toes]. || 5 ||

On the two sides, at the back, at the navel, in the belly, in the heart, and on the shoulders; then on the hump and the area below it, starting from the heart, and finally on the pair of hands and feet.
One should place the letters of the Mātṛkā in sequence upon the belly and the face; in all the letters beginning with 'ya', there is the connection with the heart as the first.
The Ocean of Knowledge has clearly explained this sequence regarding the *mālāmantra*; some say it applies likewise to the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the *mātrikā* in the *Dīpikā*. (8)
[In that case as well, there would be a connection of the heart-primacy for all four;
this is not so, because it is encompassed by a compound and because it would result in the destruction of separate syntactical connection. || 9 ||
Having meditated upon the Goddess according to the ritual procedure, one should place [the seed-syllable] accompanied by emission (sarga) along with the emission;
then, one should place the letter preceded by *ṭa* together with the bindu and the end of emission, according to the path of maintenance (sthiti).
The mantra-practitioner should know the seers and other components previously mentioned, along with the limbs;
however, if one is unable to perform everything, one may simply place the script of the emanation.
These two are the bestowers of divinity for practitioners during acts such as worship; therefore, they should be understood as essential by practitioners during worship and other such rites. (12)

By the statement from the *Kramadīpikā*, "Thus, their bodies have been rendered undecaying," and so forth, it is understood that the state of being the deity has been brought about for those two. (13)
"Having become a god, one should sacrifice to the God; one who is not a god should not worship the God"—from such scriptural statements as these, its eternality is understood. (14)
From such statements as "The recitation and so forth of all mantras," it is understood that both [recitation and fire-offerings] are individually necessary. || 15 ||

And as for the claim that "eternality alone" and "arrangement" belong to a single [entity], that is incorrect, because all four are proclaimed by means of the sublation of their respective fruits. (16)
Just as impermanence is accepted here in this world due to the occurrence of successive kalpas,
so too will there be impermanence regarding bathing, the twilight rituals, and other such acts.
What is the use of saying much more here? Worship must be necessary; if it is argued that there is a fruit [for it], then what is the status of the deposition of reality (tattvanyāsa)? (18)
Then the practitioner of mantras should perform other ritual placements (nyāsa) established for the Kalpa, just as the wise know the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa) in the Vaiṣṇava Tantra.
Then the practitioner, having conquered his senses, should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with that very same excellent mantra which he desires to recite.

Alternatively, the practitioner should perform the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇāyāma) with the Praṇava; however, by women and Śūdras, the restraint of the vital breath should be performed using the worldly [mantra].
A Śūdra and women should never recite the Veda; for one who is capable of it, the previously mentioned number applies, but for one who is incapable, it is otherwise.
One should drink the breath when properly engaged, maintain it when properly engaged, and release it when properly engaged;
by doing so, one shall attain perfection. || 23 ||
By this, the number of recitations according to one's capacity has been stated; however, the full kumbhaka [retention] should be four times that amount.
The rule common to all is that the retention [of breath] should be twice the duration of the inhalation (pūraka).
Some authorities, however, know the sequence in this prāṇāyāma to begin with exhalation (recaka) and so forth. || 25 ||
(82) "The triad beginning with *recaka* (exhalation) should also exist," say those who rely on scriptural authority (*vākya-pramāṇaka*).
That is incorrect, because in the absence of *pūraka* (inhalation), *recaka* is logically untenable. (26)
It is not appropriate to say that the expulsion of air belongs only to the bodily wind;
one should draw in the external air through the *iḍā* with sixteen measures (*mātrā*). (27)

Because in such passages as these, the status of being an external action is heard in reference to inhalation (pūraka) and the others, and because of the instruction on the sequence [in the statement], "They call this prāṇāyāma," [it is established that it is external]. || 28 ||
Nor is its manifold meaning determined by its weightiness, whether it occurs at the beginning, in the exhaling breath, or in the remaining restraint of the vital air. (29)

In *kumbhaka*, the desire for *recaka* (exhalation) is dispelled by the breath itself; therefore, the statement that [the breath] does not [proceed] from *recaka* has the sequential process as its intended meaning. This is like a foolish woman asking for a son after having married a eunuch. (30)
The practitioner of mantra should dismiss the ṛṣis and others, and then perform breath control (prāṇāyāma);
thereafter, he should perform the placement of the Mātṛkās—so it is stated in certain tantras. (31)
Then, in order to perform the internal worship (antaḥpūjā), one should perform the ritual placement of the seat (pīṭhanyāsa).

Beginning with Ādhāraśakti and ending with the pedestal (vedikā), one should place [the deities] within the heart. One should duly place Dharma and the others on the two knees, and Adharma and the others on the two thighs.

The practitioner, having performed circumambulation clockwise on the face, the sides, and the sides of the navel, should place [the mantras] from Śeṣa to the end of the Pīṭha-mantra upon the heart and meditate upon Him.

In some cases, the worship and the ritual placement (nyāsa) are taught with reference to the Dharma; thereafter, one should recollect the seer (ṛṣi) and other components of the mantra, up to its specific application (viniyoga).
Whatever mantra was seen by a particular seer and by whom indeed perfection was attained—that [mantra] is declared to belong to that seer; such is the nature of the ārṣa [type].
Because it conceals, it is designated as "chanda," like two garments for the body; in ancient times, the Self was concealed by the gods out of fear of death. (36)
By means of the Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras, those very Vedic meters were established; for whichever mantra there may be, its presiding deity is likewise ordained.
Its form becomes that [of the deity]; its divinity is called "deity-hood. In a former aeon, mantras were produced solely for the purpose of ritual action. (38)
"By this, this must be performed"—this is called *viniyoga*.
The *ṛṣi*, *chandas*, and *daivata* [should be assigned] to the head, face, and heart respectively. (39)
If the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) requires the placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*), then, having performed that placement,
one should perform it on both hands with the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) prescribed in that specific ritual procedure.
One should place those [syllables] upon the palms, starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger; first, "Hṛdayāya Namaḥ," and for the head, "Vahnivallabhā" (Svāhā).
"Vaṣaṭ" is said for the tuft (śikhā), "Hūm" is uttered for the armor (kavaca), "Vauṣaṭ" is said for the two eyes, and "Phaṭ" for the weapon (astra) in due order. (42)
The limb-mantras have been taught once for all by those who know the Agamas;
likewise, the entire science of mantras has been acquired by the wise one through the mantra. (43)
Whatever nyāsas are to be performed for a mantra by one desiring success—even when the mantra has been perfected through recitation, libation, fire-offerings, and worship—[those must be done]. (44)

Devoid of the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and other such rites, these [mantras] will not yield their fruits; therefore, their performance is proclaimed as absolutely necessary in every respect. (45)
Having placed that weapon-mantra upon those two, one should then perform three claps; by means of those very claps, one should bind the directions on all sides.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the weapon-mantra on the five limbs, beginning with the little finger;
one should place the five limbs upon the five fingers in the Dīpikā [mudrā].
According to this statement, one should place the weapon-mantra on the palms of the hands;
thus, the statement from the Śāradā-tantra regarding this must refer to the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).

Thus some say; others, however, maintain that for a practitioner, even in the case of a mantra consisting of a hundred thousand [recitations], there is a restriction of the general rule imposed by a specific injunction. (49)
And there is no sublation whatsoever here; the lamp does not sublate this.
In accordance with the introductory statement, there must be a focus on the specific meaning. || 50 ||
The restriction of that universal attainment must be postulated due to its logical impossibility; for, in the absence of that [attainment], there is the certainty of its non-existence. (51)
Having thus composed the mind, the disciplined practitioner should visualize [the mantra] upon the chest, head, crest, armor, eyes, and even the palms of the hands. 52.
Then one should assign the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) to the five limbs, omitting the eye;
for a mantra that lacks a limb, one should fashion its limbs by means of itself alone. (53)
At the commencement of the recitation of mantras, however, there is a general procedure for their visualization:
in the placement of the limbs upon the two hands, one should delineate the limbs beginning with the thumb of the forefinger.

Some who possess superficial knowledge say that, because there is no distinction, the hands and other limbs should be worshipped everywhere in the same manner as the heart and other parts, according to their respective positions. 55.
It is said that the heart-mantra and the others, when joined with the feminine suffix *ṅī* and preceded by "namas," possess the nature of a genus (*jāti*).
How then can the mention of the thumb and other [limbs] be desired therein? (56)

If it is argued that they [the letters] serve as the substratum, then by the force of that same equality, there would likewise be an inscription on the forehead and other parts during the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of the Mātṛkā-letters.
Furthermore, the lack of connection between the meanings here is not described in that same way. || 58 ||
The heart is that which is accessible to the intellect, and the word "namas" constitutes a salutation;
therefore, by means of the heart, this act of salutation is made accessible to the intellect. (59)
The head is said to signify height, while the two eyes (dviṭha) signify the grasping of sense objects;
by means of the mantra of the head, it is elevated, and the grasping of sense objects is thus described.
The crest-lock (śikhā) is declared to be splendor (tejas), and it is said to exceed the rain [in intensity]; that splendor is called the body of this practitioner through the crest-lock mantra.
From the verbal root *kav-agrahaṇa* (the grasping of armor), the kavaca [mantra] arises; thus, by means of its splendor, the deity is grasped as the kavaca through the syllable *hūṃ*.
The eye is designated as *dṛṣṭi*, and the vision is called *vauṣaṭ*. That splendor by which vision occurs is the denotation of the "eye. (63)
In that [mantra], there are two root-letters beginning with *s*, having the meanings of "casting" and "shaking.
Having cast what is undesirable by means of those two, one should shake it with the fire of the syllable *phaṭ*.
The wise have declared these limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) in all the tantras;
indeed, the Śrīgārgyasaṃhitā has also directly stated this very meaning.
One should perform the placement of mantras on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and the hands (*karanyāsa*) with the limb-mantras; this was proclaimed in the *Chinnamastā-tantra* with a resonant voice.
Now I shall explain to you the mudrās of the six limbs according to the rule:
for the heart and the head, the fingers of the hand are used, excluding the thumb. (67)
A fist formed with the thumbs tucked underneath is considered the *mudrā* for the crest (*śikhā*).
The fingers of both hands are proclaimed to be the *mudrā* for the armor (*kavaca*). (68)
Where the two eyes are considered, there the index finger and middle finger are considered; where the three eyes are present, there the ring finger is likewise prescribed.
Then, having raised his two arms with his fists,
the knower of the ritual procedure produced a sound in all directions by means of his thumbs and index fingers.
That is proclaimed by those who know the Agamas as the Vibhakta Astra-mudrā.
One should employ these six limb-mudrās in all mantras. (71)
Then, when the practitioner also performs the arrangement of the mantras and so forth,
as well as the placement of the feet and other rites specifically prescribed in the ritual manual (kalpa), || 72 ||
One should perform other installations (nyāsa) as specified in the various particular Kalpas. || 73 ||
Then, the knower of mantras should perform the placement using the letters of the Mātṛkā together with the bindu, encapsulated by the syllable *maṃ*, according to the path seen in the scriptures.

Then, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Ṛṣi, the Aṅgas, and the Kara-mantras, one should display the mudrās; thereafter, the wise practitioner of mantra should perform the binding of the directions (digbandhana) with the Astra-mantra.
Oṃ, namaḥ sudarśanāstrāya; this is declared as the mantra ending with the weapon (astra).
Then, having meditated upon oneself in the form of one’s chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), one should perform worship. || 3 ||
When one, permeated by devotion, performs the worship according to the ritual rules with mental offerings such as water for the feet and so forth,
that worship with mental flowers is considered to be *sāttvika* and auspicious.
Another [form] is stainless, pure, auspicious, bestowing liberation, and granting success;
therefore, with every effort, one should perform the auspicious mental worship.

Some authorities maintain that the Vaiśvadeva rite applies to both the self-sacrifice (ātma-yāga) and the internal sacrifice (antaryāga); furthermore, one should perform the internal Vaiśvadeva immediately after the meal.
In the triangle situated at the root-support (mūlādhāra), blazing with the fire of the deity and endowed with merit and demerit,
[one should perform the rite] preceded by the root mantra.
I offer this great supreme nectar, filled to the brim in the vessel of "this-ness" (idantā), into the fire consisting of supreme "I-ness" (parāhantā), while abiding in the form of Śiva.
Having thus reflected with his mind, the supreme master of mantras should then offer oblations one by one, saying: "I sacrifice this; svāhā! (9)
Egoism, falsehood, backbiting, lust, anger, and so forth are the oblation; the mind alone is declared to be the sacrificial ladle, and Suṣumnā is said to be the sacrificial grass.

At the conclusion of that, having become one with it (tanmaya), one should recite [the mantra] according to one's desire; one should then offer that recitation for the sake of all prosperity with the words "O Secret One," and so forth. || 11 ||
Then, having assumed the form of the deity, one should remain for some moments;
however, in the established doctrine of Vijñāneśvara, the worship of the self is taught otherwise. (12)

The offering of the body, the intellect, and the functions of the vital breath into the Deity— that alone constitutes the three supreme offerings, beginning with *argha*, in the sacrifice of the mind.
The ritual sprinkling with waters flowing from the circle of white rays within the great lotus at the *dvādaśānta* is here intended as the bath. (14)
O Maheśvarī, in the services of worship, the fragrance offered to the deity constitutes the dedication of the entire qualified (saguṇa) worship.
The worship of the deity with sky-flowers (nabhaḥpuṣpa) is described here as being performed with the mind, joined with all words, even toward the sky itself.
The knower of the mantra, with a steady mind, should mentally conceive the incense and the lamp as being composed of air and fire respectively, and offer them all around.
The respectful offering of the entire water-element, endowed with various flavors, is a pleasing oblation that bestows delight. || 18 ||
In this context, the differentiation of the elements (*bheda*) is to be characterized within the fire of the deity Śiva;
dance arises from the state of ignorance, while song is the perfection of speech. 19.
The traditionalists say that the mental worship described in the *Dīpikā* and other texts is likewise accomplished in this manner.
Thereafter, one should respectfully perform the installation of the *argha* for the sake of the chosen deity,
using fragrant paste, flowers, unbroken rice, barley, tips of *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and mustard seeds.
This is declared to be the *arghya* for all the gods, offered with *dūrvā* grass. Having washed the conch with the *astra-mantra*, one places it to the left of the fire-mandala.
Having placed there with the heart-mantra perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and so forth, and having cast them in reverse order while reciting the Mātṛkā at the end of the root-mantra.

One who is proficient in the Yoga scriptures should fill [the vessel] with pure waters, perceiving the world-seed-syllable (bīja) together with its nasal drop (bindu) as nectar flowing from that bindu.

According to the view of the *Dīpikā* and other [commentaries], the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) is not recited here; however, some indeed recite the root mantra of the *Mātṛkā-mantra* in the ritual procedure.
Having meditated upon the support, fire, the conch, the sun, water, and the moon,
one should contemplate their respective digits (kalās) in each of those locations.
Then one should take refuge in the fire-mandala, which consists of ten digits (kalās),
and likewise in the solar mandala, which consists of the digits of the sun.
One should likewise worship the one whose self is a digit of the moon and the lunar deity; "Ma" is to be known as the first seed-syllable, and "A" is proclaimed as the second.
The third is called Amba (Muṃ); one should first employ these [syllables]. Then the practitioner of mantra should invoke [the deity] with the Tīrtha-aṅkuśa mudrā.
From the orb of the sun, a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) is conceived right there: "O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, be present in these waters! (10)
This is declared to be the Tīrthamanu, which destroys the flood of sins; having made [the fingers] straight and middle-sized, [one places them] upon the middle joint of the index finger.
Having joined [the fingers] and slightly contracted them, this mudrā is known as the *aṅkuśa* (goad).
Therein, the practitioner of mantra should [invite] the chosen deity even from his own heart-lotus. (12)
Having invoked [the deity], one should display the Gālinī mudrā with the Śikhā mantra:
the little fingers and thumbs of the two hands are joined to one another.
The index, middle, and ring fingers joined together and not bent— this is declared to be the Gālinī mudrā,
which is moved over the conch.
Having veiled this with both hands and rendered it nectar-like by means of the mudrā,
one should then consecrate the water with the Surabhī root-mantra.
The fist is firm and held to the right, with the index finger extended and pointing downward; this is considered the *avaguṇḍana* mudrā when it is rotated all around. 16.
Furthermore, when the little fingers and ring fingers are joined facing one another, and likewise the index and middle fingers,
this is declared to be the Dhenu-mudrā.

Having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) by means of the placement of the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*), one should provide protection with the weapon-mantra (*astra*). There, one should worship the chosen deity with perfumes and other offerings while reciting the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).
Having worshipped that water as the form of the deity with the *matsyamudrā* gesture, one should cover it and, while touching it, recite the root mantra eight times. Then, [proceed as follows].
With the right hand facing downwards and the left hand likewise positioned, this is declared to be the Matsya-mudrā,
intended for the consecration of the conch.
Having placed the *prokṣaṇī* vessel to the south, he should fill it with water;
having added a little *argha* water to it, he should [sprinkle] his own limbs with his hand. (21)
The practitioners should perform the consecrations and then carry out the worship of the body; one should worship one's own Lord in the region of the head and Gaṇapa at the base (ādhāra).

Having worshipped that [deity] with devotion according to the rite of Nyāsa for the sake of the seat (pīṭha), one should worship the Mūla-mantra in the foundation (ādhāra), the heart, and between the eyebrows.
By means of the root mantra, the threefold energy is unified with that seed-syllable;
its form is entirely distinct according to the specific methods described for each respective ritual manual.

The mantra-practitioner should worship with seats and other offerings, and then adorn that body; he should worship the limbs and so forth according to the procedure revealed in the respective ritual manual.

One should worship [the deity] with offerings such as perfumes and other services, even without the formal food offering (naivedya). Having worshipped with perfume and flowers, one should [offer] the essence of nectar flowing from the *bindu*. (26)
This indeed pleases the God; thus the Kramadīpikā has said: "Having performed worship and restrained the breath, one should recite the mantra for as long as the occasion permits. (27)
Having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) once again, one should offer the recitation itself;
one should recite the seed-syllable one hundred and eight times, encased within the Praṇava.

One should perform the remaining rites in a manner that is consistent with the prescribed path; however, the worship of the surrounding deities (āvaraṇārcana) has been described in the Agastya-saṃhitā.
Having performed the sacrifice of the self (ātma-yāga) as prescribed, and likewise the intermediate worship (antara-pūjana), one should then inform the Lord of Gods and worship his retinue.
Thus worshipped, the God grants all desires; thereafter, one should indeed perform the external worship for the sake of prosperity in this world.
And this is logical: when the principal is being worshipped, the worship of its members is [implied]; by what authority is it sublated?
Nor is there a non-statement [of the rule], because it is presented [in the scriptures]. (32)

According to the maxim "whatever one is devoted to," those learned in the Tantras know that just as the planets themselves include their presiding and counter-presiding deities by the very term "planets," so too are the deities included in rites such as the great gifts (*mahādāna*).
One should perform all this with the water contained in the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, having first released [the deity].
One should fill the *prokṣaṇī* vessel with water from those waters. || 34 ||

Having offered some water for the *argha* here, one should arrange the ritual services (*upacāra*). To the north of the *argha* water, the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*) should be prepared. (35)
In the same manner, he should offer the madhuparka and again perform the sipping of water (ācamana) and so forth; then, being well-composed, he should place a conch shell to his east.

It is said in some places that one should arrange vessels for the purpose of the water for the feet (pādya) and so forth; or alternatively, one may prepare the pādya and other offerings in a single vessel. || 37 ||
The supreme characteristics of a worthy recipient (pātra), as proclaimed in the Tattvasāgara, are as follows: [a vessel] made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, or a leaf of the Palāśa tree. (38)
A vessel made of precious gems, or born of conch, or even from a lotus leaf—these eight types of vessels are proclaimed as supreme, bestowing all accomplishments. (39)
Among all vessels indeed, the conch vessel is distinguished as superior;
a vessel measuring thirty-six finger-breadths is proclaimed to be the best. (40)
The middle [size] is that minus one-third, and the lowest is twelve finger-breadths;
one should never have a vessel made that is less than eight finger-breadths.

The practitioner of mantra should place a vessel of flowers on the right side, and then again in front; he should set down all the ritual materials for the practice, such as perfumes, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and so forth.

Now, out of a desire for the welfare of practitioners, I shall describe the external worship; first, one should draw the king of diagrams (yantra) according to the form prescribed in the respective ritual manual (kalpa).
Because it completely restrains the impurities of the mind, such as desire and anger, they call this a "yantra"; when worshipped, the Divine is pleased within it. (44)
One should draw this unsurpassed yantra with the specific substances prescribed for each respective kalpa, upon a pedestal made of gold, silver, or copper, or on birch bark, cloth, or the ground.
If the deity is not pleased by worship without a yantra, and no yantra was prescribed in the ritual manual (kalpa),
then it should be accompanied by a *bhūpura* (fortified square).
Having drawn an auspicious eight-petalled lotus adorned with four gates according to the procedure prescribed in the Tantra, one should worship the chosen deity.
And this drawing of the lotus is performed in accordance with the requirements for the worship of Śakti;
because it is stated to be the substratum for worship, it is declared here as being necessary.
Then, in the north, the Guru; in the south, Gaṇanāyaka; and then the wise one should worship them in ascending order from the center. || 49 ||
Below, one should worship Ādhāraśakti, who stands upon the Tortoise-stone, possesses a splendor resembling a hundred moons, and holds two lotuses.
Then the mantra-practitioner should worship Prakṛti according to the method prescribed in the ritual manual (kalpa);
he should worship the dark-blue Kūrma seated upon her head.
Above, one should worship Ananta, who is seated upon the Brahma-throne, resembles a kunda flower, and holds a discus on his head while supporting the earth.
There, one should worship the Earth, dark as the tamāla tree, bearing blue lotuses, and girdled by the shimmering ocean.
(92) One should worship the Ocean of Milk, the Island of Jewels, and then the wish-fulfilling trees; below these, one should worship the altar-platform, radiant with its mandala.
One should worship those who are red, dark, yellow, and the luster of sapphire, whose forms are the feet [of Viṣṇu],
and who take the forms of the bull, the lion, and the elephant, being superior even to Dharma.
One should worship those limbs, which possess characteristics not previously mentioned; then one should worship the lotus in the corners starting from the southeast and in the cardinal directions.

Having first worshipped the bulb of bliss (ānandakanda), immediately thereafter the stalk of consciousness (saṃvinnāla), and after that the lotus consisting of all the principles (sarvatattvātmaka); || 57 ||
The minister (mantrin) should worship the petals as the primary nature (prakṛti), the filaments as consisting of transformation (vikāra),
and the pericarp as enriched with the seed-syllables of the fifty letters.

But at the conclusion of the worship of Dharma and the others, having proclaimed the worship of Ananta, some have stated that the worship of Padma is performed by means of the word "Padma" itself. 59.
One should worship the solar orb and the others with the three parts of the *praṇava*.
Having worshipped the solar [deity] with the first part, one should worship him along with his *tāpinī* and other digits (*kalās*).

Having worshipped [the deity] with another [mantra], one should worship the digit of the moon consisting of nectar and the rest; [one should worship] Uṣarbudha with the third [mantra], and the digits beginning with Dhūmrārcis.

The qualities (guṇas) situated upon the seat (pīṭha) are said to be white, red, and black; they are declared to be sattva, rajas, and tamas. One should worship them with their primordial seed-syllables (bījas). 62.
One should reverently worship these— the Self (Ātman), the Inner Self (Antarātman), and the Supreme Self (Paramātman)— beginning with the primordial seed-syllables, according to the prescribed rule.

The practitioner of mantra should worship the one whose nature is knowledge (jñānātman), and then he should worship Māyā and the others; likewise, he should worship the Śaktis upon the filaments and in the center, in due order.
Then, the practitioner should fashion the seat with his own mantra and the image with the root-mantra,
or else with the mantras prescribed in the ritual manual, having first uttered the root-mantra.
In the shade of the Kalpa tree, one should worship the embodied form with perfumes and other offerings; thereafter, one should meditate upon the deity in the form described in the Kalpa.
Meditation (dhyāna) is considered to be the mental perception of one's chosen deity as the Self; that too is said to be of two kinds:
with attributes (saguṇa) and likewise without attributes (nirguṇa).
(93) The realization that "I am He" when there is oneness of the individual soul and Brahman—that indeed the knowers of Brahman understand to be meditation upon the attributeless (nirguṇa). || 68 ||
One's own heart-lotus, complete with its pericarp and filaments, is in full bloom and resplendent with the circles of the moon, sun, and fire. (69)
There, one should meditate upon one's own chosen deity as known from the scriptures;
such knowledge is indeed called meditation with attributes (saguṇa-dhyāna). || 70 ||
One should contemplate the divine splendor, resembling a lamp, at the mūlādhāra; by means of the root mantra, O Śivā, that splendor [should be led] through the path of the suṣumṇā.
Having joined it and led it to the forehead, one should contemplate it as resembling the moon;
then, having emerged through the path of the nostril, it is most beautiful.

Having joined [the deity] with the Brahma-randhra according to the prescribed rite, within that form which consists of a mass of Karaṇḍa flowers and has the nature of the lotus of the Mother (Mātṛkā); || 73 ||
The wise one should perform the invocation with the *āvāhana-mudrā*; having invoked, he should properly establish [the deity] with the *saṃsthāpana* mudrā. (74)
Thereafter, having brought it near with the *sannidhāpana* mudrā, having restrained it with the *nirodhinī* mudrā, and having made it face [the practitioner] with the [appropriate] mudrā; || 75 ||
After performing the rite of manifestation (*sammukhīkaraṇī*), the practitioner should perform the rite of totalization (*sakalīkaraṇī*);
after the rite of totalization, he should [perform] the rite of veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*) with the appropriate mudrā.

Having veiled [the offering] and rendered it nectar by means of the *amṛtīkaraṇa-mudrā*, and having bound the *paramīkaraṇī* [mudrā], one should perform the act of supreme transformation (*paramīkṛti*).
Now, their characteristics are stated according to the order of their enumeration: having formed the añjali with both hands, [one places the thumbs] upon the root joints of the ring fingers. (78)
One should extend the thumb; this is considered the *āvāhanī* (invoking) mudrā. If this same mudrā is turned face downwards, it is considered the *sthāpinī* (establishing) mudrā.
From the joining of two fists with the thumbs raised, it is the *sannidhāpinī*;
that same mudrā, when the thumbs are inserted within, is considered the *saṃbodhinī*.
The *sammukhīkaraṇī* [mudrā] is considered to consist of two hands with palms turned upward; the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs upon the body of the deity is the *sakalīkṛti*. (81)
The *avaguṇṭhanikā* mudrā is proclaimed as the *dhenu* mudrā; it is formed by interlocking the two thumbs while extending the other fingers. (82)
This Mahāmudrā is the supreme joy for the wise in the act of bringing [the deity] to perfection; one should employ these mudrās in the rite of invoking the deity. 83.
In the case of the Śālagrāma and the stationary [liṅga], there is no invocation or dismissal; for Hari is eternally present within the Śālagrāma stone. 84.
Thus some say here, following the instruction of Baudhāyana, that in all cases it is the light of the complete nature of reality [that is present]. (85)
"Calling forth (āvāhana) is declared to be the act of appearing before [the deity] with reverence"—in accordance with this statement from the *Siddhāntasāra*. (86)
Some wise ones perform the invocation even upon stone and other materials;
one should understand that when Śiva has been thus invoked, his presence resides here within this body.

Stabilization (sthirīkaraṇa) is prescribed as the act of fixing [the deity] with devotion during worship; having accepted the worship being performed, including even acts such as restraint (nigraha), one should perform the installation (sthāpana). || 88 ||
In this world, his capacity to act is said to consist in his presence; for as long as the worship continues until its completion, there is indeed the presence of Śiva.

This [state] is taught as the unified form of even this All-pervading Lord through devotion; it is the abode of bliss, the reality characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss. That which pervades all here should be meditated upon as the *avaguṇṭhana* (the veiling).

Even for constituent parts that possess distinct natures, their transformation into nectar (amṛtīkaraṇa) together with the whole, which they serve, is considered to have that same non-distinct purpose. 91.
Forgiveness of his offenses should be understood as the supreme form [of worship].
This meaning of the rites beginning with the invocation has been revealed. || 92 ||
The filaments are formed by the vowels [the "sons of the sky-moon"] and the consonants [the "navels"], each in two groups;
likewise, they are formed by the letters beginning with *ya*, *śa*, *na*, and *la*.
The petals are adorned in the cardinal directions and intermediate points in sequence;
one should know that it is likewise for the city of Kṣoṇī, excluding the [central] finger. 94.
The lotus of the Mātṛkā has been declared to be the warder-off of all calamities. (95)
The wise practitioner, having visualized the retinue of attendants as having emerged from the body of the deity in the form of sparks,
should seat them in their respective places while reciting the mantra.
Then one should perform the ritual services preceded by the root mantra; having recited the root mantra, one should offer the seat to her.
In each of those instances, one should offer water at intervals between the ritual services. But then, where would this offering of water be required, and who is its regulator? 98.
Without the observance of restrictive rules, giving [water] would lead to over-extension; therefore, where water should be given and how—what is the definitive conclusion on this? (99)
It is said: "In that [place], in that [situation]"—because two instances of repetition (*vīpsā*) are heard in this sentence, one restricts the location while the other indicates totality. (100)
And likewise, it is understood that wherever there may be a gift or an offering, water should be given in that very same manner. (101)

If one thinks that there is no superior [merit] in the offering of ritual services when all the articles for worship are absent, then one should indeed meditate upon them with the mind during the presentation of those services. (102)
One should recite the name of the deity beginning with "Tārā" and so forth, joined with the syllable "ṅe," and ending with "namaḥ";
this mantra is proclaimed as the root and so on. (103)
Then the practitioner should utter words of welcome and well-being, and thereafter offer water for the feet (arghya) upon the head, consecrated with the head-mantra (śiromantra). 104.

One should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) to the lotus-feet of the Lord with the *Hṛdaya-mantra*; that [water] is prescribed as consisting of water mixed with *śyāmāka* grain, *dūrvā* grass, lotuses, and *viṣṇukrāntā*. (105)
Then, with the *svadhā* mantra, one should offer water for sipping (*ācamana*) three times into the mouth;
this is what has been taught by those who know the mantras, using nutmeg, cloves, and kakkola.

In some cases, it is prescribed that after the offering of the *argha*, one should provide the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*); however, there is an option regarding these two.
One should perform the rites such as the swift sacrifice (tūrṇayāga) and others, as well as the offering of water for honor (argha) and so forth;
it has been stated therein by the practitioners of mantra that the mantras must indeed be accompanied by the word "namaḥ."
Having first uttered "namas," "svadhā," "svāhā," and "vauṣaṭ" in their respective order,
one should offer the water for the feet and the other articles of worship.

Then, with the heart-mantra, one should offer the *arghya*—consisting of *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice—at the head, saying "Arghyaṃ namaḥ"; and one should likewise offer the *pādya* at the feet. (110)
The phrase "preceded by the heart" would otherwise be inconsistent, were it not for this statement intended for its subsequent utterance. (111)
Some maintain that the seed-syllable is indicated by the word *svadhā*; with the utterance "svadhā," one should offer water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) three times into the lotus of the mouth. (112)
In accordance with such statements as "vidhi" and so forth, Manu is considered [the author];
those whose feet are worshipped by the Svadhā [mantra] have clearly stated this in the *Pradīpa*. (113)
Then, with the *svadhā* mantra, one should offer the *madhuparka* into the lotus of the mouth; clarified butter mixed with curd and honey is declared to be the *madhuparka*. || 114 ||
But when the object as described cannot be obtained, one should accept that which resembles it, just as wheat is accepted for barley or rice for paddy. (115)
Even if those [specific items] are unavailable, one should imagine something similar using perfumes and other substances; with that very mantra, one should offer the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka).
Having requested [the deity] for the bath, one should offer a most beautiful bathing garment;
one should perform the anointing and massaging with unguents in the manner of the royal service of a great king.
One should cause the bath to be performed with scented waters and offer water for rinsing the mouth;
having given a garment of fine silk, one should perform the cleansing of the hair and limbs.
Then, having provided the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra), one should again offer water for sipping (ācamana);
and having established [the deity] within a beautiful mandala adorned with divine garlands and unguents.
Then, having adorned [the deity] with various divine ornaments endowed with many jewels, as prescribed in their respective ritual manuals, the mantra-practitioner [should proceed]. (120)

One who knows the ritual procedure should worship the limbs and other parts upon the body of the deity. [He should offer] sandalwood produced in Malaya, which is cool and has not been previously smelled.

Then the mantra-practitioner should offer [the oblation] mixed with camphor and agallochum, using the letters of the Mātṛkā encased by the mantra according to the sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa). || 122 ||
"In some tantras it is said that one should worship him with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, sequentially upon the head, the heart, the base (the navel), the feet, and all the limbs. (123)
Then, with a one-pointed mind, he should offer five handfuls of flowers:
two *kamala*, two *karavīra*, two *kumuda*, and two types of *tulasī*. (124)
The two *jātī* flowers, the two types of *ketaka*, the *kalhāra*, *campaka*, *utpala*, *kunda*, *mandāra*, *puṃnāga*, *pāṭalā*, *nāga*, and *campaka*. (125)
Āragvadha, karṇikāra, pārantī, navamālikā, saugandhika, koraṇṭa, palāśa, aśoka, and mallikā. || 126 ||
The practitioner [should offer] dhūtthura, sarjaka, bilva, arjuna, and munipatraka, as well as other fragrant flowers and leaves. (127)
A wise person should accept those items prescribed for worship that are not soiled, nor touched by the ground, nor defiled by worms, hair, and the like. (128)
One should discard a flower that has been touched by the body, smelled, half-bud, or withered; one should always place a flower upon the head of the Deity.
At the time of worship, one should not wave the hand over the deity; however, in the worship of Gopāla, one may do so during the fivefold offering of handfuls of flowers.
That method, as proclaimed otherwise by the wise, is now being described: one who knows the ritual procedure should offer a pair of *tulasī* leaves at the two feet.
In the center, one should place a pair of horses, and likewise a pair of lotuses on the head; one should bestow all these upon the entire body and then worship the retinue.
In the ultimate sense, there should be only one añjali at the feet;
however, because of the statement "even with six," there should be two añjalis on the head. (133)
The meaning of the *Dīpikā* has been clearly established here by those such as myself.
Now, having obtained permission from the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), one should worship the limbs (*aṅga*). Generally, these come first, though in some cases it may be otherwise. (134)

One should worship the heart and the other limbs beginning from the southeast corner on the filaments; the eyes in front and the weapon-mantra in the cardinal directions, using the limb-mantras ending with "namaḥ. (135)

The *Gārgyasaṃhitā* states that during worship, the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) is used in the cardinal directions and the eye-mantra (*netra*) in the region of Īśāna; this is indeed clearly established. (136)
Some maintain that one should perform the very limbs [of the ritual] ending with "namaḥ," [visualizing them] as having the lusters of frost,
crystal, dark-blue, blue, black, and ruddy.

The wise practitioner should meditate upon the deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatās) as women who are the primary forms [of the deity] and who bestow boons and protection, according to this very sequence. (138)
Now, should the directions such as east and so forth be taken from the perspective of the deity or from that of the self? Since there is no regulating authority, doubt arises in this matter. (139)

To this it is replied: the wise should understand that for the deity, the directions beginning with the East are to be grasped; the gods face the sacrificer, while the ten directions, starting from the East, are to be known as facing the gods in rites such as worship and fire-oblations. 140.
Thus, in accordance with the statement accepted by everyone, wherever there may be an inconsistency, it is in that very place that such a conceptualization of direction [is applied]. (141)

"Except for those [already mentioned], only the directions such as the East and so forth should be taken as they occur in the context," say some practitioners; others, however, say that [they are to be understood] in every direction. (142)
In accordance with the stated injunctions, they declared the rule for the directions;
thereafter, the modes of livelihood as prescribed in the Kalpa shall apply in sequence for the purpose of worship.
Then one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) together with their primary retinues, provided with their weapons, classes, and presiding deities;
otherwise, some desire it differently.

[One should worship] those [deities] endowed with their respective leaf-seated lords, colors, weapons, retinues, and limbs; and for Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt and lord of the gods, the word "pada" [is used]. 145.
Afterwards, one should likewise extract the word for the vehicle and the word for the retinue for the others as well, ending each with "namaḥ," beginning with the vehicles and so forth. 146.
Thus, the worship of Indra and the other deities has been fully described for the Tūrṇā sacrifices: Indra, Agni, Yama, Yakṣa, Varuṇa, Pavana, and Vidhu. (147)
Īśāna, the lord of serpents, is below; the Grandfather (Brahmā) is above. They are yellow, red, black, smoky, white, and both smoky and white respectively.
These are proclaimed in sequence as being white, tawny, and ruddy by color. || 149 ||

With their own weapons resting in their lotus-like hands, divinely attired and radiant with garlands, one should know their weapons in sequence to be the vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, the goad, the mace, the trident, the discus, and the lotus. (150)
Yellow, white, sky-colored, lightning-red, white-black, and the luster of kuruvinda and pāṭala are proclaimed as the characteristics of diamonds and the other [precious stones]. || 151 ||
Their lotus-hands are joined with their respective weapons and the gesture of fearlessness, and they are most beautiful.
[Their vehicles are] Airāvata, as well as a ram, a buffalo, and one known as a *preta*. (152)
The wise know that the animals of these [deities] are, in order: the one called Makara, a deer, a serpent, a bull, a tortoise, and a swan. (153)

In some places, the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇārcana) is prescribed at the conclusion of the offering of food (naivedya); this is indeed traditional and may be performed as an optional alternative.
He who is not capable of performing the ritual worship of the entire retinue should, in this case, worship his chosen deity with Aṅga, Indravajra, and the others. (155)
Having fully worshipped the garments, one should then present incense and other offerings; one should offer incense from a low vessel made of copper, bell-metal, or similar materials.
In an auspicious vessel shaped like a lotus with a bent stalk and containing two parts,
[one should offer] incense made from guggulu and aguru trees, cast along with heartwood and charcoal.

Furthermore, this incense made from substances such as resinous exudates (niryāsa) and other fragrant materials that have been described is recommended for the act of worship when it has not been offered to another [deity]. 158.
The lamp, like the incense, should be placed in a vessel fashioned in the shape of a lotus, with each petal illuminated by a wick soaked in cow's ghee.
A bright and highly fragrant lamp filled with camphor should be offered aloft;
the characteristics of incense and lamps are very clearly stated in the Śāradā [Tantra]. (160)
The preceptor should fumigate the deity from below with guggulu, aguru, uśīra, sugar, honey, and sandalwood, mixed with clarified butter.
Having placed wicks filled with camphor in either clarified butter or sesame oil,
one should display tall, fragrant lamps.
Then, having offered a handful of flowers, water for the feet, and water for sipping, one should pray to the chosen deity for the purpose of offering the food oblation.
Having placed the food offering—soft, warm, and well-cooked—in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, or fashioned from gems and other materials; || 164 ||
Sweet snacks, pure milk-rice with sugar, plantains, jackfruit, mangoes and the like, curd, milk, and refreshing drinks. || 165 ||
Having established [the deity] before him and sprinkled [it], one should place flowers with the *tāra* [mantra].
Sprinkled with the *astra* [mantra] and protected by the *cakramudrā* and the wind and water [mantras]. (166)
Having dried it with fire and burned it with the right hand, one should [visualize] the left hand filled with a stream of nectar,
consecrated by the root mantra as nectar.
Having touched [the offering] three times while reciting the mantra with the *dhenusamjñā* mudrā,
one should consecrate it as nectar (*amṛta*) and then worship the food offering (*naivedya*) with perfumes and other articles.
Then, one should pray in this manner so that a great radiance may issue forth;
having recited the root mantra ending with "svāhā" and offered water, one should present the offering. || 169 ||
"I offer this oblation to you; may you accept it, O Hari. This is the mantra for the offering of the gift (nivedya-arpaṇa) in all forms of worship, using one's own name [in place of "Hari"]. 170.

Then, with the mantra "Thou art the underlayer of nectar," he should cause [the guest] to sip water; meanwhile, with his left hand, he should form the mudrā of the morsel, resembling a blossoming lotus petal.

One should display [the gestures] with the right hand and likewise show the Prāṇa and other [vital winds]; one should touch the little finger, the ring finger, and the tip of the thumb with the [respective] mudrās.
By that, the first [mudrā] arises among them; the second is between the index and middle fingers; the third is between the ring and middle fingers;
[the fourth consists of] the middle, index, and ring fingers. (173)

The fourth consists of those [fingers] together with the little fingers; these five are proclaimed as the Pañcī. They are preceded by the Tāra and correspond to the vital breaths: prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna. || 174 ||
These mantras of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, joined with the fourth [vowel] and the fire-bride (agni-vadhū), have been declared;
the mudrās beginning with prāṇa should indeed be displayed in their proper sequence. 175.
Having brought the two hands together facing each other, joined and fully extended, with the little fingers and thumbs joined, this is the mudrā known as the Cakra. || 176 ||
Then, while touching his own ring fingers with both hands using the primary [mudrā], he should display the offering-mudrā (nivedyamudrikā) while reciting the mantra. || 177 ||
Dhvauṃ; having uttered "Salutation to the Supreme," one should say "to Vāmana"; and having uttered "to Aniruddha," one says "I offer this oblation. || 178 ||
This mantra is for the Vaiṣṇava Tantra; one should apply it similarly in the Śaiva and other systems. Then, [one should offer] those made of flour, accompanied by *samavarti* [grains]. || 179 ||
The mantra-practitioner should display lamps ignited with ghee and other substances, which possess intense brilliance and appear like the circling flight of pigeons. (180)
Taking [the lamp] with his hand and meditating, he should perform the *nīrājana* (waving) of the Lord over his head; this, preceded by the ringing of a bell, is called *ārātrika*.
To the south, he should prepare a sacrificial mound; having established the fire there and consecrated it according to the rules, the learned man should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite.
There, having worshipped the deity whose form has been described with perfumes and other offerings,
the knower of mantras, having offered oblations with the *tāra* and the *vyāhṛti*s, [should offer] with the root mantra.
Having offered twenty-five portions of milk-rice mixed with ghee,
one should again worship [the deity] with the vyāhṛtis and with perfumes and other offerings.
Having joined that [offering] and placed it upon the pedestal, one should dismiss the fire within the image;
with the remaining oblation, one should scatter the bali offering all around.

One should offer scents, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata) to the attendants of the deity; if one is unable to perform the fire-oblation (homa), one should perform a recitation (japa) twice the number of oblations required.
"Whichever limb may be deficient, the recitation (japa) should be double that number"—according to this statement, the wise declare this to apply in all cases. (187)
Some say: "We have no consensus on this matter, because their word does not proceed toward the application of a deficiency in the constituent parts of the ritual honor. (188)

Otherwise, there would be an over-extension; for if it were not so, there could be no restriction. Nor can there be a restriction of the logical principle of this statement without any basis in valid cognition.

Since its necessity is established by the requirements of the preliminary practices (prayoga) and so forth, it is nevertheless not approved by the learned (śiṣṭas) at any time for rites such as the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).

It should not be said that there is room for an alternative procedure (*anukalpa*) in this obligatory daily fire-sacrifice (*nityahoma*); for since the undesired consequence [of such an alternative] would follow, there is no restrictive rule for this obligatory rite. Therefore, established custom (*ācāra*) alone must be the refuge in its performance. || 191 ||
Having turned the water into nectar by means of the *dhenu-mudrā*, [one offers] a mouthful of water with the mantra:
"Thou art the covering of nectar," followed by the two *ṭha*s.

p. 102) Having given this [offering] into the hand of the deity from that which has emerged from the mouth, one should cause the face to rise by offering the essence of light and water, and then one should contemplate that the food offering (naivedya) has lost its essence; thereafter, one should remove it. || 193 ||
Having given that leavings to him, one should purify the area in the northeast;
Viṣvaksena is remembered as the splendor of Viṣṇu, and Caṇḍa is [the splendor] of the All-pervading One.
Likewise, Caṇḍeśvarī belongs to Śakti, and Caṇḍeśa belongs to Śaṅkara; Lambodara belongs to Gaṇapati, and Abhī belongs to Ucchiṣṭabhojin.
Rinsing the mouth, cleaning the teeth, sipping water, wiping the face, anointing the hands, perfuming the mouth, and wearing garlands and ornaments— (196)
Having offered those [flowers], preceded by the gift of water, the wise man should present betel-leaf mixed with pieces of camphor.
One should worship again with the services beginning with sandalwood paste and ending with the lamp.

This is declared to be the "Worship of the Gracious One" (Prasannārcā), which propitiates all the gods. Having offered the *argha*, one whose mind is focused on no other should present a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*).
"Others know that one should worship with the five-fold offerings (pañcopacāra); in this regard, some dispute concerning the worship of the attendants (pārṣada) during the ritual of worship. (199)

With perfumes and other offerings, one should worship [the deity] together with his retinue according to this verse from the *Kramadīpikā*. Since the secondary rites (*anukalpa*) follow from this very statement, they are not described extensively here.
Having praised each respective deity with hymns, one should then perform a circumambulation.
A single prostration with one hand or even a single circumambulation [is meritorious]; however, visiting Viṣṇu at an improper time destroys previously accumulated merit.
Then one should perform prostration, either with eight limbs or with five limbs:
with the two arms, the two feet, the two knees, the chest, the speech, and the eyes.
Prostration with the head and the mind is declared to be the eight-limbed (aṣṭāṅga) salutation.
With the two arms, the two knees, the head, speech, and the intellect—this is the five-limbed (pañcāṅga) salutation;
these two are the most excellent for acts of worship.
Now, the characteristics of the service mudrās are correctly explained: the lotus mudrā is said to be placed at the heart; that same [mudrā] becomes the seat. (204)
(103) With the right hand slightly bent at the fingers, the fingers should be joined in the best manner;
this is the Svāgata-svastika mudrā, with the fingers reaching to the base of the middle finger. || 205 ||
The Svastika-mudrā is performed with both hands; it is proclaimed as the mudrā for the arghya offering. Those same two hands, when extended, are declared to be the pādya-mudrā.

With the index finger resting on the base of the right thumb, and the little finger of the right hand extended, the three middle fingers [are held together]; this is proclaimed as the mudrā for the ritual rinsing (ācamana).
The ring finger and thumb joined together, with the other three fingers extended—this is the mudrā for the *madhuparka*; having thus consecrated the water-pot in one's hand. (208)
Having formed a fist for the bath with the middle finger and the thumb joined together, while the other three fingers are extended—this is proclaimed as the mudrā of the garment. (209)
The little finger and the thumb joined together, with the three middle fingers extended—
this is called the *yajñopavīta* mudrā by those who have mastered the Vedas.
The *madhuparkī* is considered the gesture with the palm turned upward and adorned with a seal; the *muktā*, which is a fist with the index finger extended, is proclaimed as the *gandha* gesture.
When the middle finger is raised with its face downward and the others are bound with the thumbs, it is declared to be the Puṣpa-mudrā (Flower Mudrā),
which increases the merit of offering flowers.
The thumb joined with the index finger while the other three fingers are contracted; this mudrā, when offered as incense, brings satisfaction to the gods. (213)
The *pauṣpikī* mudrā with palms facing upward is celebrated as the *dīpa* (lamp) mudrā, provided that the tips of the five fingers are joined together and knotted while facing upwards. (214)

This mudrā, bound in three ways, is proclaimed as that of the food offering (naivedya). With both hands joined back-to-back, one should rotate them with the fingers interlaced; this is known as the *chotikā*, and one should employ it during prostration.
Now, therefore, in the worship of Viṣṇu,
the wise one should perform the rite of offering to Brahman (brahmārpaṇa) with handfuls of water while reciting the mantra known as Brahmārpaṇa.

One should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) before and after the recitation; with the mind restrained, purified, observing silence, contemplating the mantra, with an undistracted mind and free from defects, one should keep the deity constantly in mind. || 2 ||
The best of practitioners should perform the recitation (japa) in the presence of the sun and other such objects for the sake of attaining all perfections;
thus says the Mantradevaprakāśikā. (3)
One should recite facing forward in the presence of the sun, a preceptor, the moon, a lamp, water, Brahmins, and cows.
Having performed the recitation according to one's ability, one should offer that recitation into the right hand of the deity for the sake of all accomplishments with this mantra: || 5 ||
O you who guard the secret more secret than the secret, accept this recitation performed by us; O Mother, may success be mine;
you, O Supreme Goddess, are my refuge. 6.

This mantra is for the Śākta tradition; one should likewise employ it in the Vaiṣṇava and other traditions. One should gratify [the deity] with the services due to kings, such as the white umbrella and the fly-whisk.
Whatever may be difficult to obtain among all the ritual services, one should mentally visualize all of that and provide it by means of scattering flowers.
Nārada said: "In the absence of the two types of ritual substances, one should offer water; with pure water alone, there is fullness. (9)
Having again offered a handful of flowers, the wise one should prostrate with the eight limbs;
having praised each respective deity with their specific hymns according to the prescribed rite.

Then the practitioner should entreat her with the gesture of supplication: "Whether through ignorance, negligence, or deficiency in the ritual practice, whatever has been omitted or excessive, you should forgive it all. (11)
O Treasure of Compassion, please forgive all of that out of your mercy—[that which was] devoid of material offerings, devoid of ritual action, and lacking in faith and mantra. (12)
Whatever action is performed by me in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—may all that become worship of you, O Lord, and may it lead to my prosperity. (13)
Whatever action I perform, whether it be very great or even very small, all of that is for the sake of compassion; may it be forgiven—here I join my palms in reverence.
Having risen and ascended to his seat, he should dissolve the entire host of the retinue into that form by means of the mudrā of withdrawal (upasaṃhāramudrā).
Having placed the right hand with its face upward into the left hand which is turned downward,
one should join the fingers with the fingers and rotate them.

This is the withdrawal mudrā (saṃhāramudrā), which is considered appropriate for the rite of dismissal (visarjana). Saying "Forgive me," one should perform the pervasive [mudrā] three times with the root mantra.

Having subsequently established the deity within the lotus of one's own heart, the wise person should, after inhaling the flower through the path of the *suṣumṇā*, perform the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*).
Having placed the remaining fragrance into the water of the conch and stirred it with sandalwood paste, the wise one should hold it in his hand and recite the root mantra seven times.
Having meditated upon all the founders of religious traditions, the wise man should sprinkle his own body with the water remaining from the worship of the deity,
which is held within a conch shell.
It removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin from those on whose limbs it has adhered.
The remains of the offering (nirmālya) should be worn upon the head, and the unguent should be applied to all the limbs. (21)

Having offered it to one who possesses devotion for Him, one should partake of the food offering (naivedya) after worshipping with mental perfumes and other offerings, preceded by the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the sages and so forth.
Having meditated upon oneself in the form of one's chosen deity, one who is devoted and of steady mind should recite the mantra according to the procedure seen in the scriptures. (23)

"At the completion of the count, one should again perform the *ṛṣi*-contemplation and the breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*); thus says the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā* at the conclusion of the dismissal (*udvāsana*). (24)
If a man performs an action prescribed by rule according to an improper method, he obtains no fruit at all; for that act results for him in nothing but mere suffering.
Whatever action is performed by men endowed with faith and devotion, with a perfectly pure disposition, that conduces to infinity. (26)
Whatever is performed devoid of ritual rules, corrupted by intention, and done without faith—that is seized by the asuras from that deluded person of wicked soul. (27)
By means of specific acts of worship, in accordance with the ten times, according to one's capacity, according to what is right, and in a manner not censured by the world. || 28 ||

One who is healthy and capable should perform [the rite] with the most excellent materials; one of middling capacity should use middling materials; and one who is inferior should proceed with inferior ones.
Accompanied by fire-rituals, oblations, and ornaments,
and joined with the purification of materials, this shall be the supreme worship.

One should offer the *kālasarga* (the offering at the appointed time) even if devoid of the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*); when accompanied by all the ritual services (*upacāra*), it constitutes the middling form of worship. || 31 ||
Having set aside various forms of splendor such as garments and ornaments, the worship consisting solely of an offering of flowers is indeed the lowest form of veneration.
If the practitioner is unable to perform this worship, then he should indeed meditate upon the deity alone and worship him perfectly. || 33 ||
Alternatively, the wise one should perform mental worship, or even self-worship; or else, he may perform purely external worship.
But one who is incapable of even the mere act of worship should give the materials for worship; and he who is not even able to give those should perform the viewing of the worship.
If one is unable to perform each preceding [duty], one should resort to each subsequent one; if one were to act otherwise than this, it would result in an undesirable fruit, as stated in the Śruti.
The master of the primary rule who conducts himself by means of a secondary rule— no fruit pertaining to the next world arises for that person of evil intellect.
He who does not possess even one [of these] goes downward; of this there is no doubt. Thus it has been stated by someone that this occurs for one who has not performed the mental worship.
One should not worship an external deity as that which generates the state of divinity; this is merely the prattle of the ignorant, for [it does not produce] the nature of that deity. 39.

One should accomplish [the rite] through the ritual ending with the placement of the *kalās*; for it has been declared that the success of that [mantra] depends upon the placement of the *mātṛkā* and the mantra. (40)
The *Tattvasāgarasaṃhitā* states a specific rule regarding birth-impurity (*sūtaka*): "Now I shall describe the worship of one who is under birth-impurity, as taught in the *Āgama*. (41)
Having bathed daily and having completed the supreme mental rite,
one should worship by means of the sequence of external worship and through the yoga of meditation.

If one is not a seeker of sensual pleasures, one should perform the worship of the deity like a regular obligatory rite (*nityakarman*); for he who performs the worship of the deity outside of the prescribed rules [is at fault]. (43)

Even a slight offering made by one who worships with devotion according to the rules, even with materials brought from others, yields no fruit at all, just like an oblation poured into a heap of ashes. (44)

For one who performs worship, the fruit shall be only half; the full fruit will not accrue. However, the wise person who, with devotion and effort, personally prepares the entire ritual apparatus and performs the worship, shall obtain the full fruit.
Having personally brought and prepared the articles for worship, one should perform the worship;
for this is indeed the best method, the supreme one that grants all desired objects.

Whatever has been accomplished through one's wife, sons, friends, and others, and that which is the intermediate form of worship—by means of those [deities], the fruit of that [worship] shall be attained together with them. || 47 ||
That which is performed by others and given to one, or that which is purchased by means of it, is considered secondary; through such [service], the fruit shall be only one-quarter. || 48 ||
One may bring flowers from trees planted by others and perform worship; however, for one who does so without informing the owner, that worship is fruitless.
Only those who perform what has been prescribed are the recipients of the fruit;
for all desired objects, it is not otherwise. (50)

A twice-born man should perform acts such as giving gifts, fire-offerings, and worship with means acquired through righteous means; for if he does not do so, even while performing them with devotion, he goes downward.
Thus the common procedure for worship has been correctly described. Thereafter, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) every day with a tenth part of the number of recitations (japa).

Furthermore, their status as a tenth part may occur only in certain cases otherwise; or rather, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) once the number [of recitations] has reached one hundred thousand.

Alternatively, when one's recitation [of the mantra] has reached its full extent, one should perform a fire-offering (homa). One should perform the homa as a tenth part [of the recitation], uttering the mantra ending with "svāhā. (54)
In the rite of fire-offering (homakārya), the mantras end with the wife of Agni (svāhā); in worship (pūjā), they end with "tanu" (tanno).
The wise one [should act] with a mantra purified by the syllable Om (oṃ) and ending in svāhā.
"One should offer oblations at the conclusion with 'svāhā', while meditating upon the deity of the mantra"; by such statements, the rule that all [mantras] end with 'svāhā' is established. (56)

The claim that one should utter "svāhā" again even at the end of a mantra where "svāhā" already occurs is the opinion of certain [authorities] who are enveloped by the deep internal darkness of ignorance. (57)
"Namaḥ," "svāhā," "svadhā," "vauṣaṭ," and "vaṣaṭ" are used for the offering [of oblations]. This is their application;
why would there be another [application] for this alone? (58)
The phrase "the mantra is at the end of that" indicates that the word "that" (tat) refers to the end [of the mantra].
Otherwise, if it were taken as having an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha), there would be unnecessary complexity (gaurava). || 59 ||
Even in the fire-offering (agnau karaṇahoma), that which is approved by the practice of the Chandogas is therefore established as being complete even without the word "svāhā."
A wise person should understand that this applies even at the beginning of a word such as *namaḥ*; furthermore, a sentence distinguished by the conduct of the learned is also recited. (61)
Speech, desire, power, the syllable Om, and Śrī are said [to be the five limbs].
One should never employ the syllable Om in these initial mantras.
At the end of the two *ṭha*s, one should not utter the two *ṭha*s; at the end of *namaḥ*, one should not utter *namaḥ*.

Now, I shall describe the procedure for the fire-oblation (homa) according to all the tantras, having also thoroughly examined the ritual manuals (kalpas), the compendiums (saṃhitās), the Śāradā-tantra, and others.

The mantra-practitioner should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the prescribed rule in a square or other shaped sacrificial pit for the attainment of all goals; that procedure shall now be explained.
One should regularly perform the obligatory and occasional fire-oblations (homa) either in the fire or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
although there is no rule anywhere for performing optional (kāmya) oblations on a sacrificial mound.
Nevertheless, because this [rite] is not prohibited and in accordance with worldly convention, the optional (kāmya) oblation should also be performed by practitioners in some instances there.

Having thoroughly washed his feet after performing the fire oblation (homa) and sipped water (ācamana), and having awakened [the deity], he should bow to the Guru and others on his seat and perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaviśodhana).
Having performed the Mātṛkā-nyāsa as revealed in the respective ritual manuals (kalpa),
and having likewise performed the nyāsa of the principles (tattva) and so forth, as well as the restraint of breath (prāṇasaṃyama).
Having consecrated the site, that minister should prepare either a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or a leveled altar (sthaṇḍila);
he should make it one cubit in size and four finger-breadths in height.
It should be one cubit in measure, raised to the height of the joint of the thumb and forefinger, very beautiful,
made of sand, and square on all sides.

One should consecrate it according to the prescribed rite for the object, or else by means of gazing and other such acts; gazing is performed with the root mantra, while sprinkling is considered to be done with the weapon-mantra (śara).
Striking with those very [darbhas] and sprinkling with the *varman* mantra is prescribed. One should draw three lines each, pointing eastward and northward, with the *hṛdaya* mantra. (10)
The deities of the lines with tips pointing eastward are traditionally held to be Mukunda, Īśa, and Purandara;
those of the lines with tips pointing northward are Brahmā, Vaivasvata, and Indu.
(110) One should write the sentences pertaining to the specific section (pakṣa) according to one's own Vedic branch (śākhā).
"One should write the lines as prescribed by one's own branch," so says the *Laghudīpikā*. (12)
