It is also stated here in the *Prapañcasāra*: "One should draw [the lines] according to one's own Vedic school; however, some say that the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) should consist of two blades of *darbha* grass, with the mantra 'tenedaṃ'. (13)
Alternatively, one should draw a triangle surrounded by a hexagon there;
outside that, an eight-petaled lotus with filaments, and further beyond that.
Having constructed a square with four gates, the most excellent practitioner, within that space, should draw a triangle and [the] Śakti in its center. || 15 ||

One should write the elements suitable for the rite, the gems, and the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished, interwoven with the letters of the mantra and surrounded by the seed-syllable of Śakti.
Likewise, the practitioner should place the syllables of the wheels and so forth upon the girdles according to the ritual rule; first the word "sahasrāra," and then "kaumodaki" should follow.
After [the mantra of] Mahāśaṅkhapada, and then again Mahāśaṅkhapada,
the mantras of one's own [deity], ending with the armor (varma) and weapon (astra), are indeed proclaimed in their proper sequence.
First [he saw] the great Pāñcajanya conch, immediately after that the great plow, then the great mace,
and after that the great trident.
One should know that the mantras for the conch and the other [emblems] end with *svāhā* in their respective order.
The discus and the others are situated in the cardinal directions, while the conch and the others are located in the intermediate corners (koṇa).
Afterwards, one should sprinkle the ritual materials, the oblation, and so forth—all of them—with the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*).
Then the practitioner of mantra should worship the Vāgīśvarī-pīṭha.
Beginning from the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) and ending with the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra), I shall respectfully describe the powers of Bhuvaneśvarī, as well as her seat-mantra.
Jayā, Vijayā, then Ajitā and Aparājitā, Nityā, Vilāsinī, Dogdhrī, Aghorā, and Maṅgalā—these are the nine. 23.
"Salutation to the essence of the yoga-pīṭha of Vāgīśvarī and Īśvara. This is the pīṭha-mantra beginning with *hrīṃ*; having invoked [the deities] into this, one should worship them. (24)
Vāgīśvarī, having bathed after her menses and wearing blue lotuses,
together with Vāgīśvara, [should be worshipped] with ritual offerings in due order.
Then, one who knows the procedure should contemplate the body of Vāgīśvarī; as it has been stated in the *Tattvasāgara-saṃhitā* and other texts, one should perform worship. (26)
There, one should contemplate Lakṣmī as being in her menses and the Lord Nārāyaṇa; from their union according to the worldly rite, the fire is produced there.
One should understand the specific [fire] through its respective designations in due order,
whether it be that produced from sun-crystals and the like, or that born in the house of a Vedic scholar.
Having brought the fire in a vessel made of bell-metal or similar material,
one should take a small ember with the Astra-mantra and [protect it] with the Kavaca-mantra.
Therefore, for the sake of accomplishing all goals, the practitioner of mantras should abandon the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (kravyāda).
Some have declared here that the renunciation consists in saying, "I abandon the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters. (30)
One should then consecrate the remainder with the four [rites] beginning with inspection (vīkṣaṇa),
while contemplating the unification of the fire of the sacrificer with the fires of the stomach and the moon.
With this seed-syllable *raṃ*, the practitioner of mantras should unite consciousness with the fire;
it is consecrated by the *oṃ* mantra and rendered nectar-like by the *dhenu-mudrā*.
Protected by the arrow-mantra and enveloped by the armor-mantra, he should diligently circumambulate it three times from left to right.
Preceded by the proper utterance of the Praṇava,
with his knees touching the ground, he should face the fire.
While Vāgīśvarī, full of desire, was sleeping in the presence of Śiva, the Goddess,
perceiving it as the seed of Śiva, should deposit this [mantra] into her womb.
The practitioner, having duly cast into the fire a fuel-stick measuring a span and saturated with clarified butter, and having burned it in this rite of oblation; || 36 ||
"O Brahman, you shall be the supervisor of what has been done and what remains to be done here"; having spoken thus, the officiant (mantrin) should sit upon kuśa grass to the south of the fire.

The excellent practitioner, if unable [to procure the actual items], should likewise imagine these things: a water-pot, an upper garment, a silken cloth, and a young brahmin student (baṭuka). || 38 ||
If he is capable, he should indeed choose a Brāhmaṇa for the office of the Brahmā priest, and [present him with] three garments along with flowers, sandalwood paste, and betel-leaf. (39)

The wise say that the "ornament" (alaṅkaraṇa) is the provision of the [two] garments; with the thought that it is for the sake of sexual union, one should offer the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) to those two. (40)

In the Dīpikā and other texts, however, the binding of the bracelet (kaṅkaṇabandhana) is prescribed here: having sprinkled the fire with the Astra-mantra and having covered the sacrificial pit (yoni) with excellent kuśa grass.

The practitioner should place a bundle of arrows in the cardinal directions with the weapon-mantra; with that same mantra, he should consecrate it for the protection of the womb using the root-mantra.
One should tie a *darbha* bracelet upon the hand as an auspicious charm (*kautuka*), reciting for the protection of the pregnant woman:
"O Śakti, protect, protect! (43).
"One should display the Jvālinī mudrā"—this is the opinion of the Ratnāvalī; its definition is stated in that very work, and it is now described here. (44)
Having made the wrists even and the hands with fingers fully extended, one should join the two middle fingers and place the two thumbs in their midst. 45.
The Jvālinī mudrā is considered the kindler of fire;
then the practitioner should ignite that fire with this mantra. (46)
Having uttered "cit piṅgala hana daha paca yugmāni," one says "sarvajñājñāpaya svāhā"; this is the mantra beloved by the Fire-god: [cit piṅgala hana daha paca paca sarvajñājñāpaya svāhā]. || 47 ||

While intending to offer an oblation and while the oblation has already been offered, one should not blow upon the fire with the hand, a winnowing basket, the mouth, or a wooden tool; rather, one should fan it with a fan or similar means.
"One should blow upon the fire with the mouth alone, for this [fire] was born from the mouth. As for the statement "not with the mouth," they apply that to worldly [fire]. (49)
Then the mantra-practitioner should display the mudrā called Saptajihvā, [reciting]:
"I bow to the blazing fire, to Jātavedas, the consumer of oblations. (50)
Having worshipped the fire with this mantra— blazing, golden-hued, and facing in all directions—
the three types of tongues of the Vasu [Agni] are addressed.

One who knows the ritual procedure should place [the mantras] throughout the body of oneself— in the genitals, anus, head, mouth, vital breath, and eyes— according to the method that is about to be described.
The letters from *sa* to *ya*, joined with half-portions of fire (*ra*) and accompanied by the bindu, are declared to be the seven mantras of the tongues in their respective order. (53)
The third is Padmarāgāsuvarṇā, followed by Bhadralohitā; then Lohitā, Śvetā, Dhūminī, and Karālikā. (54)
The tongue of fire intended for the rājasī [nature] is prescribed for the rite of subjugation (vaśya); it is golden, sky-colored, red, black, and another is considered to be of beautiful luster.
The sattvic tongues are remembered as being multiform and intensely red;
they possess the universal form, emit sparks, are smoke-colored, and have the speed of thought.
Lohitā, Karālā, Kālī, and Tāmasajihvikā— these are the Sāttvika goddesses for divine worship, while the Rājasa goddesses are for rites performed with desire.
These [mantras] belonging to Tamas should be employed by the wise in cruel deeds against the gods, along with the Pitṛs, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Nāgas, and Piśācas. (58)
And these Rākṣasas, having successively taken refuge in the tongues of the fire,
performed the placement of the hands and limbs of the fire with these mantras, just as before.
Sahasrārcis, Svastipūrṇa, Uttiṣṭhapuruṣa, Dhūmavyāpin, Saptajihva, and Dhanurdhara—these are the ones who have been proclaimed. (60)
The limb-mantras, associated with their respective seed-syllables, should be deposited in due order; likewise, the eight forms of Jātavedas [Agni] should be placed upon one's own body.
One should place [the syllables] in sequence upon the head, the limbs, the sides, the buttocks, the lower back, the hips, the sides, and the shoulders; these are now described in their proper order.
Jātavedas, Saptajihva, he who is known as Havyavāhana, the one named Aśvodaraja, and likewise the one called Vaiśvānara—[these are his names]. (63)
Kaumāratejas, Viśvamukha, and Devamukha—these, beginning with the word *tārāgnaye* and ending with *namaḥ*, are the forms of Fire (Vahni-mūrtis). (64)
Beginning from the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) up to the circle of fire (vahnimaṇḍala), the practitioner of mantra should worship the sacred seat (pīṭha) together with its nine powers.
Yellow, white, reddish, black, speckled, intensely radiant, emitting sparks, beautiful, and flaming—
these are declared to be the nine powers of the fire.
Having offered a seat with the seed-syllable (bīja), one should fashion the form (mūrti) with the root-mantra (mūla),
[visualizing the deity] holding the gestures of boon, power, auspiciousness, and fearlessness with his sprout-like hands.

(114) One should [visualize] him as golden-hued, with the luster of vermilion, seated upon a lotus, three-eyed, and endowed with the tongues that will be described hereafter, in accordance with the sequence of rites. 68.

One who knows the ritual rules should meditate thus upon those with their hair tied up in matted locks: she is golden-colored when presiding over gold, black when presiding over a Rakshasa, and blue-hued when presiding over a Nila.
The golden one has the color of beryl; the red one follows the fire;
the one situated in the water has the luster of the rising sun and resembles a ruby.
Suprabhā, Vāyubhāgī, Raktikā, Rajanaprabhā, Yathārthā, Bahurūpā, and Dakṣottaranivāsinī. (71)
That [line] in the middle of the *kuṇḍa* is praised; they declare its fruit to be as follows:
it is used for attracting gold and the like, while *Kanaka* is used for paralyzing (*stambhana*) and other such rites. (72)

She is considered red for acts of hatred and so forth, black for the rite of killing; she is said to be of beautiful luster (suprabhā) for pacification, and intensely red (atiraktikā) for driving away.
In the Bahurūpottara [direction] one attains success and supernatural power (ṛddhi), and likewise in the south; she always extends auspiciousness in the center—of this there is no doubt. (74)
Then, one should sprinkle pure water upon the girdle,
and spread *darbha* grass with their tips pointing inward across the middle of the girdle.
For in the rite of strewing [the sacrificial grass], one should discard the cow-tail hair and the *īṣikā* reeds; this has been stated by Bhaṭṭanāga in the *Tripurāsārasaṃgraha*: || 76 ||

Having set aside the cow's tail and the blade of grass, the wise man should spread another kind of grass; he should then place the enclosing sticks (paridhis) in the various directions, excluding the eastern one.

Having worshipped them in a clockwise direction, one should place those three [deities], Brahmā and the others, [upon arrows] produced from a single tree, which are fresh, not too straight, and auspicious. (78)
One should take staffs made of Khadira or Udumbara wood, measuring either a forearm's length or equal to the girdle;
in the absence of the former, one should take each subsequent type in order.

The practitioner, having meditated upon the fire, should worship the fire in the center with the fire-mantra; he should then worship the tongues, preceded by their seed-syllables, in the center and in the six corners.
One should worship the deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatās) upon the filaments according to the stated method; one should worship the Mūrtis, who bear the Śakti and the Svastika, upon the petals.
Then [he should place] the world-protectors in the directions, and outside of them their weapons;
afterwards, having taken the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with his two hands, he should hold them facing downwards. (82)
Having heated them three times in fire and taken darbha grass,
the practitioner should purify their tips, roots, and middles with them in due order.
Having taken them with the left hand, the practitioner of mantra should sprinkle them with the right; he should heat them again and cast the darbha grasses into the fire.
One should place those two within the kuśa grass on the right side of oneself;
then, taking the vessel for the clarified butter (ājya), one should sprinkle it with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (astra).
One should place two strainers into a vessel measuring a span; having poured clarified butter into it, one should consecrate it with the rites of inspection and so forth.
Having lifted the embers with the Heart-mantra, one should cast them there;
this is designated as *tāpana* (the heating rite) by practitioners skilled in the Tantras.

Having ignited a pair of *darbha* blades and cast them into the clarified butter (*ājya*), the wise one should then throw them into the fire with the *hṛdaya-mantra*; this indeed is the rite of purification (*pavitrīkaraṇa*).

Having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) with ghee using a pair of blazing darbha grasses while wearing the armor-mantra, one should cast the darbha into the fire; this is declared to be the "illumination" (abhidyotana).
Then, having displayed blades of *darbha* grass ignited in clarified butter while reciting the *astra-mantra*, one should consign them into the fire; this is considered the "kindling" (*pradyotana*).
Having taken clarified butter and cast embers into the fire, one should touch water with the thumb and the ring finger, holding two *darbha* blades measuring a span (*prādeśa*).
Having held it, one should purify the ghee with the Astra mantra; this is considered the purification of the ghee.
Likewise, with two Kuśa blades and the Hṛdaya mantra, [one should purify] facing oneself.
One should perform the immersion in clarified butter; these are declared to be the six purificatory rites (saṃskāras).
A pair of darbha blades with a knot, measuring a span (prādeśa), should be placed within the clarified butter.

Having cast [the breath] out and divided it into two parts, one should contemplate [them] on the dark and the other on the bright fortnight; then, one should place the iḍā channel in the left part and the piṅgalā in the right.

Having meditated upon the Suṣumnā in the center, the wise one should perform the oblation according to the prescribed rule; taking clarified butter from the southern portion with the Sruva spoon while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra.
One should offer oblation to Agni with the mantra "Svāhā to Agni" into the right eye of the Fire; likewise, taking [the substance] from the left, one offers it into the left eye of the Fire. (96)
Then, with the heart-mantra "svāhā to Soma," one should offer oblation from the center, taking clarified butter and offering it into the eye on the forehead of the fire.
One should offer oblations into the Vaiṣṇava fire with the mantra "svāhā to Agni and Soma," for the true presence of the Three-eyed Lord exists in that fire, except when it is Nṛhari.
Some, however, recognize this oblation as belonging to Viṣṇu in every respect; for the three-eyed nature of the Fire-god is not said to be dependent upon [the status of] the deity. (99)

If that were so, how could this oblation be performed with another mantra? Taking clarified butter from the southern portion with the *sruva* ladle while reciting the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra), [he should offer it]. 100.

One should offer oblations into the mouth [of the fire] with "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā! and then one should cause the remnants of the clarified butter to fall upon the portions according to the sequence of the oblations.
This has also been stated by Śrī Somaśambhu in another Śaiva Āgama:
"The practitioner, having taken clarified butter from the three portions in sequence with the *sruva* ladle... (102)

The wise practitioner should perform the opening of the mouth and eyes of the fire by sequentially pouring the remaining clarified butter into the fire with the mantras "svā" and "he," according to the respective divisions. 103.
One should contemplate the central, eastern, southern, western, and northern sectors as having the nature of Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Sadyojāta, and Vāmadeva respectively.
At the time of the fire-oblation (homa), having meditated upon the form of Agni, the practitioner of mantra should perform the daily oblation at the western face. 105.

For subjugation, attraction, good fortune, nourishment, and so forth, as well as for pacification and the purification of cooked offerings, the excellent practitioner should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) on the left side.

But for the purpose of slaying with a sword and so forth, as well as for the desire for victory and for the sake of producing what is desired, one should sacrifice facing the east, just as previously described.
For the purposes of killing, eradication, inciting hatred, and paralyzing, [the practice] is on the right; however, for liberation, the expiation is performed in that very same fifth [position].
The arrangement of the portions is fully described in the *Mantramuktāvalī* treatise;
thereafter, one should offer oblations of clarified butter with the *sāvitrī* and the *vyāhṛti* mantras. || 109 ||
The best of practitioners should offer oblations into the fire three times with the fire-mantra;
he should then perform the rites for the fire, beginning with the impregnation (garbhādhāna), in their proper sequence. (110)
With eight oblations of clarified butter, each accompanied by the Praṇava, and with the Mūla-mantra according to the Jñānārṇava,
the rites beginning with Garbhādhāna are performed.

In the *Mantramuktāvalī* treatise as well, it is proclaimed in this very same way: "Having offered seven oblations with the *hṛdaya*-mantra, [one performs] the rites beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*). (112)

Some mantra-experts say that one should perform each of these rites individually: first the *garbhādhāna* (conception), then the *puṃsavana* (ensuring a male child), and thereafter the *sīmantonnayana* (parting the hair).

Immediately thereafter, the birth-rite (jātakarma) should take place, as well as the naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa); after that, the rite of going outside (bahirniṣkramaṇa), and finally, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) is prescribed.

Furthermore, for him there are the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā), the initiation (upanayana), the Great Observance (mahāvrata), likewise the secret doctrine (upaniṣad), followed by the parting of the hair (godāna), marriage, and death. (115)
Those rites ending with marriage are prescribed for auspicious acts; those ending with death are designated for cruel deeds by those who know the Agamas of fire.

Since it is well known from the *Candrikā* that there are exactly sixteen preparatory rites (*saṃskāras*), the author has stated [the limit] as ending with the gift of the cow (*godāna*); thereafter, the return home (*samāvartana*) is described. (117)
The specific procedure for the naming ceremony (*nāmakarman*) in the *tūrṇāhoma* and other rites has been declared;
having likewise performed the naming ceremony by offering eight oblations of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*), [the rite is complete]. 118.
One should perform the visualization with the root mantra, "You are the guide, O Fire. Then, having fully worshipped his two parents, one should unite them within oneself.
One should offer five fuel-sticks (samidh) drenched in clarified butter at the base and the tip;
however, one should avoid those produced from the *śleṣmātaka* tree and the *piśāca* tree.
This has also been stated by Bhaṭṭanāga in the *Sārasamuccaya*:
"Having abandoned the *śleṣmātā-piśāca* tree, one should take it from others. (121)
The best of mantra-knowers, according to the prescribed rite, should offer one oblation for each of the tongue, the limbs, and the forms of the fire, in their proper sequence, using the mantras.

Some Tantrikas maintain that there are subsidiary mantras (aṅgamantra) for Nṛtya and the other [arts], while others who understand the meaning of the tantras hold that the subsidiary mantras belong to the root mantra (mūlamantra). 123.
(118) Likewise, the offering of water for honor (*argha*) and so forth, as well as the fire sacrifice (*homa*), are mutual indications;
here, tradition (*sampradāya*) is the refuge, and nothing else remains. || 124 ||

Having taken up clarified butter with the *sruva* spoon four times into the *sruc* ladle, the practitioner, standing before the fire with a disciplined mind, should offer it while holding the *sruc* with his hand. (125)
One should offer oblations with the fire-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* for the sake of prosperity; one should offer ten oblations with the mantra of Vighneśvara.
Then, one should offer oblations both individually and collectively;
this is considered the common "mouth of the fire" for all mantras.
Then, having worshipped the seat of the chosen mantra together with its Śakti within the fire,
one should worship that deity in the form of Agni, the bestower of desired boons.
The practitioner of mantra should offer oblations into its mouth twenty-five times with clarified butter using the root mantra; this is known as the unification of the faces.
Contemplating the identity of the fire and the deity along with one's own self, one should offer eleven oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra.
This junction of the channels has been taught by those who know the traditional scriptures;
one should offer oblations to the principal limbs in their proper sequence. (131)
The best of practitioners should properly offer each oblation with clarified butter,
or else with sesame seeds mixed with the three sweets as prescribed in the ritual manuals.
Or, for the sake of accomplishing his desired object, he may perform a fire-oblation (homa) as he wishes;
then, the knower of the ritual rules should perform the oblation with the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
"Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ," preceded by "svāhā," and joined with "agnaye ca pṛthivyai ca mahate ca. (134)
These Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis) are endowed with greatness derived from the moon, the stars, and the directions; they are in every respect composed of the deities.
In the Śāradā [Tantra], however, it is declared that one should then offer oblations with the *vyāhṛtis*;
therein, the *mahāvyāhṛtis* are said to be as follows: [136]
The wise should consider both these positions as mere conceptual constructs; the practitioner should offer the full oblation with the ladle using the root mantra. (137)
(119) Its characteristic has been proclaimed specifically in the context of the *pūrṇāhuti* sacrifice:
having filled the *sruva* ladle with clarified butter, and then having filled the *sruc* ladle with that [same butter]. 138.
Then, having turned it face-downward, the knower of mantras should rise;
with his body upright, he should place the bases of those two [the sruk and sruva] at the root of his navel.
Having uttered the mantra beginning with the root syllable and ending with the *nādānta*, preceded by the left foot,
and accompanied by fruit, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), [one should offer it] with an uninterrupted stream of clarified butter (*ājya*).
The practitioner of mantra should again perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the thought that it is supreme nectar;
such is the definition of the complete oblation as proclaimed by the venerable Somaśambhu. 141.
Having placed the *sruva* ladle face down upon the *sruc* which is filled with clarified butter,
and having fixed a flower at the tip of the *sruc*, [he should then act] with his left hand.
Again, holding those two with the left hand in the mudrā resembling a conch shell,
one should remain with the upper body straight, the feet even, and fully composed.
Fixing the root of that [channel] at the navel, with his eyes fixed intently on the tip of the *sruc* ladle,
he emerged through the *suṣumṇā*, having abandoned the causal deities such as Durgā and the rest.
Having brought [the mantra] up to the end of the left position, one should unweariedly extract the root of those two;
above the root mantra, one should utter the ending "vauṣaṭ."
Then one should offer clarified butter into the fire with a stream of ghee as thick as a barleycorn,
using the mantra known as Brahmārpaṇa, and furthermore, eight oblations.

One should perform oblations with the most excellent mantra for the sake of liberation from the bondage of karma; [this applies] to everything from here on, by virtue of one's life-force, intellect, body, and authority over dharma. (148)
At the end of the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, one should utter the Vastu-mantra; thereafter, one should proclaim it with a well-disposed mind, speech, and action.
One should declare whatever has been thought with the hands, the feet, the belly, and the penis, as well as whatever has been spoken and whatever has been done. (150)

Having spoken thus, "all that," one should utter the words "brahmārpaṇam"; at the end, the phrase "may it be" (bhavatu) should be added twice—this is considered the mantra of the offering to Brahman (brahmārpaṇamanu). || 151 ||

Then, having performed the ritual dismissal (udvāsana) of one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) along with its limbs and enclosures, one should again [perform the worship] of the tongues and other parts of the fire according to the prescribed procedure.
Having offered each oblation one by one and sprinkled water upon oneself, one should unite the fire with one's own self, along with the enclosing sticks and the surrounding grass mats. (153)

The practitioner of mantras should burn these [substances] during occasional rites (naimittika), but he should not burn them during daily rites (nitya). After the oblation has been offered, the preceptor should subsequently present the bali offering upon the maṇḍala.
One should respectfully offer oblations to the constellations, together with the zodiac signs and the days of the week, in their proper order, preceded by perfumes, flowers, and incense.
The collection of stars beginning with Aśvinī consists of two and one-quarter [nakṣatras];
immediately following this, excluding the signs starting with Aries, they are designated by the names of the constellations. 156.
Having uttered the word "to the deities" (*devatābhyaḥ*), one should then say the word "day and night" (*divānaktaṃ*).
Then, one should say "to all wandering beings" (*cāribhyaḥ*) and "obeisance to all spirits" (*bhūtebhyaś ca namaḥ*). || 157 ||
Thus, when that zodiacal sign is complete, one should apply [the ritual] therein; likewise, one should apply it for the planets who are the lords of those respective signs. || 158 ||
One should offer oblations to the seven instruments during the interval between Pisces and Aries;
thus is the bali-offering prescribed for the rite of homa.
One should construct the mandala of the heaps with a division into inner and outer sections; some authorities describe it as circular, while those who know it as such describe it as square.
Or if the twelve zodiac signs were circular in shape,
they would be shaped like ants or resemble citron fruits.
The wheel may be circular or square; it should consist of twelve sectors, resembling the petals of a lotus, as described by the wise. (162)
Mars, Venus, Mercury, the Moon, the Sun conjoined with Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and Rāhu are the lords [of the houses] in order. (163)
These have been declared as the lords of the zodiac signs; their forms are now described here: ruddy, white, green, and likewise pale-red. (164)
Pāṇḍu, Vicitra, Sitetara, Piśaṅgaka, Piṅgala, Karbura, Babhru, and Malina follow one another in sequence according to their respective lusters. (165)
The weekdays, the lakes, and the seven ending with Ketu are the nine planets;
likewise, Vava, Mānava, Kaulava, and Taittila [are the karaṇas]. (166)
Gada, Vāṇija, and Viṣṭi—these are said to be the seven Karaṇas. Thereafter, the practitioner of mantras should worship the deity according to the prescribed rule. (167)
Then the wise practitioner should satisfy the Brahmins with garments, ornaments, and other gifts;
the mantra-practitioner should also employ the "Fire-mouth" (agnimukha) rite, as prescribed, even in the daily fire-oblation.
Regarding this, some superficial thinkers say: "This rule does not apply to the obligatory [rite], for a distinction between the obligatory and the optional rites is observed everywhere. (169)
Moreover, since this rite is a constant duty, the days have passed by this very procedure; what is the use of other rites, such as those performed in autumn? (170)
"Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) on the south," and so forth, is the specific ritual procedure;
because it results in the permission for the remaining rites, the ceremonies such as the conception (garbha) and others do not follow from this. || 171 ||

In this regard, it is said here that by means of which the rites beginning with the *garbha* (conception) are to be performed; having explained the entire procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*), [the remaining details] are found in the *Śāradātilaka* and other such works. (172)

The practitioner of mantras should burn these [offerings] during occasional rites (naimittika), but he should not burn them during daily rites (nitya). It is held that the only distinction regarding the enclosing sticks (paridhi) is that they are not burned [in the daily rite]. || 173 ||
Only this much distinction between the two is understood here; otherwise, why would that other distinction between the two oblations not have been stated by him? (174)
In the Saṃhitā, according to the supplementary rules for Agastya, this "mouth of fire" (agnimukha) is prescribed for the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites alike. (175)

In the Jñānārṇava it is also stated: "One should perform the rites beginning with the impregnation (garbhādhāna); thereafter, one should perform the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma), and immediately after that, the optional fire-oblation (kāmyahoma). (176)
In accordance with various statements such as these,
it should be understood that those rites apply even to the obligatory (nitya) [rites], as does any specific injunction (vaiśeṣika-vidhi).
[The view that it has the result of not permitting the remainder is incorrect; it is said to be another injunction (vidhyantara), but not a specific injunction (vaiśeṣika-vidhi). || 178 ||
When all [the oblations] have reached the mouth of the fire, two additional *vyāhṛtis* are used— at the beginning and at the end of the *homa*,
or between the two pairs of *vyāhṛtis*— each according to its own [mantra].
It is taught as moving from one station to another, or as the unification of the faces;
it is the piercing of the channel (nāḍī) and the joining [of the breaths], this being the head of the opposing side. 180.
(122) "The statement [of the opponent] should serve as a refutation of the counter-position," so say those who follow reasoning (tarkānusārin).
Now, regarding the fourfold [set] beginning with the examination of the word *saṃskāra*: 181.

It should be stated that this is the intended meaning (*tātparya*), because of its simplicity and due to the distinction between the primary injunctions; let that indeed be the primary ritual procedure (*mukhyakalpa*), while in the secondary procedure (*anukalpa*) there is a twofold injunction. (182)

To this it is replied: he should not be intent upon the inspection and so forth, because the inspection and other rites must precede the formal installation (ādhāna) according to the sequence prescribed in the scripture.

In the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), there can be neither renunciation nor the prior performance of the fire-installation ceremony; otherwise, one would have to assume another root-cause for the act of gazing and so forth.

Because of the importance [of the ritual], even in such rites as those involving fire, and because the fulfillment of optional (kāmya) rites is achieved through that very act of establishing the sacred fires (ādhāna). (185)

Thus, the expectancy regarding "how it is to be done" (itikartavyatākāṅkṣā) is not satisfied by the general [injunction] alone; otherwise, there would be no connection between the mantra and the vessel in that context. (186)

Or rather, let there be for us a "full oblation" (pūrṇāhuti) simply from the sight of the [teacher's] name; otherwise, the four [acts] beginning with the glance—the consecration, the word, and the meaning—are not required. (187)
"This is declared to be the 'mouth of the fire' (agnimukha)," according to the words of Śāradā; and it has also been stated by Bhaṭṭanāga in this well-refined [work]: 188.

By means of such words as "vidhi" (injunction) and so forth, which are connected with sound and the other sense objects, there is the communication of the entire complex of ritual action through the mediation of its purpose. || 189 ||

Otherwise, in the absence of the spreading of grass and other such items during the obligatory fire-sacrifice (nityahoma), this [procedure] would be inconsistent; therefore, one should not burn these [materials] in obligatory rites.
Or how could it be appropriate for the learned one to say "having performed the consecration according to rule"?
Therefore, this is compared to the swallowing of a husk by a bride.
Now, the summary for the homa of the Sānatkumāris is stated; I shall describe the consecration of the fire which is common to all. (1)
Listen now, O Nārada, to that by which all tasks are accomplished—whether they be daily rites, occasional rites, rites for specific desires, or the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa). || 2 ||
In ritual practice, this is praised everywhere for the sake of pleasing the deity; having first performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and having arranged the general water offering (sāmānyārgha).
Either in a sacrificial pit or upon a consecrated mound, one should place a seat in the center;
having purified it with the root mantra and through the consecratory rites such as inspection and the rest.

One should worship the queen, who has bathed after her menses, together with the king; having consecrated the fire according to the ritual rules, one should cast [the oblation] into it, kindle it, and awaken it.
Having strewn *kuśa* grass in all directions, one should also place the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). Having worshipped Brahmā and the others upon their seats, one should worship the fire.

Having purified the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and having purified the clarified butter according to the rule, he should offer five fuel-sticks (*samidh*) into the fire and four oblations of clarified butter.
The most excellent practitioner, having offered oblations of clarified butter according to the rules, should perform the purificatory rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*, each with eight offerings.
Having thus consecrated the fire, one should place the root mantra upon one's body; then, having meditated on that deity within the fire, one should also worship it according to the prescribed rite.

One should offer the prescribed substances into his mouth according to the stated number; having performed the oblation, one should then offer the "limb-portion" (daśāṃśa) and subsequently the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Thus has the summary regarding the fire-oblation (homa) spoken by Sanatkumāra been declared. In the event of inability to perform the oblation, one should perform the recitation (japa) fourfold.
The twice-born [should receive] sixfold or eightfold [the fee], according to the respective order;
however, some have stated here that the number for the *homa* should be fourfold. (12)

Because it is established by the principle of *prakrama* (contextual sequence), for the sake of brevity, and out of deference [to tradition], as stated in the *Dīpikā* regarding the rule "for those who are unable" (*aśaktānām*) and so forth, [the term applies] to the *saṃhitā* and other [Vedic recensions]. (13)

To this it is replied: the fourfold nature of the recitation itself is prescribed here; for, due to the consequence of supplying ellipses, a qualified injunction would result in excessive complexity. (14)

If that [act] were a *homa*, it would result from the violation of the syntactic enclosure (*saṃdaṃśa*) by such statements as "if thus" and so forth; therefore, in this context of *homa*, the desire for that *homa* is enjoined. (15)

Nor is there any contradiction with logic, since there is an alternative procedure for one who lacks a limb; or rather, let this option be dependent on capacity, as in the case of the alternative regarding the oblation (homa).
Just as in the worship of the planets and other deities, the sequence follows the number of oblations; the teachers have likewise declared this meaning for the subsequent [rite]. (17)

The [requirement] for the libation (tarpaṇa) and so forth should be understood as being one-tenth of the fire-oblation (homa), because that alone is the subject under discussion; it is not based on one-tenth of the recitation (japa). (18)

The secondary alternative for the libation (tarpaṇa) and so forth arises from doubling the number of recitations (japa) and the like; indeed, the mere secondary alternative for the fire-oblation (homa) is the subject matter of the statement in the Dīpikā. (19)

For the wives of the twice-born, however, it should be known that recitation is performed without fire-offerings; for a Śūdra, recitation is prescribed when directed by his master, as declared by those learned in the Vedas. (20)

If it were established that the performance of the oblation is an auxiliary part (aṅga) [of the rite] because of the attainment of honors and so forth, then even women and Śūdras would perform the oblation; such is the undesirable consequence.

However, regarding those two, the *Dīpikā* states that the procedure beginning with "that which has been described" is devoid of fire-oblation (*homa*), by means of the sentence concerning the rite of preliminary observance (*pauraścaraṇaka*) which is devoid of fire-oblation.
For, since the qualification is understood from another source, one would not take it as a qualifier; if it were taken, it would not apply in the case of the *sahomaka* sacrifice. (23)
When it is stated that this rule applies only to the *sahoma* (the sacrifice with the oblation), then its non-application would follow in the case of the *ahoma* (non-sacrifice);
thus, there would be a contradiction regarding the subject under discussion.

Furthermore, since the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) is enjoined even when the fire-oblation (*homa*) is omitted, one may possess the qualification for the goal even with respect to mantras belonging to the Vedic tradition (*āmnāya*). (25)

(125) From where [could it arise], since there is an absence of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) regarding the rite of preliminary service (*puraścaraṇa*), and because it is established in quite another way?
Thus, that [efficacy] would belong to my worship and fire-oblation (*pūjā-homa*) as well. (26)
Nor should it be said, "What is the recourse when there is a lack of food joined with the *praṇava*? for when worship cannot take place without the mantra, [this objection does not apply]. || 27 ||
When the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) have been accomplished through the attainment of worship,
let there be the qualification for that very rite of puraścaraṇa.
"Success is achieved even without the fire-oblation (homa); thus there is a great difference between the two. Even so, eligibility would apply to both of them when it comes to the homa. (29)
Then who would prevent bathing according to the Kātīya ritual? This is called the protection of cattle sold by a fool. (30)
Furthermore, they recite here a statement distinguished by the conduct of the learned: "From the chanting of the Praṇava, from burnt offerings, and from the worship of the Śālagrāma stone... (31)
Furthermore, by having sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Śūdra shall fall into the state of a Caṇḍāla;
the rule for the fire-oblation (homa) has been declared for these three castes alone.
But a Śūdra, desiring that same fruit, should perform twice as many recitations as the number of oblations;
for the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā also clearly states this meaning as follows: || 33 ||
For all castes alike, the initiation accompanied by ritual action (kriyāvatī) should be performed; likewise, for women and Śūdras, that which involves the fire-oblation (haumikī) is not recommended.

If, in this way, the eligibility for performing the oblation (homādhikāritva) of those two [the husband and wife] is understood anywhere in the ritual procedure (prayoga-vidhi) and so forth, then let it be so; what harm is there in that? (35)
Because the rule is seen [to apply] at the beginning of the Kṛṣṇa-mantra and so forth, just as with the utterance of "svāhā";
or else, if there should be an inability [to perform] either the fire-oblation (homa) or the libation (tarpaṇa). (36)
O limb, the rite of *puraścaraṇa* is indeed accomplished by these two means alone: by reciting the mantra that many times and by the propitiation of Brahmins. (37)
If any limb [of the ritual] is omitted, a recitation twice that number must be performed with devotion by one who is unable [to complete the rite], for the sake of accomplishing the limbs. (38)

If even one limb of this [rite] is omitted, then one will not attain the desired result. Regarding those recitations and fire-oblations for which no specific number has been stated by the wise, [the rule is as follows]. (39)
The number for their recitation (japa) and fire-oblation (homa) shall be eight thousand;
if no specific number is mentioned, it shall be one hundred and eight, or a thousand, or even ten.
It is declared that in the Nārāyaṇī [rite], the measure [of mantras] is used without formal honorific treatment;
in the Saṃmohana [rite], the measure is prescribed when no specific desire-based ritual action has been mentioned.
Whether it be one hundred thousand, ten thousand, a thousand, or even a hundred, the mantra-practitioner should perform the respective fire-oblations according to the gravity of the ritual acts.
In the *Tattvasāgara*, it is stated that for the daily recitation (*prātyahika-japa*), one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times, or a hundred, or even twenty. (43)
One should recite it six thousand times, or one thousand, or one hundred and eight times;
this is indeed the specific rule according to the Agastyasaṃhitā. (44)

Now, it may be objected: where there is no injunction regarding specific details such as the hands, or no restriction regarding the directions, or no conceptualization of the *prahva* and other [postures], [how can there be a rule]? (45)
In response to the inquiry, "How can the functioning of worldly convention proceed in the absence of specific injunctions? that which was spoken by the Sage is stated. (46)
Where an action is prescribed but the specific limb of the agent is not mentioned, it should be understood that the right hand is intended, for it is the hand that brings actions to completion.

Where there is no fixed rule regarding direction for recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth, three directions are prescribed there: the eastern, the northern, and the unconquered (aparājita).
Whether sitting, standing, or bowing down—wherever no such rule exists—that [recitation] should be performed while sitting, and not while bowing or standing. 49.
One should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) into the mouth of the deity with a tenth part of the oblations;
one should satisfy [the lineage of teachers] with a tenth part of that, according to the Āgama composed by Vidyānanda.
This has been stated by the Vidyādhara masters in the scripture known as the Ratnāvalī;
likewise, it is also proclaimed in the Tripurāsārasaṃgraha. (51)

Therefore, the rites of libation (tarpaṇa) and so forth are not prescribed here as being one-tenth of the number of recitations. I shall now describe the procedure for libation according to the oral tradition.
At the conclusion of the fire oblation, one should visualize the seat of the deity within the water; having respectfully gratified it with water alone, ending with the seat-mantra.
There, one should worship the God with water-based offerings such as *pādya* and the rest; and from the tenth part of the *homa*, one should offer auspicious waters into the mouth of the God. (54)

One should perform the libation with a restrained mind using the mantra that will be described hereafter; the word "tarpayāmi" (I satiate) should be appended at the end of the mantras along with their respective names.
The wise consider that for the mantras ending in the dative case, this is the rule for libation; one should indeed perform the libation with water held in the hollowed palms.
The libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed with that water; this is stated in the Saṃhitās and other texts.
And one should perform the libation according to the prescribed rule, using pure water in a quantity equal to one-tenth [of the water used for bathing].

Having worshipped [the deity] in the water as before with flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and other offerings, the wise man should offer one handful (añjali) for each unit when the count is complete.
Having offered [the oblation] to the attendants, such as the limbs (aṅgas) and so forth, one should dismiss the deity; even in the first [case], some desire the satiation (tarpaṇa) of the retinue.
Having uttered the root mantra, at its end one should add the name of the deity in the accusative case, followed by the word "aham," then "tarpayāmi," and ending with "namaḥ. || 60 ||
Some say that Manu has prescribed this for the limbs and so forth; one should perform the sprinkling with a tenth part of the libation and wipe it upon one's own head.
I shall describe the procedure for purification according to all the tantras: the practitioner, having meditated upon himself in the form of the deity, [should perform it] upon his own head. (62)
One should perform the consecration consisting of the sprinkling of water with one's own mudrā; reciting the root mantra ending with "namas," one should perform it—so say the ancients. (63)
In the view of those for whom the fifth limb is the feeding of the twice-born during a rite,
I shall now describe that procedure according to their doctrine.
Having invited the Brahmins and prepared food of six flavors,
one should invoke the chosen deity with the root mantra and offer them a seat.
Having meditated thus, the practitioner of mantra should invoke [the deity] as described into the body of the Brahmin;
he should then worship those Brahmins, who have become the forms of his chosen deity, with water for the feet and other offerings.

One should feed [the Brahmins] with various kinds of food possessing diverse flavors, perceiving them as deities; when the Brahmins have been well-fed, that [act] becomes complete in its parts and fruitful.
Since even a deficient rite becomes complete merely by the propitiation of a Brahmin,
a learned man should by all means feed one for the sake of accomplishing the rite with all its constituent parts.
Whatever task involves a person with a physical deficiency, that task is not properly accomplished; therefore, one should diligently feed the learned in all ritual activities.
Whatever other meritorious deeds there may be, they become fruitless through the feeding of Brahmins [at improper times],
like elephants on the road of kings.
For those for whom there is no obstacle to their ritual action and who provide food to Brahmins, however,
the visualization [of the deity] occurs from merely the tenth part of the recitation.
Then, having performed the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) in this manner, that most excellent practitioner should meditate upon the deity in her true form as previously described. || 9 ||
At the conclusion of that, one should perform a great worship and feed the Brahmins;
one should honor one's own guru with many garments and ornaments.
By satisfying the poor and the helpless, the mantras of practitioners are brought to accomplishment.
Alternatively, for those of limited intellect, this method serves to accomplish the mantra; having bathed during an eclipse of the moon or sun, with a restrained mind, one should proceed. (1)

Relying on one of the two paths mentioned by the wise, the practitioner should then perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) with kuśa grass, unbroken rice grains, and water, after which he should worship the deity.
Having worshipped with single-minded devotion by some means or another, one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind, from the time of touch until liberation is attained. (3)
Then one should perform the fire-oblation and other rites according to the rules and as is convenient; at the conclusion of that, one should perform a great worship and the satiation of the Brahmins.
Then, for the sake of the mantra’s accomplishment, one should worship and satisfy the guru; when this is done, the supreme accomplishment of the mantra arises.

Or else, having previously observed a fast, one should stand in water reaching up to the navel in a river flowing toward the ocean and recite the mantra with undistracted mind; this would be the superior alternative in the ritual procedure for the *puraścaraṇa*.
In the Dakṣiṇāmūrtitantra, however, it is stated regarding the Dakṣiṇāmūrti mantra: "One who has fasted for three nights and is pure"; thus say the Tantrikas. (7)
If the mantra should not become effective even when this is done,
one should perform the preliminary service (puraścaraṇa) until the mantra becomes perfected.

Then, one should accomplish all the desires and ritual applications (prayogas) declared in the Kalpa; for even a man who constantly recites [the mantra] will fail if he does not know their application (viniyoga).
The mantra falls away from its potency; therefore, one should be intent on effort. And thus, the application [of the mantra] at the beginning of the *saṃhitā* and so forth is prohibited.

That [knowledge] has the Rāma-mantra as its object, because it is understood by beginning with that; for this very reason, he says: "As a supplement to the ritual procedure for the application of the mantra" (verse 11).
Just as there may be the occurrence of sin for one who employs the mantras of Śrī Rāma, such is not the case with the mantra of Lakṣmaṇa; rather, he attains the supreme goal. (12)
Alternatively, this prohibition is considered to concern prohibited objects; for this very reason, killing and so forth are cited in the concluding summary. (13)
This mantra does not bestow liberation; let it be employed for killing and the like. It has been said that for those who perform such ritual applications, the next world does not exist.
If it were not the case that [the action] has a prohibited object, how could that [prohibition] be established?
In the performance of a rite enjoined for the sake of the next world, that fruit will certainly not arise; thus, one or the other [of the two positions] must necessarily be sublated. (15)
This is called the "rope with snares at both ends"; therefore, it must necessarily be admitted that its object is indeed prohibited. (16)
Furthermore, that [scripture] is intended to negate resting in those [objects] alone;
it is postulated out of fear of the contradiction posed by various [other] statements. (17)
If one should somehow perform what has begun otherwise due to delusion,
one should complete it from the very point at which it became altered.
If, upon completion, I should realize that I have performed this otherwise, I would do it again at that very moment;
there is no repetition of any ritual act.

Where there is the non-performance of the principal act, that rite together with its subsidiaries must be performed again; however, where there is the non-performance of a subsidiary, there should be neither a repetition of the whole nor the performance of that specific subsidiary.

Now, for the sake of accomplishing mantras, I shall explain the *vīrasādhana* (heroic practice), by means of which the desired success is attained even when there is no success through mere exertion in [other] mantras. (21)
When that occurs, the heroic accomplishment (vīrasādhana) should be performed with great effort;
for one who has perfectly mastered a single mantra, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be achieved.
What need is there to speak of a man who possesses many mantras? He who, being well-composed, performs the *vīrasādhana* is Śiva himself. (23)
One attains the supreme accomplishment; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Therefore, the Vīrasādhana should be performed with every effort. (24)
Becoming fearless and pure, this [mantra] bestows the accomplishment of all goals; there exists nothing superior to it that grants such swift success. (25)
Therefore, with every effort, the Vīrasādhana must be performed; its unsurpassed procedure is now being told according to common worldly usage. (26)
In former times, Bhairava proclaimed this supreme rite which grants all accomplishments; having prepared it right in one's own home with honey, meat, molasses, and rice.

Having taken sacrificial offerings of rice mixed with ghee, a goat, unbroken grains, flowers, and so forth, along with milk, during the latter half of the night after one and a half watches have passed; || 28 ||
Though alone and accompanied only by his sword in hand, he was free from fear; having approached the funeral pyre and seen him from a distance, he held him back at some distance behind.
Having sat down on a portion of the funeral pyre, facing either the east or the north,
the wise man, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and joined his palms in añjali, should mutter this mantra.
And those gods and terrifying rākṣasas who dwell right here—may they grant me success out of compassion and a sense of kinship with me. (31)
Having repeated this three times, one should arrange the offerings in the vessels; those four [offerings] are placed at the four openings of the funeral pyre, beginning from the north.
Having performed the circumambulation while holding [the vessel], one should offer the bali-oblation with milk and the mantra: "Hūṃ!
O Śmaśānasambhu, accept this bali of meat and rice! Thus one should say. (33)
"Seize, seize! O couple who causes [them] to be seized, then ward off obstacles! Grant me success—svāhā! This is considered the mantra, ending with *svāhā*. (34)
At the end of *māyā*, having uttered "Bhairava," one should speak the word "bhayānaka. Having said "śmaśānādhipa," the subsequent [mantra] begins with "imam" and so forth. (35)
Having uttered "HŪM Kālabhairava," one should invoke the Lord of the Cremation Ground;
another mantra beginning with "imam" and so forth is intended for the southern direction. (36)
Having uttered "HŪM Mahākāla," [recite] "in the cremation ground" and so forth as before; this is the mantra for the western direction, and with it one should then present the offering. || 37 ||
O dweller in the cremation ground, O most terrifying Kālikā of dreadful hissing! Accept this offering, O Mother; grant me supreme accomplishment. (38)

With "HŪṂ KĀLIKE DVI-CĀ[ṬHĀ]" at the end, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) and so forth near Mahākāla; then, having meditated upon one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), [one should proceed]. || 39 ||
“HŪṂ! O you who arise from the cremation ground, accept this offering of food with meat; cause it to be accepted, cause it to be accepted! Ward off obstacles! Grant me success, svāhā!
One should recite this with an undistracted heart, free from fear, and with a pure mind.
For a single-syllable mantra, ten thousand recitations are required; for a two-syllable mantra, eight thousand.

For a mantra of three syllables, the number is fifty thousand; from that point on, it is eight thousand more for each additional syllable. This is the number prescribed for all mantras at the conclusion of the recitation, provided the deity is present.
Having worshipped her, she appears in person; when she says, "Give!
Give!", the wise man should then offer a goat as a sacrifice and earnestly pray for his boon.
Alternatively, the practitioner may perform the Heroic Sadhana (vīrasādhana) upon a corpse; some say it should be one that has been dead for more than five years. (43)
After midnight, during the latter half of the night, the wise man, free from fear, should carry the corpse to a crossroads or to the bank of a river.

Having summoned [the deity] with the syllable *hūṃ*, one should bathe [the image] with that same [substance] and seat it; having worshipped one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) according to the rules upon the corpse, [one should proceed]. (45)
One should recite the mantra ten thousand times everywhere, as previously prescribed for the bali offerings and other rites;
however, at the end, when offering the goat-bali to Bhairava, the ring finger is considered appropriate.
In the case of a Yoginī, the index, middle, and ring fingers are prescribed; for Kṣetrapāla and Gaṇeśa, the middle fingers are used, while in other cases it may be according to one's desire.
There exists nothing superior to this for bestowing swift accomplishment;
it has been declared by sages and deities alike as that which is desired by practitioners.
Fearless, pure, free from anger, with senses conquered, mighty in strength, and compassionate— such a person is described as an overseer.
Then the practitioner should perform the ritual applications (prayoga) according to his own desires.
Now, the measure of the substances for the fire-oblation (homa) is set forth here, both in detail and in brief, according to various tantras.
One karṣa of ghee is prescribed for the oblation, and one śukti of milk is likewise recorded; the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are declared by the wise to be equal in measure to those.
An equal amount of honey, milk, and food is declared to be the size of an akṣa; some say that the milk should be the size of a cupped handful (culuka) and the honey likewise.
Now, an objection might be raised: "Since the *sruva* ladle is prescribed for a liquid substance, how could it be that honey, milk, and so forth are taken in a mere mouthful (*culuka*)? (4)

It is said that by means of the prescribed method using leaves of the *aśvattha* tree and so forth, that [offering] becomes supreme; this is the fundamental rule regarding the use of a *sruva* ladle when it is unavailable for rites such as the daily *homa*.

"It should be offered even with a mere mouthful" is what is indicated by the Sūtra. Some traditionalists say that the mention of "a mouthful" (culluka) is intended to include [all such small quantities].

The curd should be the measure of a handful (prasṛti); the parched grains (lāja) should be commensurate with a fist; the flattened rice (pṛthuka) should be of that same measure, and the roasted flour (saktu) is likewise declared to be so.

Jaggery (guḍa) shall be half a pala in measure, and sugar (śarkarā) is likewise declared to be so; the portion of sacrificial porridge (caru) shall be half a mouthful, and sugarcane is considered to be measured by the joint.
One should prepare each leaf and flower, as well as cakes, one by one;
the wise know that plantains and oranges should likewise be offered individually.
Some here have stated that the citron fruit should be divided into four pieces and the jackfruit into ten, with one portion for each of the citrons.
The wise know that coconuts are cut into eight pieces;
a wood-apple fruit is made into three parts, and a kapittha fruit is cut into two.
In the fire sacrifice (homa), the fruit of the *urvāruka* is said to be cut into three pieces;
other fruits should likewise be cut into pieces, and the sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*) should be ten finger-breadths long. || 12 ||
The fuel-stick should never be thicker than a thumb; it must not be stripped of its bark, nor infested with insects, nor split. (13)

A sacrificial twig used by one who knows the rules should not be longer than a span, nor shorter; likewise, it should not have two branches, nor possess leaves, nor be devoid of potency during the oblations.

For the purpose of pacification, [the wood] should have its bark intact and be fresh; for one wishing to kill, it should be the opposite. Furthermore, it should be shattered, split, short, crooked, and likewise full of holes.
Long, thick, and infested with woodworms, these destroy all success;
Śrī Somaśambhu has also stated this as the criterion regarding roots and other materials.
One should offer three pieces of each type of root and fruit according to their respective sizes,
half a morsel of food, and five *akṣa* seeds as oblations.
One should offer according to the supreme rite a measure of sugarcane equal to one joint, two finger-breadths for creepers, and an eighth part for bulbous roots. 18.
Three blades of dūrvā grass are prescribed, as well as gulūcī and caturaṅgulā; there should be a handful of vrīhi rice, along with mudga, māṣa, and barley.

Some state that the measure for mung beans and the like is otherwise than this: they hold that mung beans should be one *karṣa* in weight, or that seven or eight barley grains (*yava*) are considered equal to one [bean]. (20)
Five or six barley grains are said to be one *tāra* (or *veṇu*); cakes (*pūpa*) are each [weighed] individually;
rice grains are declared to be half a *muṣṭi*, though by some they are said to be half of that half.
Kodrava grains should be one handful; the measure for barley gruel and milk is the same; wheat and red śāli rice are prescribed at the measure of one handful each. (22)
Sixteen rājamāṣas [make one] godhūma; red śāli rice is said to be equal in measure to a rājamāṣa—so say other experts in the Tantras. (23)

Sesame seeds should be the size of a handful (a *culuka*), and a mustard seed (*sarṣapa*) is likewise declared [to be that size] by some; however, others state that for oblations, a mustard seed is half of half a *karṣa*.
In the Jñānārṇava, however, the number for those two is declared to be one hundred;
the measure of salt is a śukti, and there are twenty-one marīcis.
The guru should be the size of a jujube fruit; asafoetida is recorded as being equal to that.
The side dish, *kṛsara*, should likewise be the measure of four thumb-breadths. (26)
Likewise, the paste of sesame seeds has been prescribed by those expert in mantra and tantra;
as well as sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and saffron. (27)
The wise have stated that [the quantity] is equal to the seeds of the tamarind; Śrī Somaśambhu has declared this to be the measure for sandalwood and other substances.
These should be the size of peas; guggulu should be like the kernel of a jujube fruit; and camphor, sandalwood, musk, and saffron [should be used]. (29)

Other experts in the Āgamas have stated that [the size of the offering] is equal to a chickpea; however, when no specific sacrificial substance is mentioned, sesame and clarified butter are said to constitute the oblation.

When the substance for the collyrium is not specified, they know that clarified butter alone is the collyrium; when the number is not specified, it should be one thousand, and likewise, when the substance is not specified, it is clarified butter.
In matters where no specific wood is mentioned, sacrificial fuel (samidh) is declared to be made of Palāśa;
however, the Gārgyasaṃhitā states this in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtitantra.
Clarified butter (ājya) is prescribed as the substance for oblations when no specific material is designated; one should proceed in this manner according to the path seen in the Smṛtis.
The oblation of parched grain and other substances is prescribed to be performed with the hand including the thumb;
the offering of fuel-sticks, flowers, fruits, and so forth, should be done with the *mṛgamudrā* gesture.
For liquid substances, the *sruva* ladle is prescribed by those expert in mantra and tantra;
one should join the tips of the ring finger, the thumb, and the middle finger together. (35)
One should raise the remaining fingers; this is declared to be the *mṛgamudrā*. In oblations with fuel-sticks (*samid-dhoma*), the practitioner should meditate upon Vaiśvānara standing. (36)

If [the fire] lies down during ghee oblations and remains seated during other rites, disease arises from an oblation offered at the ear, and blindness is declared to result from one offered at the eye. (37)
Then there should be a fire on the nose, and then a cutting of the substance on the head; with that, one should perform the oblation (homa) daily into the mouth of the Fire-god.
Where there is wood, there is the ear; where there is smoke here, there is the nose;
where there is a small flame, there is the eye; and where there are embers, there is the head. (39)
Where the blazing flame is the tongue of Jātavedas, he who offers oblations with inferior mantras while possessed by hunger, thirst, anger, and haste [is as described]. (40)
If it is not fully kindled, or if it smokes, he would become blind in another birth; likewise if it is small, dry, emitting sparks, turning counter-clockwise, or terrifying. (41)
When the fire was filled with wet wood, he likewise licked the earth as the flames turned black,
emitted a foul stench, and hissed.
For one who offers oblations into a fire that lacks flames, or into one that has been extinguished, his destruction is certain. (43)

One becomes weak in digestion, afflicted by disease, and even impoverished; therefore, one who desires health, long life, and ultimate prosperity should offer oblations only when the fire is well-kindled, never when it is unkindled. (44)
Resembling gold, vermilion, the morning sun, saffron, and honey—this is proclaimed as the auspicious color of Suvarṇaretas. (45)
The sound of a drum, or like the roar of clouds, an elephant king, or fire, brings auspiciousness; it resembles the scent of the nāga, campaka, punnāga, pāṭala, and yūthikā flowers. (46)
"Resembling a lotus, a blue water-lily, a white lily, clarified butter, and bdellium—the auspicious fragrance of fire is thus described by those who know the tantras. (47)
Cocks whose crests turn clockwise, are free from trembling, and resemble umbrellas bring auspiciousness to the sacrificer and especially to the kingdom. (48)

Smoke that resembles *kāśa* grass brings auspiciousness; smoke resembling a *kunda* flower is auspicious for fire. Smoke that is reddish-brown (*piṅga*) always causes disease, while smoke with the luster of silver brings about the destruction of the kingdom.
A flame with the color of fire (red) that is black destroys the sacrificer;
a sound resembling the cry of a donkey or a crow is a destroyer of what is desired.
An odor resembling excrement causes suffering from fire; one like urine causes loss of strength;
and one with the appearance of sweat destroys auspiciousness. (51)
If the fire has a foul odor, it will bring about suffering; if its flame is broken or covered, it will cause death and the total loss of wealth.
Smoke resembling the color of a parrot's wing or having a luster like that of a pigeon portends the eventual loss of horses and cattle. (53)

A clockwise whirlpool always bestows auspiciousness according to the rules of circumambulation. However, if lightning strikes during the time of an oblation, or if sparks from the fire appear in that same manner, it shall result in misfortune and the arising of inauspiciousness. (54)
In the event of such faults as these, the practitioner should perform expiation by offering oblations twenty-five times with the root mantra.

For the sake of pacification, the wise practitioner should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter; the excellent adept should perform the worship of the wheel with the Astra-mantra.
This expiation has been proclaimed in the Tripurāsārasaṃgraha. || 57 ||
Now, as a digression, the measurement as stated by the Teacher is set forth:
five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*, and sixteen of those make one *suvarṇa*.
Four suvarṇas make one pala, and one hundred and eight [of those] make one niṣka;
thirty-two palas make one prastha—this was spoken by the Self-Existent One himself.
Some say that a *niṣka* consists of a *māṣaka*, while others say it is a *pala*; two *guñjās* make a silver *māṣa*, and ten *palas* make a *dharaṇa*. (3)
An āḍhaka consists of four prasthas, and a droṇa consists of four āḍhakas;
that same measure is the quantity for a heap (rāśi), and a khārī consists of sixteen of those.
Twenty of those [kumbhas] make a vāha, and ten of those make a khārī;
three khārīs are declared by the scriptures to be a bhāra in due order.
Two thousand palas is declared to be the correct weight; some, however, desire a necklace weighing one-tenth of a bhāra.
A handful (muṣṭi) shall be the measure of one pala; two palas shall be a handful (prasṛti);
eight handfuls shall be a kuñca; and eight kuñcas shall be a puṣkala.
Four *puṣkala*s make one *āḍhaka* in that sequence; eight *puṣkala*s likewise are said to be a full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*).
One should declare that sixty-four *palas* constitute a *kumbha*, which is four *prasthas*. Two *palas* make one *prakubja*; two of those make a *prasara*. Two of those make a *kulava*;
twice that is a *prastha*, and in sequence, it is a *pātra*.
Likewise, some say that an āḍhaka is equal to a śiva, a droṇa, or a khārī. Five guñjās make one māṣa; sixteen of those [māṣas] make one akṣa, which is a karṣa.
Viṣṇu has stated here that twelve māṣas indeed constitute one akṣa; this is a technical definition belonging to the Vedic tradition and is not employed in the Āgamas. (11)

Therefore, those who know the scriptures maintain that worldly measures such as a handful (prasṛti) or a fistful (muṣṭi), like a conch-shell or a handful of water (culuka), are to be accepted [as valid]. 12.

Since the fire-oblation (homa) must be accomplished by means of a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), that [pit] is now defined; and it is determined according to the type of oblation as well as by the force of the specific desire. (1)
The characteristics of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) as well, in their various forms, are being elucidated according to the scriptures— both in detail and in brief, even more concisely.
One who desires the fruits of that [practice] should proceed from the pavilion of worship toward the northeast direction; for the accomplishment of auspicious goals occurs in due order.
Now, that which directly assists the initiatory rites (*dīkṣā*) and other such ceremonies—the meeting point of the throat and the navel—is briefly described [as follows]. (4)
The sacrificial pavilion (maṇḍapa) and the fire-pit (kuṇḍa), which have many varieties, are now explained; for experts state that there are many defects if these are either deficient or excessive.
Having exerted effort, one should perform what has been declared by Viśvakarman: if the excavation is excessive, there will be illness; if it is deficient, there will be loss of cattle and wealth.
In the case of a curved sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), there is suffering; in one with a broken girdle (mekhalā), death; in one lacking a girdle, grief;
and in one that is excessively large, the depletion of wealth.
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that is devoid of a yoni is said to cause the destruction of one's wife;
a pit that is lacking a neck is said to cause the destruction of one's offspring.
Excess of pride leads to death, while a deficiency of pride leads to poverty; these defects of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) have also been declared to you with effort by Bhairava.
If the thread is excessive, there will be hatred; if it is deficient, poverty. If it is devoid of knots, one will be prone to anger; if the girdle is too short, there will be failure.

If [the site] is torn apart or riddled with fissures, there will be censure; therefore, first perform the purification of the ground according to the rules, beginning with the ritual of digging. || 11 ||

Having understood the equality of the ground, one should perform the construction of the pavilion and other structures. I shall now describe the method for achieving that equality as taught in the Śuddha [Tantra]. (12)
When the bases of the two staffs, which have fine and equal tips, are joined at one corner,
and their tips are brought close together, a horizontal line marked at the center is drawn across them.
The staff should be joined with a peg and so forth, balanced equally at both ends; it should be heavy like a weight, with its base not touching its own cord.
When the two foremost lines are on the ground, one should dig from the middle mark toward the horizontal staff-line,
filling it with earth or otherwise lowering it according to the proper method.
As long as the thread reaches the lap, the ground itself shall thus attain levelness.
Alternatively, one may ascertain the levelness of the ground in another manner: having dug up the site that has been acquired, one should have the removal of any hidden obstacles performed.
Having made the ground level and smooth on all sides, resembling a mirror, one should place a jar filled with pure water in the center of an opening.

Having made it well-balanced, one should place it level in the middle of the ground. Then, when the surface of the earth has been evenly sprinkled with water that has flowed around [the vessel], the unevenness of the site— whether deficient or excessive—
is to be known by means of that water.
Now, the procedure for determining the directions such as the east is correctly explained: one should firmly plant a straight peg with a needle-like tip in the center as a shelter. (20)
Having made a mandala of that measurement, one should place a marker at the point from which its shadow enters and likewise at the point from which it exits.
The sūtra should be the same as the previous sūtra; thus, having determined the directions such as east and so forth, one should unweariedly construct the pavilion and other structures.
That which is used at the beginning of the initiation (dīkṣā) and other rites is called the pavilion (maṇḍapa).
It should be erected on an auspicious day favorable to the lunar mansion, the day of the week, and the zodiac sign. || 23 ||

Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited, one should construct a beautiful pavilion; having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should cause the Brahmins to pronounce blessings.
One should address a Brāhmaṇa with the syllable *oṃ*, a king without the syllable *oṃ*, a Vaiśya in a whisper, and one should employ the word "svasti" for a Śūdra. (25)
The distance between the pillars should be measured as five, seven, or nine [cubits].
It is joined with sixteen pillars, four of which are situated in the center. (26)
Twelve [pillars] should be erected on all sides, eight cubits in height;
they should measure five cubits [in girth], be without gaps, straight, and auspicious.
The best of experts in the tantra should bury one-fifth of that [measure] in the earth and cover it on all sides with coconut leaves or bamboo.
With two hands each, there should be four doors in the cardinal directions;
it is taught that for the central [deity] and the one to be worshipped, there is an increase of four and eight finger-breadths [respectively].
At the gates, there should be arches (toraṇas) made of milk-tree wood in sequence; their pillars (stambhas) are recorded as being five, six, or seven cubits (karas) in height.
In this manner, following the sequence beginning with the inferior [measurement], the circumference increases by ten finger-breadths;
one should place a crest at the top for the purpose of inserting the transverse wooden beam.
The measurement of the diagonal pegs (tiryakkanaka) should be half the measurement of the pillars; one should arrange the stakes at the door of the Vaiṣṇava pavilion in this manner.
On the pillars, according to the prescribed measurements, one should install conch shells, discs, maces, and lotuses made of excellent wood, arranged in order starting from the east.

One should fashion the tridents on the Śaiva arch (toraṇa) according to the measurement of one cubit; the length of the trident should be nine finger-breadths, and its width should be one-fourth of that.

The central prong should indeed be straight, while those on the two sides should be slightly curved; this is declared to be the case for the inferior [type], and one should likewise fix it at a distance of two finger-breadths.
Except for an increase of two finger-breadths from the increase of each finger-breadth for the Īśa [corner], one should fasten the directional banners,
which possess a splendor equal to that of the world-protectors.
In the center is a banner equipped with small bells, and at the doors there are pairs;
the jars are proclaimed to be endowed with fragrant substances, jewels, garlands, and the like.
The width of the banners is one span (vitasti), while their length is five cubits (karas);
for the standard (dhvaja), the measurement is said to be double that.
It should be made multicolored and pleasing to the eyes of all onlookers; one should decorate the pavilion with canopies, garlands of *darbha* grass, and other ornaments. (39)
Then, on a field measuring one-third of that [area], one should prepare a square altar (*vedi*) one cubit (*aratni*) high for the sake of the mandala. (40)
In the pavilion described above, the wise man, having divided the area outside the altar into three parts,
should designate the eastern and other directions within the central portion.
In the eight directions, sacrificial pits of beautiful form should be arranged in sequence: square, yoni-shaped, half-moon, triangular, and perfectly circular.
These [fire-pits] are hexagonal, lotus-shaped, and octagonal by name;
the fire-pit for the Preceptor (ācārya) should be in the middle, between the Lord of Gaurī and Mahendra.

In the northeast, for paralyzing, it is square; in the southeast, for enjoyment, it is shaped like a vulva; in the south, for killing, it is a half-moon; and in the southwest, for hatred, it is a triangle.
A hexagon is prescribed for pacification in the west,
an eight-pointed star for eradication in the northwest, a lotus for nourishment in the north, and an eight-sided figure in the northeast bestows liberation.
One should place a five-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the northwest for the subjugation of spirits and the like, as well as for the suppression of planetary influences;
for the purpose of pacifying malevolent magic (abhicāra), one should install a seven-cornered pit in the northeast.
