Likewise, two [fingers] are used for eating, two for liberation, and similarly two for restoring the worn-out;
likewise, one [finger] is always used for the *homa* and for pacification, directed toward the quarter of Varuṇa (the west).
A quadrangular pit, beautifully adorned, brings about all accomplishments; one resembling a half-moon destroys enemies; and a triangular pit is for the rite of killing.
Some say it should be hexagonal for the pacification of diseases, while others say it should be octagonal; however, a square shape is prescribed for Brahmins, and a circular one for kings. (49)
For Vaiśyas it is said to have the appearance of a half-moon, for Śūdras it is triangular;
some Tantrikas desire it to be square for all classes.
One should lay down a cord extending from east to west, measuring one cubit; then, having set aside half of that half, one should draw two fish-shaped figures on either side.
Having taken hold of the eastern and western ends with two half-moons, one should lay down a thread between them running from south to north.
One should know this north-south cord; from that, one should proceed to form a square. Taking hold of the tips of the four cords, one should act from the center toward the four cardinal directions.
Having fashioned half-circles, one should draw fish-shaped figures located at the corners; upon those fish, one should drop threads whose tips follow a curved path. (54)
Thus it should be quadrangular; otherwise, it would be impure. The measurement of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is desired according to the requirements of the fire-oblation (homa).
One should fashion a square as the basis for all the others; then, the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) such as the yoni-shaped and so forth should be made with dimensions equal to that field.
One should have it made with great care, for there is a great fault in deficiency or excess; having divided the Brahma-thread into one hundred parts, [one should proceed].
One should extend nineteen parts outward in front; having made a mark there, one should likewise [draw] the thread toward the west, south, and north.
The wise one should increase [the measurement] on both sides by nine and a half parts; having made a mark on those two sides, the intelligent one should proceed with great care. (59)
Starting from the eastern mark and extending to the two marks at the hips,
when two threads are laid down, a triangle is subsequently formed therefrom.
The practitioner should take half the measurement that exists between the mark at the tip of the previously drawn thread and the mark at the tip of the rear hip-thread.
Starting from the tip of the two buttocks and revolving as far as the western tip of the central line, there shall be two half-moons; this becomes the yoni-kunda,
auspicious when neither deficient nor excessive.
Having divided the square field into twenty-four parts,
one should then discard two and a half parts from below.
Then, having made a mark, one should again leave upwards two and a half parts less a sixteenth part of a part, and there too one should make a mark.
Having fixed the eastern mark and laid down the chord-line from south to north,
one should then [mark] to the east at a distance equal to the measurement of the lower mark.
Then, using a cord [measured] by a crab, one should rotate it to form a half-moon; this sacrificial pit, resembling a half-moon, shall be beautiful.
One should divide a square field into twenty-four parts;
one should extend the cord five units at the front and separately at the hips.
(145) Having increased the eastern thread by one-tenth and by eight and nine [units] respectively,
and having made marks at three places, one should lay down three threads;
by means of those marks, one should draw an excellent triangular *kuṇḍa*.
Having divided this [line] into sixteen parts, one should project the central thread outward. With a compass, using this measurement, one should draw a circle from the center;
this shall be pleasing to the sight of all.

Having divided the central line into nine parts by a portion of the Jina (one-twelfth), one should lay it out from the front; then, using that measurement from the center, one should draw a circle with five and a half [parts].
Then, having divided that [circle] into six parts, one should rotate it over all six marks;
thereafter, one should lay down six lines to form the excellent hexagonal sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The wise one should divide the square field into eight parts; then, with a compass set to the measure of one-eighth part, [he should draw a circle] from the center.
One should rotate it into a circle; this is the pericarp (karṇikā), while the filaments (kesarāḥ) are formed by rotating from the center using two-eighths [of the measurement]. || 73 ||
The middle ground of the petals is considered to be one-eighth of the third [unit],
and the upper ground is one-fourth, following the sequence equal to the layout of the field.
Having divided the central quality of the field into twenty-four parts,
one should take one part and divide it again into sixteen.
[The fifth and eighth squares] are reduced by five of these sixteen parts.
Having taken that portion, the wise one [should draw] the fifth mandala outside of it.
The practitioner of mantra should rotate it from the center; the tips of the petals are considered to be the earth. Then, according to the previously mentioned rule, he should draw the lotus.
Although the excavation for all types of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) has been shown previously, the specific method of excavation for this [particular pit] is now being described.
Having set aside the height equal to the width of the pericarp (karṇikā), one should bury the remainder;
that is the circle of filaments (kesara).
Having dug out the interior to that shape, one should dig out the leaf-surface; the expert should do so in such a way that the leaf-shapes are properly produced. (80)

(146) Some maintain that this lotus-pool is to be situated outside [the sacrificial ground]; however, the drawing of such a lotus for the pit (kuṇḍa) is not appropriate, since it is understood that the form [of the pit] is to be contemplated accordingly. || 81 ||
One should divide the square field into twenty-four parts; of that which is divided by thirty-two, thirteen [parts] constitute one portion.
One should increase the other four [sides] by those same parts;
having made the middle line measure that same amount, one should then draw the others.
Outside, within the square area, one should join two lines for each direction and mark eight signs in the intervals between the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Leaving one mark between each, one should drop eight straight lines so that their intersections meet one another. (85)
One should erase all the lines of both squares, as well as the lines of the eight cords and the additional eight corners.
One should cleanse this pit known as the eight-cornered; thus it has been described.
One should divide the half of the previously mentioned Brahma-thread into twelve parts; these [parts] should be provided with the twentieth part of nine such divisions. (88)
Having taken three parts, one should extend the Brahma-sūtra;
the wise man should then fashion a circle with a diameter equal to that measure.
Having divided that [line] into five parts and then omitting two portions,
one should apply the remaining measure as the chord-line (jyāsūtra) and project it five times.
In the circle, the bowstrings should intersect at their tips so that there are five bows,
with the arrows being one-sixth of the length of the strings.
But from the remaining five strings, the five-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is most excellent. || 92 ||
One should divide half of the previously mentioned Brahma-sūtra by thirty-six; having increased the other seven [lines] within that sūtra by that same amount.
Then, one should construct the mandala with a width equal to half the diameter;
having divided it into twenty parts, the arrow (the central line) shall consist of one-twentieth of that.
In this manner, one should apply the bowstring to all the bows;
its two ends should meet together on all sides at intervals of nine units each. (95)
Seven cubits are produced; having then wiped them away, because seven bowstrings remain, there is an excellent seven-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

A knower of numbers should reflect that there exists the defect of deficiency or excess in the characteristics of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) described in the commentaries on the Śāradā and other [Tantras]. || 1 ||
Having prepared the sacrificial pits according to one's desire, one should perform the excavation; the depth of the excavation is said to be equal to the width of the pit.

This very same thing is proclaimed in the *Divyasārasvata* treatise as well: "Having first laid out a square with four compartments according to the previous method, one should dig a trench of that same depth and length in its center, measuring one cubit. (3)
This very same meaning has been clearly stated in the *Śrīsārasaṃgraha*; for this alone is the established doctrine, proven even by logical reasoning. (4)
Some maintain that it should be performed together with the first girdle for that duration as well.
In the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*, it is stated regarding the northern [fire-pit] for the oblation: "One should dig one cubit deep horizontally, together with a girdle above."
Likewise, the pit [should be measured] in *jināṅgulas* along with the upper girdle;
this very same thing is proclaimed in the *Mantramuktāvalī* treatise as well. (7)
Thus, that which has been asserted by someone—that this doctrine is rootless—is merely a manifestation of the ignorance of the author of the *Mantramuktāvalī*. (8)
The excavation of the *kuṇḍas* beginning with the *yoni* is considered to be square or oblong;
having set aside a space of twenty-four units from the circumference of the field on all sides, the wise one should fashion the *mekhalā* (girdle) in all the *kuṇḍas*.
That place which has been relinquished is called the throat;
some tantrikas maintain that it is [measured] by one-twelfth of the width.
The end of the girdles (mekhalās) should be at a distance of one finger-breadth all around the rim (nemi); a wise man should increase this proportionally for a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) of one cubit.
For others, up to ten cubits, the measurement is distinct according to the increment of half a finger-breadth;
the throat is declared to be one part in the Kāmika [Tantra], while that which follows is for those desiring specific results.
Thus someone says: "In ultimate reality, there is no distinction between the two; one, two, or three girdles may be used according to one's desire, corresponding to the number of elements. (13)
One should construct [the altars] in the yoni-shaped and other types of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) according to the specific dimensions of each pit;
when the diameter is divided into twenty-four parts, there should be three girdles (mekhalās).
The nine planets—Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Rāhu, Ketu, the Sun, and the Moon—are formed by portions of four, three, and [one] moment respectively;
indeed, some say their height is equal to their width. (15)
Whatever the form of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) may be, such should be the form of the girdles (mekhalās);
one should construct three beautiful girdles in all the sacrificial pits.
The single girdle should be known to have a width of six and a half [units];
the measurement of the two girdles is the same as that of the first two girdles.
The girdles (mekhalās) should be made fivefold, with widths increased by six, five, and three parts respectively;
they should be known as being raised, starting from nine finger-breadths.
The fifth part of the nine parts is the first; the second is considered to be elevated by four parts less than that, and the other is considered to be elevated by two parts less than those.
The fourth [line] shall consist of three fewer [syllables], and the fifth of the remaining [syllables]. That which is their measurement in the Śāradātilaka is stated here. (20)
In a pit measuring one cubit (aratni) in height and length, the [stones] are each one and a half finger-breadths;
in a pit of that same measure, they are fifteen finger-breadths each.
In a pit measuring one cubit, the measurements are four, three, and two finger-breadths; in a pit of two cubits, they should be known as six, four, and three finger-breadths.
In a four-cubit sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), those [lines] are eight, six, and four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) wide;
in a six-cubit pit, they are ten, eight, and six finger-breadths wide.

In a pit measuring eight cubits, the measurements are eight fingers by the sequence of the Manus; in a pit measuring ten cubits, they are ten fingers by the sequence of the Manus and the Suns (twelve).
Those learned in the Tantras should know that the girdle (mekhalā) is equal in width and height; however, in the divine *Sārasvata* treatise, the measurement is stated otherwise.
The first girdle is of the nature of *sattva*, elevated by twelve finger-breadths;
the second is to be known as of the nature of *rajas*, elevated by eight finger-breadths. (26)
The third is declared to be the dark (tāmasī) girdle, measuring four finger-breadths [in height];
the width of each of these is four finger-breadths in measure.
The altar-base (yoni) for the fire-pits located in the east, southeast, and south is said to face north;
that situated on the right side of the eastern and southern pits faces east, while that in the west and north is situated in water.
"The yoni of the ninth pit is situated in the southern direction; for the remaining ones, it is said to face the east"—from such statements as these, it is understood in this way. (29)

One should avoid the vulva in the *yoni* pit and the navel in the lotus-shaped (*abja*) pit; as for what was previously stated regarding the directions starting with east and southeast, that which has available space should be used otherwise.
For it is thus: because it awakens [the practitioner] in all directions, and since it accomplishes all aims, the square is so described. (31)
The girdle is in the middle, and the womb (yoni) is half the measure [of the pit];
it is twenty-four parts in length and breadth, according to the measurement of three parts.
The rim is raised by one part from the middle of the pit;
as if it had entered [the pit], its edge is curved, and the girdle is made with a portion of one *jina*.
For the sake of the girdle, a separate piece of ground should not be taken;
rather, it should be taken from the middle of the field of the womb (yonikṣetra), resembling two jars at its base.
It may be contracted at the front, or shaped like a leaf of the holy fig tree (aśvattha),
or it may belong to fire-pits (kuṇḍas) measuring one fist, one cubit, or one forearm in size.
It should possess a length, width, and height of six, four, and two finger-breadths respectively; one should make the tip of the yoni one finger-breadth wide and slightly downward-facing.
In other sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one should increase the width of the vulva (yoni) by one finger-breadth for each successive pit;
likewise, its tip should also be increased by a sequence of two barley-corns (yava). || 37 ||

Within the womb-like cavity, there should be a channel like a sacrificial ladle (sruk) capable of pouring out clarified butter; starting from the base, the stalk should extend to support the root of the womb.
A wise man should likewise make an opening above the second girdle for the purpose of placing the enclosing ring (paridhi) between the two girdles. (39)
One should fashion within the fire-pits a navel resembling a lotus;
its measurement is said to be either conforming to each respective pit or as follows: || 40 ||
The navel is said by the wise to have a height equal to one-twelfth of the pit (kuṇḍa), a width of one-eighth of the pit, and a length of the same number of parts.
Alternatively, for pits measuring one fist, one cubit, or one forearm in height, they should be provided with four or three finger-breadths [in width];
in other cases, one should increase these dimensions accordingly.

The one of noble intellect, following the sequence of two *yava*s, should separately [mark] the navel; having divided the field of the navel into three parts, he should place the pericarp in the middle.
One should fashion eight petals using two external segments; thereafter, one should form the tips of the petals, thus completing the characteristics of the *kuṇḍa*.
In this context, the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) have been described according to the number of oblations: a pit measuring one fist (muṣṭi) is prescribed for fifty oblations.
For a hundred oblations, the pit should be one aratni in measure; for a thousand, one cubit; for ten thousand, two cubits;
and for a hundred thousand, it is declared to be four cubits.
A pit of six cubits is prescribed for ten lakhs, and one of eight cubits for a crore;
a pit measuring one cubit is ordained for one lakh.
One should increase [the size] by ten cubits up to ten hundred thousand [lakṣas];
from ten lakṣas until the time of striking (ākoṭi), it is prescribed to be ten cubits.
There is no other oblation superior to one measured by ten million;
nor is there any sacrificial pit superior to one measuring ten cubits. (49)

In all matters, such as honoring [the teacher] and so forth, the square [mandala] is the appropriate application; for it has been declared by the wise that this brings about all accomplishments for everyone. (50)

The mention of the yoni and other types of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) follows as a matter of course; regarding sacrificial pits of two cubits and so forth, some who are overly zealous have said: || 51 ||
Having made the Brahma-thread measuring two cubits and so forth, and having formed two corners there,
one should cause other sacrificial pits, such as the yoni-shaped ones, to be constructed.
When the question is asked, "How many cubits long is this house? and the other replies, "It is ten cubits," this is indeed a worldly illustration. (53)

Because that [word] is not seen in such cases as "the pot (kuṇḍa) is made from that (tad-asat-dvika)," the insertion of an ellipsis (adhyāhāra) is not appropriate, precisely due to the absence of expectancy (ākāṅkṣā). || 54 ||

As for what was stated [earlier] regarding "ten cubits," that is said here because of the context; however, it is not seen at all in such passages as "the sacrificial pit is two cubits at ten thousand [repetitions]," and so forth.
Whether it be the length, the width, or both, this instruction is stated as follows: "The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) shall be two cubits [in measurement]," and so forth. (56)
However, it is determined that only the fruit of the field is doubled; this is our accepted position, and its method is now explained. (57)
In the field of the hand, the middle line is twenty-four finger-breadths;
it is joined with thirty-three finger-breadths and seven barley-corns.
Four lice, along with four likhyās and a half,
constitute the measurement for a two-cubit middle cord; this same measurement for a three-cubit cord consists of forty-one finger-breadths and four barley-corns.
Four lice, slightly less than four *likhyās*,
constitute that which is forty-eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in a span of four cubits.
Having marked fifty-three finger-breadths (aṅgulas) and six less-yavas, that measurement is declared for a five-cubit field; for a six-cubit field,
its base is said to be fifty-eight aṅgulas and six yavas.
The square root of seven cubits is sixty-three finger-breadths (aṅgulas) together with four barley-corns and slightly more than two yūkas. (62)
Likewise, for a [mandala] of eight cubits, the middle line is said to be sixty-seven finger-breadths and seven barley-corns, slightly less than that.
In a pit measuring nine cubits, the base is considered to be seventy-two finger-breadths;
in a pit measuring ten cubits, that base is the middle cord. One should increase it by seventy-five finger-breadths and seven barley-corns.
Thus it is proclaimed that one should construct the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) with great effort, starting from two cubits and so on, together with those slightly more or less [than that]. 65.

p. 153) Since manifestation is difficult to accomplish for those who possess forms such as two hands and so forth, one should know the form of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to be the supreme body of primordial nature (prakṛti). 66.
The head is declared to be in the east, the arms in the south and north;
the belly is said to be the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and the feet are in the west.
There, eighteen consecrations for the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are taught:
inspection with the root mantra and sprinkling with the [mantra of] the arrow are considered [the first two].

Striking with that same [mantra], sprinkling with darbha grass, and protection with the armor-mantra (varma) are prescribed; digging and lifting up with the weapon-mantra (astra), and filling with the heart-mantra (hṛd). || 2 ||
Sprinkling with the *samīkaraṇa* mantra and the *varman* mantra is prescribed; pounding with the *heti* mantra and wiping with the *varman* mantra [are likewise performed]. (3)
Anointing, the fashioning of the artistic forms, and immediately thereafter the drawing of the three lines; following that, worship with the Heart-mantra is prescribed. (4)

The making of the mouth with the Astra-mantra, the cutting of the auspicious Kuśa grass with the Hṛdaya-mantra, the clearing of the crossroads with the Kavaca-mantra, and the cutting of the right side with the Tattva-mantra.
In the sacrifice, one should consecrate the sacrificial pits with the consecrations prescribed; or else, one should consecrate them with the four [rites] beginning with inspection.
Having examined various treatises and extracted the essence from them all,
the procedure for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and other matters is here stated with care, like butter from curds.
Now, the method taught in the scriptures for the purpose of understanding the cubit, the span, and so forth, as well as the divisions of the finger-breadth and other units, is set forth.
In this regard, there is much disagreement among disputants concerning the middle phalanx of the right hand of the Creator, such as Śaradā and others. (2)

A *trasareṇu*, an *anureṇu*, the tip of a grain of barley, and a *likhya*—along with a louse (*yūkā*), a barley-corn (*yava*), and a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*)—form a sequence each eight times the size of the preceding one. (3)
When the sun shines through a lattice, that subtle particle which is seen is called the *trasareṇu*, the first among all measures of magnitude.
A *trasareṇu* should be known as that which consists of eight *paramāṇus*.
A closed fistful of *prakoṣṭha* [grains] is here called a *muṣṭi*, and eight *muṣṭis* are called a *ratni*.
Ratni is declared to be a kara minus one-sixteenth part; this has been stated in the *Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana-saṃgraha*. (6)
The forearm is the hand with the fingers extended; it becomes a *saratni* when the fist is clenched. That same measure without the little finger is an *aratni*. || 7 ||

In reality, since works such as the *Parīśiṣṭa* are of the nature of Smṛti, one should understand that the auspicious rites mentioned therein apply to rituals prescribed in the Smṛtis; however, regarding rituals taught in the Āgamas, one should understand the characteristics of the hands and so forth according to the procedure stated in the *Śāradātilaka* and other such texts. (1)
Likewise, it is stated in the *Pañcarātra* regarding the characteristics of the hand and so forth:
"The distance between the joints in the middle of the middle finger of the teacher’s right hand is declared to be a *mātrāṅgula*. (2)
An *aṅgula* is said to be eight times the size of a *yava* according to the sequence of atoms; this is declared to be the *mātrāṅgula* by the measurement of the middle finger's length. (3)
In the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*: "Regarding the definition of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*),
whenever the measurement of the thumb-finger is prescribed, one should always measure it there by means of the knots at the joints of the large fingers."
Likewise, Kātyāyana has also stated the definition of a finger-breadth (aṅgula): "The measure of a finger-breadth consists of six barley grains placed side by side. (5)
This statement of the learned is also accepted by everyone:
"The authoritative cubit (prāmāṇika-kara) is the distance between the middle finger and the elbow. (6)
Twenty-one finger-joints of a jewel are counted as one *ratni*; ten finger-joints of the thumb are proclaimed to be a *prādeśa*.
Having thus deliberated upon the established doctrines, while composing the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*, this doctrine has been formulated here regarding rites such as the offering of one's hand.
The final conclusion here shall be derived from the words of the Kalpaka; for the statement of the Kalpaka directly depends upon the Veda as it has been perceived.
The authors of the Smṛtis composed their legal treatises by inferring the sacred tradition (Āgama);
for that which exists in its entirety, whether in the state of lying prostrate or with the hands raised, [is the source].
The fifth part [of a finger] is a *hasta*; a *jināṃśa* (one-fourth of that) is its *aṅgula*. A sixteenth part of that is a *yava*;
this is declared to be the definition of the *hasta* and so forth. (11)
A *bhāna* shall be one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), and twelve *aṅgulas* make a *vitasti*. Two of those are declared to be a *hasta*; such is the supreme opinion. (12)
The scope of these two has been explained there regarding finger-breadths; indeed, one should prepare all the implements for sacrifice according to the measure of the finger-breadth (mātrāṅgula).

A wise person should fashion the implements of the oblation, such as the *sruva* ladle and others, as well as the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the handful (*muṣṭi*), and the finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), according to the scriptures using the measurement-finger (*mānāṅgula*). || 14 ||

"Or rather, for all ritual actions, the *kiṣku* alone is considered [the standard measure]," so say those who know the collection of the essence of the established tenets of reality (*tattvasiddhānta*). (15)
The measurement of finger-breadths, cubits, fist-widths, and so forth, is stated here as pertaining to the sacrificer; it never applies to the preceptor or to the other officiating priests.

In the Chandogapariśiṣṭa, the sage Kātyāyana has stated: "When the procedure for measurement has been declared but the measurer has not been specified, the sacrificer shall be the measurer; this is the settled conclusion of the learned. (17)

One should fashion the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) for the sacrifice according to the method that will be described hereafter, using wood from the *kāraskara*, *āmalakī*, *palāśa*, or *khadira* trees. (18)
The wise man, having taken one of the trees— either Śrīparṇā, Śiṃśapā, or Śīraśākha—
should divide it into thirty-six parts, each measuring one cubit in length.
The edge (anta) should be made with twenty parts, and the altar (vedī) with eight of those parts.
The neck is measured by one part, and the mouth is measured by seven parts;
the width of the neck is proclaimed to be three parts of the pedestal.
The opening at the mouth should be made level with the throat;
one should fashion a passage for the exit of the clarified butter according to the measurement of the little finger.
In the center of the altar, the pericarp (karṇikā) should be fashioned with one part; one should then fashion a lotus stalk (vaṭa) all around it with one part on the outside.
The pit for that [stūpa] should be divided into three parts; outside, it should be half a part in width, and one part all around should be fashioned as the petals.
Some [authorities] have stated that one should also dig out the leaves;
however, since this is not taught here, it does not appear to be compelling. (25)
The girdle (mekhalā) should be around the mouth and the altar (vedī), measuring half a part on all sides;
at the base and tip of the teeth, there should be two sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) measuring three and four finger-breadths respectively.
The *dantī* (tooth) portion consists of two pairs of parts; this is declared to be the *aṇḍa* (egg).
With six parts, the tail-section (*pucchabhāga*) of the altar (*vedī*) takes the form of a tortoise (*kūrmākṛti*). || 27 ||
One should draw the face of a swan, an elephant, or a bird; behind the face of this [image], the characteristic of the *sruk* ladle is said to be located. (28)
One should fashion the *sruva* ladle with twenty-four parts;
the measurement of its handle is declared to be twenty-two parts. (1)
With four parts one should fashion the swelling [of the base], with a karṣa of clarified butter the head should be grasped;
with two parts one should bury it in the mud in the shape of a deer's footprint.
The *guṇḍī* should be adorned with a ring at both the base and the tip of the handle;
thus is described the characteristic of the *sruva* according to all the Tantras.
"A wise person should fashion the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles according to the rules from gold, silver, copper, or even iron; such is the doctrine of the *Phetkāriṇīmata*. (4)
It is said that [a sruk] at its base causes harm, likewise at the middle it causes grief, and at the tip it is said to cause disease;
how then can one hold the sruva?
Having abandoned four finger-breadths in front and likewise sixteen [finger-breadths] at the sides,
one should hold [the space] in the middle with a measurement of four finger-breadths using the conch-gesture (śaṅkhamudrā).
The sacrificer indeed suffers loss from the sight of the base of the *sruva* ladle;
therefore, the practitioner of mantras should conceal it at the time of the oblation according to the prescribed rule.
With the hand turned palm-upward, the oblation should be offered while pressing with the tip of the thumb; the fingers being held together and the speech restrained.
O Sage, one should prepare the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles from a flawless, beautiful *palāśa* leaf, or from a small *aśvattha* leaf in the case of a concise *homa* ritual.
Thereafter, one should perform the ritual applications as they were previously described as being effective;
now, I shall correctly explain here the characteristics of the six rites (ṣatkarma).

In accordance with all tantras, it bestows the accomplishment of the fruits of practice; the wise praise the six rites ending with killing: pacification, subjugation, immobilization, inciting hatred, expulsion, and then [killing]. (11)
The pacification of diseases, sorcery, possession, and the like is proclaimed;
the subjugation of all people, making them obedient, is also declared. (12)
The obstruction of the activity of all [senses] is declared to be "stambhana" (paralysis). Causing mutual hatred among those who are affectionate is considered "vidveṣaṇa" (inciting enmity). 13.
Uccāṭana is proclaimed as the expulsion from one's own country and so forth; māraṇa is declared to be the taking away of the life-force of living beings. (14)
Having understood one's own deity, the directions, the time, and so forth, one should accomplish the rites. Rati, Vāṇī, Ramā, Jyeṣṭhā, Durgā, and Kālī are declared to be the deities of the six rites;
one should worship them at the beginning of each rite. (15)

The directions are assigned to Īśa, Candra, Indra, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Agni. Beginning from sunrise, the seasons—Vasanta and the rest—occur in succession every ten *ghaṭikās* throughout each day and night. 16.
From spring, summer, and the rainy season come autumn, winter, and the cool season; winter is prescribed for rites of pacification (śāntika), while spring is for rites of subjugation (vaśya).
In the winter season, conciliation (sammāna) is to be known; in the summer, hostility (vidveṣa) is said to be effective.
The rainy season is to be known for the rite of eradication (uccāṭana), and autumn for the act of killing (māraṇa). 18.
The wise call the lotus (padma), the swastika, the formidable (vikaṭa), the cock (kukkuṭa), the crooked (vakraka), and the auspicious (bhadra) the names of postures (āsana).
One should extend both arms between the knees and the shanks;
this is known as the vikaṭāsana, performed while seated in the utkaṭāsana posture.
First, having assumed the utkaṭāsana with both feet even, one should then place both hands between the knees; this is declared to be the kukkuṭāsana. || 21 ||
One should place the two ankles below the scrotum along the sides of the perineal seam;
with the hands holding the feet against the sides, this constitutes the Bhadrāsana posture. || 22 ||
The other mudrās, beginning with the Svastika, were indeed previously described in their proper order; now the six mudrās known as Padma, Pāśa, and Gadā should be understood in sequence. (23)

The mudrās previously mentioned in order are named the pestle (musalā), the thunderbolt (aśani), and the sword (khaḍga); now the lotus (padma), the noose (pāśa), and so forth are described, as well as the characteristics of the thunderbolt (aśani).
The mudrā formed by joining the little finger and the thumb is triangular and belongs to Śani.
Water is recommended for rites of pacification (śānti), while fire is declared to be used for subjugation (vaśya). (25)

For the rite of immobilization (stambhana), earth is to be known [as the element]; for inciting enmity (vidveṣa), space is proclaimed; for eradication (uccāṭana), air is remembered; and for killing (māraṇa), fire is further considered [the appropriate element]. || 26 ||
During the respective emergence of each element, the mantra-practitioner of sharpened mind should properly perform the corresponding rite, joined with its respective maṇḍala. (27)
The movement of the earth is in the form of a staff beneath both layers; that of water is upward;
and that of fire is horizontal. (28)

The movement [of the breath] through the center of the sky is known as the arising of all beings; upon the arising of the earth, the knower of the Self should perform the rites of immobilization and subjugation.

The rites of pacification (śāntika) and nourishment (pauṣṭika) belong to the water element; those of killing (māraṇa) and so forth belong to the wind element, as do the rites for the eradication of adversaries.
The destruction of poison and other such things is recommended at the rising of the sky; the rising of the spirits has been declared, and I shall now describe their maṇḍala.
The circle of the sky is marked with six dots; that of the wind is a triangle endowed with a svastika;
and that of fire is joined with a crescent moon.
The wise know that the mandalas are the lotus for water, the square with a vajra for earth, and those having the appearance of their respective elements. (33)
They say that these [elements] are adorned by their respective colors and enveloped by their own names:
the sky is transparent, the wind is black, fire is red, and water is clear.
The earth is yellow; thus the five elements have been described according to their form. Their colors were previously declared for the purpose of examining the *kula* and *akula*. (35)
The syllables of the moon, water, earth, sky, wind, and fire are the seed-syllables for the six rites, respectively. (36)
Grathana, vidarbha, sampuṭa, rodhana, yoga, and pallava—these are the arrangements for the six types of ritual acts. (37)

One should interpose the letters of the name with the syllables of the mantra according to the prescribed rule; one should know that this is "stringing" (grathana), which is highly recommended for rites of pacification (śāntika).

One should write the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished situated between pairs of mantra-syllables; this is to be known as *vidarbha* by practitioners for the rite of subjugation. (39)
The mantra should be at the beginning and at the end of the name; this is considered a "casket" (sampuṭa).
This is declared by those who know the mantras to be excellent for the purpose of paralyzing.
The mantra should be placed at the beginning, end, and middle of the name; this is considered the method for immobilization (stambhana).
This is declared to be highly recommended in the rites of inciting enmity (vidveṣaṇa). || 41 ||
The name should be at the end of the mantra; this is considered the "yoga" for expulsion. The mantra should be at the end of the name; this is considered the "pallava" for killing.
White, red, yellow, mixed, black, and smoke-colored are proclaimed as the colors of the deities mentioned in the mantras for the six types of ritual actions.
The fifth, second, third, and likewise the seventh lunar days,
when conjoined with Mercury, Jupiter, or the Sun, are highly esteemed for rites of pacification (śāntika).
The sixth, the fourth, and the thirteenth lunar days joined with Jupiter and the Moon are auspicious for rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika), as are the eighth and the ninth.
The tenth and the eleventh [lunar days], when joined with Sunday or Friday;
for the purpose of attraction (ākarṣaṇa), the new moon day, the ninth, and likewise the first [tithi].
The full moon day joined with the moon and the sun is for the rite of incantation;
likewise, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight and the eighth day when the stars are dim.
They are highly recommended for the rite of eradication (uccāṭana), especially during the evening twilights,
as well as on the fourteenth, eighth, and new moon days of the dark fortnight.
The day of Nandā joined with a Sunday, as well as the fifth, the seventh, and the full moon— these lunar days are to be known for the rite of immobilization (stambhana).

One should perform auspicious acts when the planets are auspicious, and inauspicious acts when there is an inauspicious rising. For fierce rites, one should act during the Riktā lunar day, on a Sunday, and during the Mṛtyu-yoga.
The substances for writing mantras for the purpose of killing are sandalwood, bezoar, turmeric, soot from a house, charcoal from a funeral pyre, and the eight poisons. (51)
The fumes of a hawk, fire, hemp,
and dhattūra, along with house-soot and the three pungents (trikaṭuka), are declared to be the eight poisons.
Having correctly understood the deities, the times, the mudrās, and so forth, the wise practitioner should employ the six rites for the sake of attaining the results as described. (53)
The knowers of mantras should perform the rites outside the sixfold ritual; "these are the procedures for pacification (śāntika)," so have the traditionalists declared. (54)
If one does not obtain success because of an obstruction caused by a powerful opposing karma, one should perform the rite again two or three times. (55)
One who is utterly struck down by fate should not perform worldly rites; there is no fault in this, yet he may incur ridicule. (56)
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the mantras hidden within the tantras—
both those that are well-known and those that are obscure, such as the Nīlasārasvata and others.
[These mantras] are those declared in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtti-tantra, as well as those found in the Phetkāriṇī[-tantra],
and those situated in various well-known chapters of diverse treatises.
I do not speak thus to certain others due to the influence of time; first, one should extract the Vāgbhava seed-syllable of Tripurabhairavī. (3)
The knower of mantras, having encased the supreme goddess with the *tāra* (oṃ), [recites] "sarasvatyai namaḥ" at the end; this mantra consists of eleven syllables, the number of Rudras.
The seer is Dakṣiṇāmūrti; the metre is declared to be Gāyatrī;
and the deity is proclaimed to be Vāṇī, the Mistress of Pārijāteśvara. || 5 ||

Atri, who was restrained by Varuṇa, [perceived] this pair of syllables uttered while speaking downwards; this ten-syllable mantra of Vāgīśvarī bestows the power of speech. Kaṇva is the seer (ṛṣi), Virāṭ is the meter (chandaḥ), and Vāk is declared to be the deity (devatā).

At the end of *hṛdaya*, one should likewise utter the word *bhagavati* twice; then, preceded by the *vāgbhava* syllable, one should extract the mantra ending with the wife of Fire (Svāhā) and addressed to Vāgdevī. This mantra, enriched with sixteen syllables, bestows the fruit of mastery over speech. (7)

The Tāra (Om), Māyā (Hrīṃ), Dhava (Śrīṃ), Bindu (Ṃ), Śakti (Aiṃ), the Tāra (Om) again, and Sarasvatī (Vāgīśvarī) in the feminine dative case— this eleven-syllable mantra is declared to be the ultimate.
"O Vācaspati! O Immortal One! Again, Plūvaḥ, Plūḥ—thus one should recite.
This mantra, consisting of eleven syllables, beginning with 'Vāk', has been proclaimed by the sages. (9)
The bed of Viṣṇu situated in the water (toya) together with the solitary four-faced one (Brahmā), the Bindu joined with the half-moon and Fire (Agni),
and Bhr̥gu who possesses the Bindu and Sadyojāta and Water— these three seed-syllables have been declared by the wise for those seeking the essence of Sarasvatī. (10)
[Vāgbhava, the left eye, and Bindu-adbhuvaneśvarī—these three seed-syllables have been stated. Its seers and other [attributes] are as before. (11)
Having first extracted the seed-syllable Śakti (Hrīṃ), one should then utter the syllable Trīṃ; with the long vowel at the end, this is the mantra of Nīlasārasvata. || 12 ||

This mantra of Tārā is said to be distinct, beginning with the *tāra* (om) and ending with *phaṭ*; if it is devoid of the *tāra* and ends with *phaṭ*, it is said to be the distinct mantra of Ekajaṭā. (13)
The seer is said to be Akṣobhya, the metre is declared to be Bṛhatī, and the deity has been explained here by the teachers in due order. (14)
The pair "Lajjā" (hrīṃ), the seed-syllable of the bride (strīṃ), followed by the long letter "Ta" (tāṃ) and the armor (huṃ)—this other four-syllabled mantra of Sarasvatī has been declared. || 15 ||
At the end of that, if there is the syllable *phaṭ*, there is another five-syllabled mantra;
at the end are the seed-syllables of Tāra, Śakti, and Vadhū, followed by the long [vowel] as the armor (*tanucchada*).

The weapon [seed-syllable] is *agnivadhū* (the bride of fire), followed by another seven-syllabled *manu*. This is proclaimed in the mantra-śāstras; likewise, the seed-syllable of the bride (*vadhū-bīja*) is encased by the long *varma* (armor) syllable, and this other one consists of three syllables. || 17 ||

The two *va* syllables joined with the *repha*, the left eye (*i*), and the *bindu*, followed by *phaṭ*—this is the three principles (*tritattva*). One should first utter the *tāra* (om) for the lotus, then the pair [of syllables] for the great lotus (*mahāpadma*). || 18 ||
Padmāvatī, ending with two *ṭha*s, having a single *jaṭā*, and joined with seven vowels—this, when the bindu is placed upon the twelfth vowel, becomes the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Bālā. (19)

The letter *va* (vānta) mounted upon fire (*ra*), conjoined with the moon of the left eye (*i*), is declared to be this seed-syllable of Śrī, like another wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*). Bhṛgu is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Nivṛt-gāyatrī is the meter (*chanda*), and Śrī is proclaimed as the deity (*devatā*). (20)
The Vāgbhava, the Vanitā of Viṣṇu, the Māyā, and the Makaraketana—this mantra consisting of four seed-syllables bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life. || 21 ||

The ten-syllable mantra beginning with *dīrghāmārādi* and ending with *sargāntau*, consisting of *brahmabhānurvasundharā vāntesinyai priyā*, is declared to belong to Agni. Dakṣa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Virāṭ is the meter (*chandaḥ*), and Śrī is said to be the deity (*devatā*). (22)
Vāgbhava, Śambhu’s consort, Ramā, and Makaraketana; the third [syllable], the two nooses of the world, and the seed-syllable of Fire, blazing brightly. (23)

(166) This twelve-syllable mantra of Mahālakṣmī, beginning with *tāra* (om) and consisting of the syllables *bhṛgu* (s), *tyai*, and *hṛt* (namaḥ), enriched by *argha* (svāhā), is declared to bestow all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*). || 24 ||
The seer is declared to be Brahmā; the meter is said to be Gāyatrī; and the deity is proclaimed to be Mahālakṣmī, the primordial source of the worlds. (25)
Śambhupatnī, Śriyāruddhā, Kāma, Bhagavatī, Mahī, Brahmāditya, Dharā, Dīrghā, Lakṣādi, Bhagavān, and Marut. (26)

The pair [of syllables] *prasīda*, followed by *śrīruddhā bhuva-neśvarī*, ending with *namas* and preceded by the *praṇava* (Oṃ), constitutes this mantra; beginning with twenty-seven syllables, it is proclaimed to bestow all prosperity. (27)
It should be adorned with Candra (the moon), Īśa (the letter I), Māda (the letter Ma), Lakṣmī (the letter L), and Vahni (the letter Ra) along with Dīrghākṣi (the long vowel Ī);
it should be joined with Bindu (the nasal dot) and Dhruveśvarī (the letter U), and encapsulated by the Śrī-bīja (the syllable Śrīm). || 28 ||
The sage is Hari, and the meter is considered to be Gāyatrī;
the deity is Mohinī Lakṣmī, who bestows great sovereignty. (29)
Nakulīśa mounted upon fire, possessing the left eye and the half-moon—this is declared to be her seed-syllable (bīja), practiced by those desiring supernatural attainments (siddhi). (30)
The sage is Śakti, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity of the mantra is said by the assembly of gods to be Bhuvaneśvarī, who is served throughout the world. 31.
The practitioner of mantras should extract the mantra consisting of the three seed-syllables— Vāgbhava, Śambhuvanitā, and Ramā— which is the means for attaining the fruits of the three aims of life.
This three-syllabled vidyā is considered to be Māyā encased within the seed-syllable Vāk. || 33 ||

The three-syllabled mantra beginning with *pāśa* consists of Ananta joined with Bindu, Māyā, Brahmā, Agni, and Tāra; it bestows complete subjugation. The Seer and other [limbs] have been stated previously, and the Deity is Bhuvaneśvarī. (34)
*Tāra*, *māyā*, the seed-syllable of armor (*varma*), *ṛddhi* conjoined with *Īśvara*; then *kūrma* at its end, the Lord (*bhagavān*), *kṣantrī* (or *strī*), and the long *tanucchadam*. (35)

The Blessed One is Saṃvarta; his seed-syllable (bīja) is Māyā (Hrīṃ); he consists of twelve syllables. He is declared to be the Sage Arjuna, and Virāṭ is said to be the meter. Tvaritā is proclaimed as the deity, who bestows the fruits of the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha). || 36 ||
The Blessed One is the armor; Meru is the end, accompanied by creation. The Vidyā known as Trikaṇṭakī consists of three syllables. (37)
This three-syllabled Vidyā, beginning with *kṣe*, is for women of the three castes and is the "Three-Thorned" spell for subjugation. || 38 ||
*Tāra* (Om), followed by *māyā* (Hrīṃ) and *vāgbhava* (Aiṃ), then *nityaklinne madadrave*; ending with *vahnijāyā* (Svāhā)—this is the fifteen-syllable mantra. (39)

The seed-syllable of Speech (Vāgbhava), the seed-syllable of Love (Mānmatha), "Nityaklinne," then "madau," "drave," and "vahni-vadhūḥ"— this twelve-syllabled mantra has been declared. Samohana is the Seer (Ṛṣi), Nivṛt is the Metre (Chandas), and Nityā is the Deity.
Immediately after the *vāṅmāyā*, [the mantra] "nityaklinne madadrave" follows; this mantra, consisting of twelve syllables ending with two 'ca's, bestows subjugation. (41)
Aṅgiras is the seer; Triṣṭubh is the meter declared by the sages; Vajraprastāriṇī is proclaimed as the deity, the bestower of desired boons. || 42 ||
Having uttered *Bhuvaneśī*, [one says] *nityaklinne madadrave*; this is the nine-syllable Vidyā, which possesses twenty-two syllables ending with two *u*s.
The mantra consisting of the three seed-syllables (bījas) was proclaimed by Śrī, Māyā, and Madana; its seer (ṛṣi) is Sammohana, its meter (chandaḥ) is Gāyatrī, and it belongs to Tripuṭeśvarī. 44.

The power [consisting of] the noose, goad, and cupped hands; Jhiṇṭīśa; the sky [ha]; and the wind [ya]. O Parameśvarī, at the end of the word "sound" [śabda], there is the letter ending in 'ca' [ṭha] preceded by the Praṇava [oṃ]. This mantra, known as Aśvārūḍha, is said to consist of thirteen syllables.
The mantra consists of seventeen syllables: *māyā* (hrīṃ), followed by *hṛdbhagavati*, then *māheśvari*, and finally *annapūrṇe* with a pair of *ṭha*s (svāhā). || 46 ||
At the end of that is the pair "parāśrīkāma," then "bhagavati," then "māheśvari," then "annapūrṇe svāhā"; this is the mantra beginning with the fixed syllables (dhruva). 47.
The sage is Brahmā with twelve syllables; the meter is declared to be Paṅkti;
the deity is proclaimed to be the perfected Annapūrṇeśvarī. (48)

The mantra consists of the syllable Māyā (Hrīṃ), followed by the word Padmāvatī, and then the beloved of Agni (Svāhā); this seven-syllabled mantra is said to bestow complete subjugation over all. || 49 ||
The seed-syllable consists of the letters *da*, *ta*, *va*, *ga*, *ṃ*, *a*, *bi*, and *dva*; in the *dhūmāvatī* [mantra], there is *dvi-ṭha*.
Pippalāda is the sage, the *nivṛt* is the metre, and *dhūmāvatī* is the mantra. (50)

At the end of "parā jvālāmukhī," there is the two-fold *dviṭha* (the letter *ṭha*), which is a seven-syllabled mantra. This [syllable] is joined with *māyā* (the letter *ī*), the third vowel (*u*), and the ear-dot (*bindu*, *m*), and then it becomes possessed of the creative emission (*sarga*, *ḥ*). (51)

Ending with the five [vowels], possessing a foundation, having Māruta as its seed-syllable and Bhautika as its seat, this mantra consists of eight syllables, beginning with TĀRĀ and ending with HṚDAYA. || 52 ||
The seer is Nārada, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Manu’s Durgā, who is proclaimed by the virtuous as the remover of misfortunes. (53)
The radiant sky together with the two eyes, and the white [syllable] standing upon the two hips—this is declared to be the eight-syllabled Vidyā of Mahiṣamardinī. 54.

*Tāre* (Oṃ), *durge* joined with *rakta*, followed by the last letter (*kṣa*) and the end of the vowel series (*au*), together with the eye (*i*), and twice the end of the vowel series (*au-au*)—this ten-syllable Vidyā, beginning with *jaya durge*, is to be known. (55)
At the end of the word "mahīṣa," one should utter "hiṃsike kūrcam" and then the weapon-mantra ending with the wife of fire (svāhā);
this mantra consists of ten syllables.

At the end of the word "jvala jvala," there are two instances of "śūlini"; then follows "duṣṭagraha" [and so on], ending with the weapon-mantra (astra) and culminating in the wife of fire (svāhā). This is the mantra. (57)
It is declared that [this mantra] consisting of eighteen syllables destroys malevolent planets, minor spirits, and enemies.
Dīrghatamas is said to be the seer (ṛṣi), Kakup is cited as the meter (chandas), and Śūlinī, who is worshipped by all the gods, is declared to be the deity (devatā). || 58 ||

Having addressed the word "arise" (uttiṣṭha), there would be the word "man" (puruṣi); then the Grandfather (pitāmaha), with the moon as his eye, would say "you shall sleep" (svapiṣi), and there would be fear for me.
Having recited what has presented itself, if it is possible [to speak further], then, O Blessed One, he should thereafter tell me that which is impossible.

The mantra consisting of thirty-seven syllables has Śamayāgnivadhū as its deity; Āraṇyaka is the seer (ṛṣi), and Atyanuṣṭubh is declared to be the meter (chandas). The deity is known as Vanadurgā, the destroyer of all misfortunes.

One should utter the pair of *tāra* (oṃ) enclosed by the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma*, klīm); within the pair of *kūrca* (huṃ), there is the *śakti* (hrīṃ), and the weapon (*astra*, phaṭ) shall be the consort of fire (svāhā). || 62 ||
One should extract the fifteen-syllable Vidyā beginning with Tārā belonging to Rāmeśvara, as well as the Śakti-tritattva, the Vāgbīja, and the Tāra-mantra. (63)

At the end of "Vajravairocanī," there is the Blessed One Māruta; followed by the Kūrca weapon-mantra, he who has two vowels at the end—this is the threefold power consisting of that many syllables. 64.

Then the syllable *tāraṃ*, then the *vajrapada*, then *vairocanī* should follow; the Lord (*bhagavān*), *māruta*, the pair of *māyā*, and the weapon (*astra*) with two *ṭha*s—this mantra of thirteen syllables is the *Chinnamastā-mantra*. (65)
One should extract the seeds of Ādilakṣmī, Śakti, Kūrca, and Vāk; for Vajravairocanīye, there should be the pair of Māyās, followed by the utterance of Phaṭ.

The mantra, ending with the wife of Vahni (the fire-goddess), should be repeated many times for each [deity]; it should be recited separately with the five seed-syllables joined at the beginning, the end, and the middle.

One should proclaim Chinnamastā by means of [her mantras] both individually and as stated in their proper sequence. Here, Samrāj is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), and Bhairava shall be the meter (chandas) of this [mantra]. (68)
The elemental [syllable] situated in ether, the lunar orb, and fire, with the bindu as its crest;
and that which is situated in ether, the first of those [elements], earth, Indra, and fire, with the left eye and the bindu. (69)
The mantra situated in space (a), the wind (ya), and fire (ra) is the creation (sarga) [kṣa], followed by the moon (i) and the khaṇva (ṭha).
Vāgbhava is the first seed-syllable, and Kāmabīja is the second. 70.
The third is called the seed-syllable of power (śaktibīja); this Vidyā, consisting of five peaks (pañcakūṭa), is proclaimed by means of three seed-syllables and is to be known as Tripurabhairavī. 71.
The seer (ṛṣi) is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the meter (chandas) is declared to be Paṅkti, and the deity (devatā) is said by the teachers to be the goddess Tripurabhairavī. 72.

The first and last [syllables] are devoid of the letter *ra*; one should omit the *bindu* at the end. In some cases, the seed-syllable of Śiva is placed below the seed-syllable of the Moon in the middle.
The end of *kānta* (the letter *m*) joined with *vānta* (the letter *au*), and the end of *akula* (the letter *ha*) together with the end of *nānta* (the letter *ḥ*);
this is declared to be the six-peaked [mantra], joined respectively with the *bindu* and the *nāda*. (74)
If the syllable *tāram* (om) is followed by *kāmaḥ* (klīm) and ends with *namaḥ*, that becomes the Heart-mantra of the Goddess.
In the previously mentioned Bhairavī-mantra, [one should place] *parāśivām* after the *kāmakūṭa*.
If one should utter [the syllables] *hi*, then the goddess becomes Bhairavī Ḍāmarī. *Tāra* (Om), *kṣmā* (LṂ), and *mādana* (KṢE) are the seed-syllables; here, Śiva becomes threefold. (76)
Gradually form that [syllable] ending in *ma* with the sun (*ar*) and a digit of the moon (*indu*); the first pair consists of *bindu* and *nāda*, while the last is like the *visarga*.
The goddess Ṣaṭkūṭabhairavī, whose ṛṣi and other [limbs] are like those of Tripureśī;
one should write the syllables of Ṣaṭkūṭabhairavī according to the order of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama). (78)
Likewise, this Bhairavī, who is eternal and universal, shall be the remover of fear;
O Goddess of the Gods, having abandoned desire for Ḍāmareśvarabhairavī, [one attains this]. 79.
One should draw the seed-syllable of Śakti, pervaded by Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā; she is proclaimed as Bhairavī, named Bhayavidhvaṃsinī (the Destroyer of Fear). || 80 ||

By adding the five arrows of Tripurā, the Vidyā becomes five-syllabled. Madana is its seer (ṛṣi), and the Gāyatrī is said to be its meter. Its deity is this Sovereign Goddess (Īśvarī), who is to be worshipped like Kāmeśvarī.

The first [syllable] is the lower [lip], enriched by Bindu and Nāda, situated in Brahma and Indra, and joined with the Moon; the second is enriched by Bhṛgu and Sarga; and the third is said to be Manu. 82.
The first with the first, the middle with the middle, and likewise the last with the last—the first with the last and so forth—that very [method] becomes one that yields swift results. || 83 ||
The nine-syllable mantra is Tripureśānī, while the ten-syllable mantra begins with the Praṇava (Oṃ).
Dakṣiṇāmūrti is its seer (ṛṣi), and Paṅkti is declared to be its meter (chandas). Tripureśānī is the deity; she is a wish-fulfilling gem for those who worship her. (84)
Then, Śiva, Candra, Agni, and Dīrghākṣī consist of the Bindu and Nāda; likewise, Candreśa, Vahni, Vāmākṣī, Bindu, and Nāda constitute [the next]. (85)
Śakti and Kalāḍhya are at the end; the four seed-syllables have been declared. Let the third be the Śrī-bīja; thus the Vidyā shall consist of twenty-four syllables.

The seed-syllable of Śakti is in Vāgbhava; the Kāma-bīja is as before. The final [syllable] joined with Śiva belongs to Tripureśī, O Maheśvarī. This is indeed the goddess Lalitā, who bestows all prosperity. (87)

The seed-syllable of desire alone is declared to be the mantra of Kāmeśī. The sage of this mantra is said to be Kāla, its meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is proclaimed to be Kāmeśvarī, the sovereign of the universe. (88)
One should place the pair of *vada* syllables within the middle of the word *vādinī*; O Goddess, one should write the single *haṃsa* in the *vāgbhava* and in the *nityakledinī*. 89.
One should write the pair of syllables MAHĀKṢOBHAṂ, followed by ŚIVA, CANDRAKALĀ, and ANALA;
then the VĀMĀKṢI, BINDU, NĀDA, and ANTĀ, and finally the seed-syllable TĀRA. (90)

Mokṣa, Kuruyuga, Haṃsa, and that which possesses the vowel *śakra* (i) and the *visarga*—this is the goddess Sañjīvanī. Its seer is Sita; Gāyatrī is declared to be its meter, and Jīvanī is its deity. || 91 ||
Having omitted the Vāgbhava [syllable] of Tripureśī, one should write that [Kāmarāja] again;
with the two Kāma-śaktis at the end, this becomes the three-syllabled Vidyā. Like Tripureśī, the Goddess Kāmeśvarī is considered to have the same seers (ṛṣi) and other attributes.

At the end of the *praṇava* (oṃ), one should write a pair of goads (*aṅkuśa*), and in the middle of that, one should write the syllable *bha* (or *bha-va*). One should then write the *ca*-group of consonants, excluding its final letter, situated within the fire (*ra*). || 93 ||
Endowed with the fourteen vowels and individually marked with the bindu and nāda, this mantra should end with svāhā; Bhareṇḍā shall be its deity. (94)
Having written "parām" at the end of the fire [syllable], one should also write "vāsinyai namaḥ".
This eight-syllabled mantra has Maheshani Vahnivasini as its deity; its sage is Vasishtha, and Gāyatrī is said to be its meter. (96)
Having written Nityaklinnā, one should write the Tāra (Om) at the beginning; at the end of Hṛllekhā, one should place Katham (Phreṃ), Māyā, and the Moon-seed (Sa) with the Visarga. || 97 ||
The fourteen-syllable Vidyā is said to have Brahmā as its Seer (Ṛṣi);
its metre is declared to be Gāyatrī, and the Goddess is Vajreśvarī. (98)

Having uttered "Bhuvaneśī," one should say "Śivadūtyai namaḥ. This Śivadūtī consists of seven syllables and is the agitator of the three worlds. Rudra is its sage, Gāyatrī its meter, and she is declared to be the deity. (99)
(172) Adorned with *jīva*, *vāruṇa*, and *tārā*, and ending with the word *maṅgalā* at the very end;
having written "namaḥ" at the end of *ṅe*: this is the nine-syllabled *Sarvamaṅgalā*. O Maheśānī, the seer is [traditionally] stated to be Gāyatrī as the metre. (100)

Having uttered the seed-syllable Oṃ, and also "Namo Bhagavati," one should write "Jvālāmālini Deveśi Sarvabhūtāntimam. This Jvālāmālinī is proclaimed as the wish-fulfilling jewel for those who worship her. (101)

Śiva, Candra, Jānta, Agni, Rudra, and Svara— adorned with these, one should extract the goddess Vijayā, the bestower of victory, according to this procedure; one should write the mantra adorned with Ka, Kā, Anugraha, Bindu, and Indu.
The seer of this mantra is Brahmā, and Gāyatrī is said to be its meter; the deity is declared to be Vicitrā, a jewel that grants the desires of those who worship her. (103)
One should likewise enclose the Nityabhairavī with this [mantra];
O Goddess of the Gods, the five arrows and the Nityā become the syllable of Śakra (the thunderbolt). Many other varieties have not been mentioned for fear of prolixity.
Mādana is below that; Śakti is at its end; and Bindumālinī follows. Then the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśānī, which is Aindra, becomes Vāgbhava. || 105 ||

Having divided the seed-syllable of Śiva into three according to the sequence of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, one should remove the first [syllable] from the first two; below the first [remaining syllable] is the syllable of Madana.
One should join the seed-syllable of Indra (L) below the Śiva situated above;
likewise, below the Ālaya-Śiva, there is Fire (R) possessing the fourth vowel and the Moon (U). Thus is this great seed-syllable, the seed of desire (Klīm), which brings about great prosperity.
O Great Goddess, O fair-faced one, having applied the seed-syllable of Māyā, the Mādana syllable joined with Śakra, and the seed-syllable of the Moon alone, [one should proceed]. 108.

By means of the yoga of the process of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama), one should extract the seed-syllable of Śakti. Having omitted the two vowels from the first seed-syllable, one should then utter Śiva and Śakti. This is called the Śrīvidyā, the deity known as Purasundarī. 109.
O beautiful one, [I shall explain] the power of the first Vidyā and its fourth state (turya). || 110 ||
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, having omitted [the syllables] from the beginning by means of Śiva and the Moon, this becomes Lopāmudrā; indeed, it is the third part of that very Vidyā.
(173) That great and primordial seed-syllable of Śakti was worshipped by Vidyāgastya;
through the power of Lopāmudrā, she is the manifest embodiment of Brahman. 112.
Alternatively, one should extract the Goddess Śakti situated between Ā and DANA; one should place Śiva in the Vāgbhava [bīja], while the Kāma-bīja begins with Śiva. (113)

The third [mantra] begins with "Candra" and this vidyā is that of Mānavī. Furthermore, many other varieties have not been mentioned due to the fear of prolixity. Dakṣiṇāmūrti shall be the seer (ṛṣi), and the metre (chandas) shall be called Paṅkti. (114)

The life-force (jīva), the pair of Śivas (śivayuga), the beloved of the life-force and its end (jīvakāntakāntā), and Śiva with the moon (śivendu)—this constitutes the first; and the middle consists of the swan (haṃsa), the yoked earth (yuk-kṣmā), the eye (akṣa), and the moon (indu). 115.
But before that, [the Lord spoke of] this Trikūṭa, adorned with six plows, the earth, the moon, and the sky, as described in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrti-tantra*. 116.
Then Lakṣmī, Māyā, and again Tāra; Parā, Lakṣmī, and Kumārikā; then Vidyā, Vyastā, Bālā, Śrī, and Parā—this is the sixteen-syllable mantra. (117)
The wise one should write the first pair of the second [group] in reverse order; then, having placed Bālā facing inward, he should write her immediately thereafter.
One should write the three peaks (kūṭas) in sequence: Tāra, Māyā, and then Lakṣī. One should enclose them with Bālā; she who is called Ramā is the Supreme Goddess. 119.

One should write separately the [syllables] ending in Candra (the Moon) and Vāruṇa (Varuṇa), together with Śakra (Indra) and the others; first, one should write them in reverse order, beginning with the left eye (I), followed by Bindu and Nāda. 120.

One should write the inward-facing maiden (antarmukhā kumārī) enveloped by five [syllables]; this sixteen-syllable mantra consisting of six peaks (ṣaṭkūṭa) has been taught in another tantra in due order. 121.
The seed-syllables beginning with Tāra and Māyā constitute the Vidyā; it consists of six peaks (kūṭas).
The seer and other [limbs] are as before; the divisions are not stated here for fear of prolixity.
Having joined together Brahmā, Ādhāraśakti, Kalā, Smara, and Purandara,
one should then join the Goddess Īśvarī into Śiva.

One should join the seed-syllable of Śiva, which stands at the beginning of that [seed-syllable] of the Moon; one should join Mādana, situated within the seed-syllable of Indra, with the Mistress of the World (Bhuvaneśvarī). 124.
One should extract the seed-syllable of Śiva situated within Mādana, joined with Indra as the sixth; then one should extract the seed-syllable of Māyā situated within the red seventh and Indra. 125.

One should also join together in one place the seed-syllable of the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī), which resides in the syllables beginning with Tuṇḍa and Akṣarīśiva, and is conjoined with Marut and Indra. (126)
Below the fourth seed-syllable from the mouth, one should join Krodhīśa; likewise Pinākīśa situated in the moon, and Ākāśa situated in the red [syllable]. (127)
Joined with the fourth vowel and adorned with the *nāda* and *bindu*, all [these] combined together become five;
thus there are five five-syllabled [mantras]. This Vidyā, consisting of five peaks (*kūṭa*), is the fifth, the Supreme Deity. (128)
Then, at the end of the expansion of Vāṅmāyākamalā, one should utter "O Blessed One, O Śrī Mātaṅgeśvarī, who captivates the minds of all people. (129)
At the beginning of all [mantras], there is *mukharājyante*; at the beginning of all, there is *mukharañjini*.
After that, there is *sarvarājavaśam*, and then the word *karisarpa*. || 130 ||
Then, [there is] the Brahmānetra, which brings women and men under control, and the Agnyāsana; then the Karī, which brings all wicked beasts under control, and the Sarvabhṛgu. 131.
"O Śaṅkarī, bring such-and-such a person from all the worlds under my control, O Śivāgrani!"—this is the mantra of eighty-eight syllables for the Jāyā fire. (132)
"Oṃ namaḥ pāśāṅkuśau dvedhā phaṭ svāhā kālikālike"—this fifteen-syllable mantra of Kālī consists of a long *tanucchada* (armour). 133.

At the end of *prāsāda*, one should utter *kāli*, and then the word *mahākāli*. [The syllables] joined with *kalā* and *akṣi* are repeated twice, and at the end of that, one should pronounce *phaṭ*. (134)

With "svāhā," this fourteen-syllable mantra becomes that of Mahākālī; then, with the seed-syllable of modesty (hrīṃ), the "kūrca" syllable (huṃ), and ending with "phaṭ," it becomes a three-syllable mantra.
The two fires of dissolution (pra-layāgni), accompanied by blood and joined with upward-pointing hair (ūrdhvakeśī), and likewise conjoined with the Nāda and Bindu—thus again are the two Krodhas. 136.
This mantra of Kaumārī, consisting of the syllables of her qualities and bestowing all desires, is like a wish-fulfilling gem;
having uttered the word "ucchiṣṭa," one should also say "cāṇḍālinī. (137)

At the end of that [is] the goddess Sumukhī, who is also the great Piśācī; then the seed-syllable of Śakti, followed by the letter ṭha at its end, with the qualities (guṇas) and the emission-point (sarga-bindu). (138)

Alternatively, one should utter the *mātaṅgī* mantra beginning with *ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālī*, followed by *sarvavaśam* at the end, and concluding with the heart of the elephant (*karin*) and the beloved of fire (*vahnivallabhā*). With these nineteen syllables, it shall accomplish all desired objects. (139)
The seed-syllable of Śakti multiplied by three, followed by Bhṛgu (S) joined with Sarga (Ḥ), constitutes this four-syllabled mantra of Mahāśvetā as it has been proclaimed. (140)
They know the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati to be the end of the fifth [letter] joined with the moon (the nasal). The sage is Gaṇaka, the meter is Nivṛt, and its deity is Vighna.
The mantra of Vighna consists of the four vowels in reverse order, joined with the bindu;
it ends with "Hṛt" for the rite of worship and with "Ṭhāntika" for the fire sacrifice.
First, one should utter the seed-syllables of Śrī, Śakti, Smara, Bhū, and Vighna; then Gaṇapati ending in the nominative case (Ṅe), followed by the word "Varada" after the word "Vara. (143)
"Having spoken thus, bring all people under my control, Ṭha-dvayam.
This mantra, beginning with Tārā, is said to consist of twenty-eight syllables. (144)

The seer is Gaṇaka, the metre is Gāyatrī accompanied by Nivṛt; "idaṃ gṛhāṇa vadato varma astrānalavallabhā" is declared as the fourteen-syllabled Mahākālī-mantra beginning with the syllable *dhruva*. (145)

The syllable *va* (or *ka*), joined with the red dot on the left eye (*bindu*), becomes threefold. Thereafter, there should be a pair of *kūrca*s and a pair of *māyā*s as the word for the right side. (146)
In the Kālī-mantra, there are three Śaktis, as well as the long and short armor (dīrgha-tanucchadau), a pair of Śaktis, and the Dviṭha;
the Kālī-mantra consists of twenty-two syllables. || 147 ||

The sage is declared to be Bhairava, and the meter is Anuṣṭubh, in due order; [the mantras consist of] those ending in *ha*, preceded by those ending in *ma*, and likewise those ending in *la* and *na*. (148)
The eleventh letter of the *ka*-group, the sixth of the *ka*-group, the end of the *kha*-group, preceded by Viṣṇu (the letter *o*);
with these eight syllables, one should meditate upon the mantra as if it were a red lotus. (149)
Having first uttered the syllable Oṃ, the sage Nārada is to be recited; the metre is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity of the mantra is Mahāmāyā. (150)

Then one should extract the pair of *tāra*s (om), followed by the power (*śakti*) and the Vaiṣṇavī mantra; with the three bodies (*tritanu*) placed between the two *tāra*s, there shall be another [form] known as Vārāhī. (151)
*Tāra* (Om), *viyat* (ha), *indu* (sa), and *repha* (ra), followed by a vowel (*nu*), constitute the three-syllabled mantra of Bhavānī known as Bhuvaneśī. (152)

It should consist of the syllables *mā*, *yā*, *vi*, *ya*, *d*, *i*, *n*, *du*, *re*, *pha*, and the nasal vowel *anusvāra*. Having discarded the vowel of this [syllable], it becomes the subsequent [syllable] through its connection with the *sarga* (visarga). || 153 ||
He is declared to be Mahāgaṇapati, the deity worshipped by the gods. || 154 ||
One should utter *māyā* (Hrīm), followed by the pair *vividpadadvandvam*, then say *gaṇapatim*. After that, one should say *khaḍgīśapāvakau*, and again at the end of *varada*. (155)
"Bring the entire world under my control at my feet, *ṭha* twice!
This mantra of twenty-six syllables is a celestial wish-fulfilling tree for those who worship it. (156)
The seer is Gaṇaka, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Manu;
Vighneśvara is proclaimed as the one who grants all desires to those who worship him. (157)

One should utter one's own seed-syllable conjoined with the Śakti, followed by Mahāgaṇapati in the dative case (Ṅe’nta), and then the consort of Agni; this is declared to be the twelve-syllabled mantra. (158)
The seer is Gaṇaka, the meter is Gāyatrī beginning with Nivṛt, and the deity declared in the Tantra by name is Śaktigaṇādhipa. (159)

"Having restrained one's own seed-syllable with the *śakti*, bring it under control with the two *ṭha*s. This mantra, preceded by *tāra* (om), is said to consist of eleven syllables. The seer (*ṛṣi*) and other elements of this mantra have indeed been stated previously in their proper order. (160)

The ten-syllable heart-mantra, beginning with its own seed-syllable, consists of the letters saṃ, va, rta, ka, na, e, tra, yu, ta, and is situated on a seat of fire with the two sides joined by the letter ṇa; it is for the purpose of propitiation. (161)
The sage of this [mantra] is Gaṇaka; Virāṭ is declared to be its meter; and the obstacle-remover Kṣipraprasādana is declared to be its deity. 162.
The ender of the five (Pa), joined with the bindu (M) and adorned with the left ear (U)—beginning with Tārā and ending with hṛdaya—this is proclaimed as the mantra of Heramba. || 163 ||
*Tāram* (Om), *Khaḍgīśvaraḥ*, *Kūrmaḥ*, *Niḥsvaraḥ*, and *Lāntaḥ* (La) are proclaimed; followed by *Bhuve* and *Natiḥ*—this mantra of seven syllables consists of one's own Brahman-nature. (164)
One should utter the *tāra* (om), followed by *hastipada*, and then the *piśācapada*. One should extract *indramakṣi* joined with [the vowel] *i*, and *durgā* enriched with the syllable *e*. (165)
One should write the ten-syllable mantra of Ucchiṣṭagaṇanātha as "svāhā.
Some say it begins with the seed-syllable; its meter is Nivṛt-gāyatrī.
The sage and the sequence of deities, beginning with Suśrī, are also proclaimed in due order. (166)
One should likewise address the Great-Souled One (Mahātman) as Śakti, Tāra, Hastimukha, Pralambodara, and the word Ucchiṣṭa ending in the feminine suffix -ī. || 167 ||

One should state the goad (aṅkuśa), which is long and rich in the letter ra, with a bindu at its side; then the spear (śakti) ending in the feminine suffix ṅi, followed by "ucchiṣṭa svāhā"—this mantra consists of twenty-eight syllables.
"Vakratuṇḍāya kavacam" is the long six-syllable mantra;
with "māyā" at the end of "vakratuṇḍāya," followed by "namaḥ," it becomes eight syllables. (169)

The letter Khaḍgī (Kha), followed by Śambhoḥ (Śa), Bhṛguḥ (Bha), Bindu (M), and the vowel of Manu (U), ending with Hṛdayam (Namaḥ) for Soma—this is declared to be the six-syllabled mantra. Bhṛgu is said to be its seer (ṛṣi), Paṅkti its meter (chandas), and Soma its deity. || 170 ||
Tāra, Ghṛṇi, Bhṛgu, followed by [the letter] adorned with the left ear (U), Vahnyāsana, Marut, Śeṣa, Sane-tra, Atri, and Tyap at the end. || 171 ||

The eight-syllable mantra of the Sun is said to bestow all desired objects. Devabhaga is declared to be the sage (ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī is stated to be the meter (chandas). The deity is Savitṛ, the origin of the worlds, who grants the fulfillment of all wishes. || 172 ||
Bhuvaneśvarī is joined with Ākāśa (H), Vahni (R), and Dīrghendu (Ī). Bhṛgu (S) is conjoined with Sarga (Ḥ); this is declared to be the three-syllabled mantra of the Sun. (173)

Ākāśa (ha), Agni (ra), Pavana (ya), Sadā (sa), Anta (kṣa), Arghīśa (i), and Bindu (m)—this is declared to be the seed-syllable named Mārtaṇḍabhairava. Encased by the Bimba seed-syllable, it bestows the fruits of all desires. 174.

That which ends in *ṭa* (ṭha), joined with fire (ra), eye (i), and moon (u), is declared as such; it is graced by ether (a) and the half-moon (candra-bindu), and begins with the letter *sa* (sarga). (175)

The mantra known as Ajapā is declared to be the celestial tree consisting of two syllables. Brahmā is remembered as its seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is said to be its metre (chandas), and the Lord of Girijā (Śiva) is proclaimed as the deity, the origin of the worlds. || 176 ||
O Agni Jātavedas, may there be the three *vyāhṛtis*; bring [the gods] here, O beloved of Agni, and having addressed all the rites, accomplish them thereafter. (177)
(178) This mantra beginning with "Tārā" is said to consist of twenty-seven syllables;
Bhṛgu is its seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī its meter (chandaḥ), and Agni its deity (devatā).
"Arise! Speak to the Puruṣa, O Havi (or Hari), Piṅgala! Next, give me the word 'lohitākṣa', and then 'dehi me' and the two 'ṭha's. (179)
The Manu of prosperity is proclaimed to consist of twenty-four syllables; the seers and other [limbs] of this Mantra were previously declared by the wise. (180)
The Praṇava, Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, and Svāhā constitute the seven-syllabled mantra.
Its seers and other [limbs] are as before; its deity is the great Pāvaka (Fire). || 181 ||
O Queen of the Gods, [the mantra] beginning with *anugraha* consists of *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*; it possesses eight syllables: *tāra*, *parā*, the word *haṃsa*, *so'haṃ*, and *svāhā*. (182)
The seer is declared to be Nārāyaṇa; the meter is said to be Gāyatrī; the deity is indeed Brahman itself, the supreme light bearing its own essential nature. || 183 ||

One should utter the syllable *tāram* (oṃ), followed by the word *namaḥ*, and then the two letters *nara* joined with the long vowel; this mantra, consisting of eight syllables, is declared to be *pavano ṇāya*. (184)
Nārāyaṇa is declared to be the object of accomplishment (sādhya), the sage is proclaimed, and the meter is cited; Gāyatrī is the goddess of the mantra, and the deity is the imperishable Viṣṇu. (185)
The syllable *praṇava* (Om) is proclaimed as "to the Lord Vāsudeva"; this twelve-syllabled mantra is indeed the primary one in the Vaiṣṇava Tantra. (186)
The seer is Prajāpati, the meter is proclaimed to be Gāyatrī, and Vāsudeva is declared by the wise to be its deity. (187)
The seed-syllable *hṛllekhā* twice, likewise the seed-syllable *ramā* twice; ending with "Lakṣmyai," followed by "Vāsudevāya," and ending with "Hṛdayāya," preceded by the *praṇava*. (188)
*Tāraḥ* (Oṃ), then *hṛt* (Namaḥ) for Viṣṇu, followed by the Lord of the Gods (*sureśvara*) ending in the suffix *ṅe*; then *mahābalāya* and the pair of *ṭha*s (svāhā).
This is the eighteen-syllable mantra. Bindu is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Virāṭ is the meter (*chandaḥ*), and Dadhivāmana is the deity (*devatā*). (189)
Having addressed him with the word "udgira" (utter) by means of the terms *praṇava* and *udgītha*,
he should then say "sarva-vāgīśvara" and finally "īśvara."

At the end of the inconceivable word consisting of all the Vedas, one should utter "sarvam. This mantra, beginning with "tārā" (om) and ending with "bodhaya," is proclaimed as having two parts at its conclusion. || 191 ||
The Seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra] is declared to be Brahmā; the meter (chandas) is stated to be Anuṣṭubh;
and the deity (devatā) is Hayagrīva, the bestower of mastery over speech. || 192 ||
The mantra for Rāma consists of the syllable "A" (Ananta), followed by the seat of fire (Ra), the moon (U), and the seed-syllable (Ma);
this six-syllabled mantra is declared to be a wish-fulfilling jewel for those who worship it. (193)
Brahmā is declared to be the sage, the Gāyatrī the meter, and Rāma, the destroyer of the Rākṣasas, the deity of Manu, as proclaimed by the foremost of teachers. || 194 ||
Having uttered "Jānakī" as the armor-mantra, this ten-syllabled mantra of the beloved Agnisundarī is a wish-fulfilling gem for those who worship it. 195.

The single-syllable mantra is *rām*, the two-syllable *manu* is *rāma*. Then, in sequence, [the mantras] beginning with *tāra* (oṃ), *śakti* (hrīṃ), *ramā* (śrīṃ), *kāma* (klīṃ), and *vāk* (aiṃ), along with their respective seed-syllables (*svabīja*), are joined. Thus, the three-syllable mantra *rāma* has been proclaimed by those who know the Tantras. (196)
The two six-syllable mantras are proclaimed as "Rāma" ending with "Candrabhadra," which has four syllables;
and those ending with "svāhā," "phaṭ," and "namaḥ," which have six syllables.

Then, the five-syllable mantra consists of the word "Rāma" ending in the dative case, preceded by the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja) and the seed-syllable of Ramā (Ramā-bīja), each encased [by them] in due order, followed by "namaḥ. (198)

The seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja), the seed-syllable of Ramā (Ramā-bīja), the seed-syllable of Śakti (Śakti-bīja), and so forth, in their proper sequence— this is declared by the knowers of Tantra to be this six-syllabled mantra.

The mantra beginning with the syllable Om, followed by "Rāmacandra" in the dative case and ending with "Namaḥ," as well as the same for the word "Rāmabhadra," is declared to be the eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣara). || 200 ||

The seed-syllable of Śakti, the seed-syllable of Ramā, and the seed-syllable of Vāc should enclose [the name] "Rāma," ending with Candrabhadra and including the fourth vowel; thus it becomes a nine-syllabled mantra. (201)

One should recite "Tāraṃ namo bhagavate rāmacandrāya" (Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed Lord Rāmacandra); or else "Rāmabhadrāya"—both of these consist of twelve syllables. There are many other mantras as well, which have not been mentioned here for fear of prolixity.
One should utter "Tāraṃ namo bhagavate varāhāya," followed by "bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ pataye. (203)
