"Grant me the status of a sovereign at your feet, and cause it to be granted at the end.
This mantra, ending with the wife of Fire (svāhā), consists of thirty-three syllables. || 204 ||
The sage is declared to be Bhārgava, the meter is stated to be Anuṣṭubh, and the deity of this mantra is said by the wise to be Divarāha. || 205 ||

The heart-mantra for the Blessed Lady should be [HRĪM]; immediately after that, for Dharaṇī, it is [HRŪM]. At the end of "Dharaṇī," the pair "dhare" follows, ending with the seed-syllable SVĀHĀ; this begins with the syllable DHRA and concludes with the Dhruva (SVĀHĀ).
The Heart of the Earth (Dharāhṛdaya) is said to consist of nineteen syllables; Varāha is declared its sage (muni), and Nivṛt is cited as its meter (chanda).
The deity is considered to be the primordial nature (prakṛti) of all beings, the Earth. || 208 ||
One should first utter "Ugra" and "Vīra," followed immediately by "Mahāviṣṇu"; then, having addressed the word "Jvalantam," one should pronounce "Sarvatomukham. (209)
Then one should utter "Nṛsiṃha," "Bhīṣaṇa," "Bhadra," and "Mṛtyumṛtyu.
"I bow" (namāmyaham) is said to be this King of Mantras, the celestial tree.
The seer is declared to be Brahmā; the meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh;
its deity is Narasiṃha, who is saluted by gods and asuras. (211)
The letter *kṣa* mounted upon the fire-vowel (*r*), conjoined with the nasalized vowel (*anusvāra*),
its head shimmering with the *bindu* and the *nāda*— the wise know this to be the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Narasiṃha.

The seed-syllable is "namo bhagavate narasiṃhāya" (Salutation to the Blessed One, Narasiṃha), followed by "jvālāmāline" (to the one garlanded with flames), and thereafter "dīptadaṃṣṭrāya" (to the one with blazing fangs). 213.
One should utter the word "pada" for Agnineṭra, who is all-pervasive and the slayer of Rākṣasas;
at the end of "sarvabhūtavināśa," the letter *la* (or *na*) is accompanied by a bindu and the wind (*marut*).

At the end of "sarvajvaravināśānte," there are the two syllables *lāyārṇau* (or *nāyārṇau*), followed by the pair *daha*, the pair *paca*, the pair *rakṣa*, and then *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This great mantra, known as Jvālāmālī, consists of sixty-seven syllables beginning with the fixed seed-syllable (*dhruva*). || 215 ||
The noose (pāśa), the spear (śakti), Nṛhari, the goad (aṅkuśa), the armor (varma), and phaṭ constitute the six-syllabled mantra of Nṛhari, which is said to grant all desires. || 216 ||
The seer is declared to be Brahmā; the meter is stated to be Paṅkti;
Narasiṃha is proclaimed as the deity of this mantra. (217)
The syllable *tāra* (om), followed by *bhṛgu* (bha), *viyat* (i), and again *bhūyaḥ* (bha); this is enriched with *vahni* (ra) and joined with *dīrgha* (ī).
With *pāvaka* (va) at the end of the *kavaca* (huṃ) and *astra* (phaṭ), the seven-syllabled mantra is thus remembered. || 218 ||
The sage is declared to be Ahirbudhnya, and the meter is stated to be Anuṣṭubh; the deity is said by the sages to be Hari himself in the form of the wheel. || 219 ||
Having uttered "kṛṣṇāya," followed by "govindāya," and then at the end of the word "gopījana," [one says] "vallabhāya," ending with the two *ṭha* syllables (*svāhā*). || 220 ||

The eighteen-syllable mantra, beginning with the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), has been declared; Nārada is said to be its sage (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī is stated to be its meter (chandas), and Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of the fruits of all desires, is proclaimed as its deity. || 221 ||

At the end of the word *gopījanavallabha* is *agnisundarī*. This ten-syllable mantra has Nārada as its seer (*ṛṣi*) and Virāḍ as its meter (*chanda*). The deity, as proclaimed by the teachers, is Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of Kaṃsa. (222)
Brahmā is seated upon a seat on the earth; Śānti is adorned with the moon. The seed-syllable of the god of love is said to be that which deludes the three worlds. (223)
The sage is declared to be Sammohana; the meter is said to be Gāyatrī; the deity is directly Sarvasammohana, whose banner bears the sea-monster.

"From this [state], I eternally take refuge in the feet of the glorious Mukunda"—this is declared to be the eighteen-syllable mantra of Mukunda. Nārada is its seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is its meter, and Mukunda is the deity, preceded by the word "ṛṣi. (225)
Alternatively, at the end of this entire [mantra], there is another mantra: *hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ* for the one whose nature is as fickle as a child, produced by the sound of the wind. (226)

The Gāyatrī of Nalakūbara is proclaimed as Bālakṛṣṇa; by means of this [mantra], all perfections such as those of the seers and so forth shall be attained here through recitation and other practices. (227)
At the end of the word for "form" (rūpa) that corresponds [to the deity], one should utter the word for "taste" (rasa).
[The mantra is: "Obeisance to the pair [of forms] of Kṛṣṇa, obeisance to the Lord of Food. || 228 ||
"Give food, Svāhā"—this twenty-syllable mantra is the giver of food. Nārada is its seer, the Anuṣṭubh is its meter, and the lords of food are its presiding deities. (229)
This other [mantra] consists of twelve syllables, ending with *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
The seers and so forth are, respectively, Brahmā, Gāyatrī, the destroyer of planets, and Hari. (230)
This other Manu, Puruṣottama, at the limit of the twelve [fingers], addressed Viṣṇu, the sovereign lord, saying: "Grant me long life. (231)
The mantra ending in "namaḥ" consists of thirty-two syllables; its seer is Nārada, its meter is Anuṣṭubh, and its deity is proclaimed to be Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (232)
Having spoken the word "Gopālaka" again, followed by "Veṣadhārāya" and "Vāsudevāya," there is the eighteen-syllable mantra consisting of the armor, the weapon, and the head.

Manu, Nārada, Gāyatrī, Kṛṣṇa, and Ṛṣi are declared as the seers (ṛṣis) and so forth. Having uttered the two syllables "li" in the middle of "kāvyam," and "diva" in the middle of "phaṇām"—that is, in the middle of "kāliyaphaṇām"—one should then say again: "He performs the dance; I bow to Him. (234)
Having said, "The son of Devakī," [he did so] because of the sound of the dancing.
Manu Dantalipi said that one should address King Acyuta with this mantra.
For this mantra, the sage Narada is declared by the teachers to be the seer; the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Kṛṣṇa, the crusher of Kāliya. (236)
The mantra, preceded by *Śakti* and *Śrī*, consists of eighteen syllables and twenty syllables respectively;
there is no other mantra like this one to be seen in the three worlds. Brahmā is its seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is its meter (*chanda*), and Kṛṣṇa is its deity (*devatā*). (237)
Vāgbhava, Kāmabīja, Kṛṣṇāya, Bhuvaneśvarī, Govindāya, Ramā, Gopījanavallabha, and the word "Ṅe" as the head. (238)
Above that is the white [syllable] endowed with the fourteenth vowel (au), which is creative.
This twenty-two-syllable mantra bestows the state of Lord of Speech (Vāgīśa).
One should apply all the ancillary rites, such as the ṛṣi and others, just as for the eighteen-syllable [mantra]. || 239 ||
The mantra for the head is "Obeisance to Śrī Śaktismara Kṛṣṇa.
It consists of twelve syllables, its seer (ṛṣi) and other attributes are Kṛṣṇa, Brahmā, and Gāyatrī, respectively, in sequence. (240)

The ten-syllable mantra begins with Śrī-Śakti-Kāma (Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ), followed by Aṅgajanmaśakti (Aiṃ) and ending with Ramā (Svāhā). If this same mantra is preceded by Śaktiramā (Hrīṃ Svāhā), it becomes the [next] one. || 241 ||
*Māra-śakti*, *amā-pūrva-śakti*, *śrī-māra-pūrvaka*, and *śrī-śakti-māra-pūrva*—these are the three ten-syllable mantras.
For these mantra syllables, the ritual application of the limbs (*aṅga*), the sages (*ṛṣi*), and so forth, is to be performed as in the case of the ten-syllable mantra. (242)
This mantra, ending with the word "Māra" and consisting of eighteen syllables, bestows sons and wealth;
its seer and other attributes, as well as its eighteen syllables, are declared in due order. (243)
*Tāraṃ* (Oṃ), *hṛdbhad* (Hrīḥ), the Blessed One (*bhagavān*), followed by *jenta*, and likewise the word *nandaputra*;
at the end of *nanda* is *vapuṣe*, ending with *agni* (Ra) and *māyā* (Ī)—this is the ten-syllable mantra. (244)
This [mantra] consists of twenty-eight syllables; I shall now speak of the thirty-two-syllable version:
the word *nandaputra* ending in the suffix *ṅ*, and likewise the word *śyāmalāṅga*. (245)
Likewise, Kṛṣṇa Govinda has ten syllables and the body of a child; for these two, O Nārada, the seer is the Ṛṣi Nārada and the meters are Uṣṇik and Anuṣṭubh.

With *tāram* (om) at the beginning, *hṛd* (namaḥ), *bhagavān* (the Blessed One), and *rukmiṇīvallabhaḥ* (the Beloved of Rukmiṇī), ending with *śiras* (svāhā)— this sixteen-syllable mantra is called the Rukmiṇīvallabha.
This mantra bestows all prosperity; Nārada is remembered as its sage (ṛṣi), the Anuṣṭubh is its meter (chandas), and Hari, the beloved of Rukmiṇī, is its deity (devatā). || 248 ||
The words *nīlā*, *dantā*, *daṇḍā*, and *vadhau* [are used]; then the word *gopījana-saṃyukta-doḥ-padam*;
at the end of *daṇḍa* is the word *bāla-rūpa*, and after that the word *megha-śyāma*. || 249 ||
This mantra is said by Nārada to consist of nineteen syllables; its meter is Anuṣṭubh, and its deity is considered to be Lord Hari bearing the blue staff (Nīladaṇḍa). || 250 ||
Joined with the thirteenth vowel (au), Śārṅgin, Medas, and Keśava; likewise, Māṃsa, Antaka, and Śiras—this is the seven-syllable mantra. (251)

He is declared to be the granter of desires to those who worship Him; the sage Nārada is remembered as His seer (ṛṣi), the meter is Uṣṇih, and the deity is proclaimed to be the Beloved of the Cow (Govallabha). || 252 ||
Salava, Vāsudeva, and the word Bhagavat ending with the heart-mantra (hrīṃ), followed by the pair of words Śrī Govinda—this is declared to be the twelve-syllable mantra. || 253 ||
Manu, Nārada, Gāyatrī, Kṛṣṇa-ṛṣi, and others are proclaimed [as the deities]. He possesses upper teeth, holds a Śārṅga bow and a discus, and is endowed with a right ear. (254)
Bowing down with the eight-syllable root mantra, "māṃ saṃ nāthāya," its seer is Brahmā, its meter is Gāyatrī, and its deity is Kṛṣṇa. (255)

At the end of *tāra* (oṃ), *śrī*, *śakti* (hrīṃ), and *māra* (klīṃ), one should utter the word *śrīkṛṣṇāya*. Above that, [one says] *govindāya*, then *śrīgopījana*, and then *vallabhāya*. Then *strīṃ* and *śrīṃ*; this is the *siddha-gopālaka-mantra*. (256)

The syllable *cakrī* joined with the sound of a human (*manu*), followed by the *visarga* and the letter *e*, is considered the mantra. If that same [syllable] is preceded by *kāma* (the letter *ka*), it consists of three syllables: "kṛṣṇa" (two syllables) and "kā" (one syllable). || 257 ||
That same [mantra] may consist of four syllables ending in the dative case (*ṅe*); another four-syllable [mantra] will be mentioned, which consists of five syllables: *kṛṣṇāya namaḥ*. (258)
The other five-syllabled mantra, "Kṛṣṇāya," is situated between the pair of remembrances (smara-dvandva).
The six-syllabled mantra, ending with the wife of Agni (svāhā), is proclaimed as "Gopālāya. || 259 ||

Another [mantra] for Kṛṣṇa begins with the seed-syllable of Smara (Klīm) and ends with the wife of Fire (Svāhā); another is the six-syllabled one ending in "namaḥ"; and yet another is "Kṛṣṇa Govinda. (160)
That [mantra] has four syllables and seven phonemes; another previously mentioned one has seven phonemes.
"Śrī-śakti-māraḥ kṛṣṇāya" is another seven-syllabled [mantra]. (161)
*Kṛṣṇa* and *Govindaka* ending in *ṅi*, *smara* and so forth with eight syllables; *dadhi-bhakṣaṇa* ending in *ṅe*, and another group of eight beginning with *vahni-jāya-mi*. (262)
The second octet is "namaḥ" addressed to the one whose self is perfectly serene; and the previously mentioned nine-syllable root mantra is encased by the word "smara. (263)
*Kṛṣṇa* and *Govindaka* end in the feminine suffix *ṅi*; their seer is the sage Nārada. The meter is said to be Gāyatrī, and Kṛṣṇa is declared to be the deity. (264)

This mantra arises from the word *kṛṣṇa* situated between a pair of *māra*s; one should employ the seers, meters, and deities as previously stated. If there is blood beneath the flesh of these two *māra*s, it is another mantra. (265)

The letter *sa* (Satya), the letter *śa* (Śauri), the middle of the group [the letter *va*], and that joined with its end [the letter *ma*]—these four are adorned by the peacock, the left eye, and the crescent moon. (266)
At the end of each pair of "jaya kṛṣṇa," one should utter the word "nirantara";
at the end of the word "krīḍāsakta," one should say "mucetase. (267)

Afterwards, one should proclaim the word *nityapriya* with the dative case-ending (*caturthī*), and the word *kṛṣṇa* ending in the suffix *ṅ*; at the end of *ikṣukārmuka*, there is a ten-syllable mantra. (268)
One should extract [the mantra] together with the *salavāḥ* and the goddesses born of Acala;
the mantra consists of fifty-two syllables, arranged according to the forward and reverse order.
The great goddess Lakṣmī of poetry that wins the affection of people is the hand that removes sin; Nārada, the source of bliss, is its seer (ṛṣi), and Virāṭ shall be the meter (chandas). || 270 ||

The deity is Hari alone, the cause of the enchantment of this world; the heart is the letter Ra, followed by Para (the letter La), ending with Sākṣin (the letter Sa), joined with the creeper (the vowel Ā) and Marut (the letter Ya). (271)
This six-syllabled mantra, beginning with Tārā, is declared to consist of five syllables [in its core].
Vāmadeva is its seer (ṛṣi), Paṅkti is its meter (chandas), and Īśa is its deity. || 272 ||
The six-syllabled mantra, conjoined with Śakti, is said to be the eight-syllabled mantra;
its seer and meter were declared of old, and its deity is the Lord of Umā.

The letter *sa* (s), joined with *ya* (y) and having its head adorned by the *bindu*, is declared to be the mantra known as Prāsāda, which bestows all perfections upon those who worship it. Vāmadeva is the sage (*ṛṣi*), the metre (*chandas*) is Paṅkti, and the deity (*devatā*) is Sadāśiva. (274)

The syllable *tāra* (om), followed by *māyā* (hrīṃ), joined with the sky (*vi*), a bindu, and the nasal vowel (*anusvāra*), and combined with the five-syllabled [seed-mantra], is considered the eight-syllabled mantra.

The syllable *tāra* (om), the stable *sakara* (sa), the moon (*indu*) with the ear (*karṇa*), and Bhṛgu accompanied by emission (*sarga*); this three-syllabled mantra has been declared to be the very essence of Mṛtyuñjaya. || 276 ||
The seer is Kahola; the meter is said to be Devyādiga-yatrī; and the deity of this [mantra] is declared to be Mahādeva Mṛtyuñjaya. || 277 ||
First, [the word] "to Dakṣiṇāmūrti," then immediately after that, the word "to you" (tubhyam);
at the end of the word "at the root of the banyan tree" (vaṭamūla), the word "to the dweller" (nivāsine) follows. (278)

To the one whose limbs are solely devoted to meditation, one should subsequently utter the word "namaḥ. This mantra, consisting of thirty-six syllables, beginning with "Rudrāya Śambhave" and conjoined with the power of the Tāraka (Om), is said to bestow the fruits of all desires. || 279 ||
The sage is declared to be Śakra, the meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh, and its deity is proclaimed to be Śambhu, known by the name Dakṣiṇāmūrti. || 280 ||
First the Praṇava, then the word "hṛdayam," followed by the word "bhagavate" joined with the suffix -ṅe;
one should then utter "dakṣiṇāmūrtaye mahyam medhām. (281)
"Bestow [this mantra]; this twenty-two-syllable mantra ends with two *ṭha*s.
The sage is Caturmukha, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity of the mantra is known as Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who is intent upon the exposition of the Vedas. (282)
First is the red one, the seat of fire, possessing the drop of truth; then the second is the long vowel situated in the seed-syllable of fire, adorned by the moon of peace.
The third [mantra] consists of the three seed-syllables of Lāṅgalī and Sargī;
it is declared to be the essence of Nīlakaṇṭha, the supreme remover of the two types of poison.
(186) Fire, the sun of destruction, and wind, together with the sixth bindu—this is known as the Cintāmaṇi seed-syllable, which bestows all prosperity. (285)
The sage is declared to be Kaśyapa; the meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh; and the deity is proclaimed to be Ardhanārīśvara, the Lord of the worlds. || 286 ||
The syllable *kṣa* possesses fire (*ra*), wind (*ya*), the left ear (*ha*), and the half-moon (*bindu*). This is declared to be the seed-syllable of Tumburu, by which practitioners attain success.
Then again, "māyāsphuradvayaṃ" and "prasphuradvitayaṃ";
at the end [of these], "ghoraghoratara," and then the word "tanurūpa. (288)
At the end of that, there should be two *ca*s; then, two *pracaṭa*s; then, two *ka*s and two *ra*s;
and then, again, two *bandha*s. (289)
With the words *ghātaya* and *dvitayam* followed by *varma phaṭ*, this fifty-one-syllable mantra is proclaimed as the great Aghora-weapon mantra. (290)
Aghora is declared to be its sage (muni), and Anuṣṭubh is cited as its meter; Aghoraruḍra is designated as its deity by those most skilled in mantras. || 291 ||

The syllable *tāra* (om), followed by *vānta* (ha), situated on *dharā* (la), adorned with the left eye (*i*) and the moon (*u*), joined with the side-breast (*ra*) and the ear (*ka*), ending with the armor (*vaṃ*) and the weapon (*phaṭ*): this is the six-syllabled mantra. || 292 ||

The mantra known as Pāśupatāstra, which wards off minor planetary afflictions, consists of the final letter of the [first] class (ma) joined with the letter after au (ra), followed by "kṣetrapālāya" and the heart-mantra (namaḥ). This eight-syllabled mantra of Kṣetrapāla is proclaimed to begin with the syllable Om (Tārā). || 293 ||

One should extract *vaṭuka* ending in the locative case (*ṅe*), and likewise *āpaduddharaṇa*. Then, one should again extract *kurut* twice ending in the locative case (*ṅe*), followed by that *vaṭuka*. This great mantra, consisting of twenty-one syllables, is empowered by Śakti. (294)

Arghīśa, the peak of fire (ra), situated after the letter la (la-ra), uttered with the letter da (da-ra), and ending with phaṭ—this is proclaimed as the Caṇḍa mantra, consisting of three syllables at its end. || 295 ||
Its meter is declared to be Triṣṭubh, its metre is said to be Anuṣṭubh, and its deity is proclaimed by the preceptors skilled in the Tantras to be Caṇḍeśa. (296)
One should recite the fourfold rotation of *pārśva*, *marghīndu*, and *akkoli*; the letter *ra* joined with a long vowel should be at the end of the second and fourth [syllables]. (297)
One should extract the seed-syllable *ni* from the beginning and the light vowel *u* at the end;
this fifteen-syllable mantra of Kukkuṭeśvara has thus been declared. (298)
The Śakti-mantra is "Tāram" (Om), followed by "Namaḥ", and then the word "Bhagavate"; thereafter one should utter "Aghorebhyaḥ", "Athaghorebhyaḥ", and "Rudrebhyaḥ". (299)

Salutation ending with the wife of fire (svāhā), consisting of twenty-four syllables—this is the Mahābhairava mantra, the Uḍḍīśa, which is the means for attaining supernatural powers (siddhi). || 300 ||
There are many others—Dināstra, Kṛtyāstra, Yakṣiṇīs, Tryambaka, and so forth—who are indeed virtuous; yet they do not belong to us because of our laziness and lack of initiative.
There are exactly sixteen [forms] of Sarasvatī, six Manavas of Śrī in sequence, ten and eight of Maheśānī, and another ten of Daurgā. (302)
Bhairavī, Sundarī, and Rāmā—these thirty-eight [deities] are worshipped with devotion; then thirteen for Gaṇeśa, and one for Soma, in due order. (303)
There are four for Bhāskara and three for Agni; thereafter, there are forty-eight Gopāla-mantras in sequence, all dedicated to Viṣṇu.
For Rāma as well, there are thirty-four [kalpas] followed by Nārāyaṇa and others; at the end, ninety-four are indeed stated for Śambhu, along with fifteen. (305)
Having thoroughly examined the *Prapañcasāra-siddhānta*, the *Śāradātilaka*, as well as the *Sārasamuccaya* along with its commentaries, [I shall compose this work]. (1)
Having diligently examined the *Dīpikā*, as well as the *Salaghudīpikā*,
the *Pūjāpradīpa*, and the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*.
The *Mantradarpaṇasiddhānta*, the *Mantradevaprakāśikā*, the *Mantranetra*, the *Mantrā...* [and] the *Śrīrāmārcanacandrikā*. || 3 ||
The Mantramuktāvalī, the Ratnāvalī, the Jñānārṇava, and others; the Tantra of Sanatkumāra, the Nāradīya, and the Catuḥśatī.
The Tūrṇāyāga, the Somaśambhumata, the Agastyasaṃhitā, likewise the Vaiṣṇavīsaṃhitā, and the Tattvasāgarasaṃhitā. || 5 ||
With reverence, he studied the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Kapila, the Śrīmantravara-saṃhitā,
the Tantra of Śrībhuvanaiśvaryā, and the Nayasiddhānta.
The *Kalpa* of Śrī Vanadurgā, the *Tantra* called *Saṃmohana*,
likewise the *Hayagrīvamata*, and the *Vijñānabhārata* (*Bhairava*).
And likewise the Guhyatantrarāja and the Piṅgalāmata. || 8 ||
And the entire Vāmakeśvaratantra, as well as the Varadīkṣita, the Vijñāneśvara-siddhānta,
and the Sāraśrīsaṃhitā, in due order.
The Vijñānalalita, the Pañcarātra, the Nārāyaṇīya, the Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā, the Gārgyasaṃhitā, and likewise the Bhairava; || 10 ||
With devotion, [he composed] the Divya-sārasvata, the Ciccandra-kāmika, the Homavarottara,
and the treatise on the essence of consecration (Pratiṣṭhāsāra-saṃgraha).
Likewise, he [attains] the Vāyavī Saṃhitā, as well as the Brahma Saṃhitā; the Kṛśānu Saṃhitā, and the Yāmala of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Rudra, and the others. (12)
Likewise, one should respectfully study the *Yāmaloddhāra* and the *Matsyasūkta* in their proper sequence,
as well as the dialogue between Pārvatī and Hara and the *Vārāhītantra*.
Likewise, with devotion, [he studied] the Kubjikātantra and the Tvaritājñāna; similarly, with devotion, the Phetkāriṇītantra and the Subhagodaya. (14)
Likewise, the Yoginītantra, the Tripurārṇava in due order, the Īśānasaṃhitā, and similarly the Siddhānta of Viśvakarman; || 15 ||
The Tantra of the venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā, various Purāṇas, as well as the Smṛti-śāstras and the Mahābhārata; || 16 ||
Having examined the treatises on astrology and all the manuals in their proper sequence,
the wise Devanātha extracted the essence of them all and proclaimed this "Vidhāna" (the ritual manual) for rites such as *puraścaraṇa*.
My beloved Kaumudī is adorned with anklets of rigorous logic, slow-moving due to her immersion in word and meaning, and graced by the elegance of her composition as her necklace. (18)
My mother is Kaumudī, and my father too is Kaumudī; my fame is Kaumudī, and my very life is Kaumudī. (19)
Wise men should not show indifference toward this out of their own pride; for Manu has said that a well-spoken word is to be accepted even from a child. (20)

That which was not attained even by yogis practicing with great effort, yet was beheld with rapture by the gods led by Brahmā as they bowed down; that Vedānta, which is honored for its intense embrace of the jar-like breasts of the gopīs— [that new nectar] has been revealed.
Salutation to that supreme Greatness which has been thus expounded. || 21 ||
Having placed his lotus-feet upon Mākuṇḍa’s head, his mind overcome with impetuosity,

he stood before him at a short distance and, with great reverence, embraced the weight of the dust from his pair of lotus-feet. Then, with his head rolling over the lotus-feet of his mother, he [honored] the trident-bearer with devotion.

The Lord of the Gods, whose crest-jewel hangs down like the moon, has brought about this Kaumudī festival. This *Kaumudī* was indeed composed by the son of that Govinda, who is renowned throughout the world as one whose beautiful splendor is as lovely as the science of logic (*tarka-tantra*), and who possesses auspicious fame.
May this [work], composed by the wise Devanātha for the delight of the virtuous, be auspicious. || 23 ||
In the year of Lakṣmaṇasena marked by [the digits] sky, zero, and ocean (1000), Devanātha composed this *Kaumudī* for the welfare of the world.
Thus ends the *Mantrakaumudī*, composed by the venerable Mahāmahopādhyāya Devanātha, the illustrious Tarkapañcānana.
May there be auspiciousness! May there be prosperity!
